title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
順天府鄉試錄序
天下之貢莫大乎以士每三歲
一舉
制也正德丙子秋寔維其期順天
府臣舉故事以
請
上命侍讀學士臣俊左諭德臣鼎臣
===
往主試事其同考為學正臣琦
臣翰教諭臣誥臣信臣潮臣鑑
臣銓臣鉞臣宗周其監試為御史
臣雷臣雍而提調則府尹臣韶
府丞臣潤也暨諸内外執事咸
慎選就列時挟藝而應試者幾
三千人三試之得士一百三十

punctuated:
順天府鄉試錄序

天下之貢，莫大乎以士。每三歲一舉，制也。正德丙子秋，寔維其期。順天府臣舉故事以請，上命侍讀學士臣俊、左諭德臣鼎臣往主試事。其同考為學正臣琦、臣翰，教諭臣誥、臣信、臣潮、臣鑑、臣銓、臣鉞、臣宗周；其監試為御史臣雷、臣雍；而提調則府尹臣韶、府丞臣潤也。暨諸内外執事，咸慎選就列。時挟藝而應試者幾三千人，三試之，得士一百三十
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination

Among the tributes presented by all under Heaven, none is greater than men of learning. Holding an examination once every three years is the established regulation. The autumn of the bingzi year of Zhengde [1516] was indeed the appointed time. The officials of Shuntian Prefecture submitted a request in accordance with precedent. His Majesty ordered Academician Expositor-in-waiting Jun and Left Mentor Dingchen to go and preside over the examination. The Associate Examiners were School Instructors Qi and Han, and Instructors Gao, Xin, Chao, Jian, Quan, Yue, and Zongzhou. The examination supervisors were Censors Lei and Yong, while the Proctors were Prefect Shao and Vice Prefect Run. These and all the officials serving within and outside the examination compound were carefully selected and took their assigned places. At that time, nearly three thousand men came to sit the examination, bringing their literary accomplishments. After examining them in three sessions, they selected one hundred and thirty…

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
五人并錄其文之優者二十一
篇以為
獻亦
制也俊惟
國家養士於學而抜之於科目盖
將資其才以為世用也或疑文
不足以得士盖聞古之善相馬
===
者或以齒或以頰或以目或以
股或以毛鬣其所以相者不同
見馬之一徵也而其節之高卑
足之滑易材之堅脆能之長短
舉不能逃非神且幸也其數然
也士之徵莫有過於文生於其
心而出於其口者也謂文非教
alt_text:
五人并録其文之優者二十一
篇以爲
獻亦
制也〔俊〕〔惟〕
國家養士於學而拔之於科目盖
将資其才以爲世用也或疑文
不足以得士盖聞古之善相馬
===
者或以齒或以以頰或以目或以
股或以毛鬣其所以相者不同
見馬之一徵也而其節之高卑
足之滑易材之堅脆能之長短
舉不能逃非神且幸也其數然
也士之徵莫有過於文生於其
心而出於其口者也謂文非教
punctuated:
五人，并錄其文之優者二十一篇，以為獻，亦制也。
俊惟國家養士於學，而抜之於科目，盖將資其才以為世用也。或疑文不足以得士。盖聞古之善相馬者，或以齒，或以頰，或以目，或以股，或以毛鬣，其所以相者不同，見馬之一徵也，而其節之高卑、足之滑易、材之堅脆、能之長短，舉不能逃。非神且幸也，其數然也。士之徵，莫有過於文，生於其心而出於其口者也。謂文非教
translation_en:
…five men, and also recorded twenty-one of their finest compositions for presentation to the throne, as prescribed by regulation.
I, Jun, reflect that the state nurtures scholars in its schools and selects them through the examinations, intending to draw upon their talents for service in the world. Some doubt whether literary composition suffices to identify worthy men. Yet I have heard that those skilled in judging horses in antiquity relied variously on the teeth, cheeks, eyes, thighs, or coat and mane. Their methods of judging differed, each observing a single indication in the horse; nevertheless, the height of its joints, the ease of its gait, the strength or frailty of its constitution, and its strengths and weaknesses in performance could none escape their discernment. This was neither supernatural insight nor good fortune: the regular patterns of things made it so. As an indication of a scholar’s qualities, nothing surpasses literary composition, which arises in his heart and issues from his mouth. To say that literary composition is not what education…

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之所先可也謂不足以得士過
矣雖然有司之好惡不可以不
慎也士習之升降風俗之隆替
恒必由之夫士必有忠信之質
而又明於義利王霸之辨然後
隨其材之大小皆足以有用於
世
===
上之所資而求者盖在此也而獨於
文焉是徵故視其表將以探其
中玩其華將以冀其實其志正
其氣醇其論議無所悖見於辭
者雖或未工不得而棄矣其外
燁然其中枵然割裂裝綴徒事
口耳文非無可觀也而無所於
alt_text:
之所先可也謂不足以得士還
矣雖然有司之好惡不可以不
慎也士習之升降風俗之隆替
恒必由之夫士必有忠信之質
而又明於義利王覇之辯然後
隨其材之大小皆足以有用於
世
===
上之所資而求者盖在此也而獨於
文焉是徵故視其表將以探其
中玩其華將以藁其實其志正
其氣醇其論議無所悖見於辭
者雖或未工不得而棄矣其外
燁然其中枵然割裂裒綴徒事
口耳文非無可觀也而無所於
punctuated: 之所先，可也；謂不足以得士，過矣。雖然，有司之好惡不可以不慎也。士習之升降，風俗之隆替，恒必由之。夫士必有忠信之質，而又明於義利王霸之辨，然後隨其材之大小，皆足以有用於世。上之所資而求者，盖在此也。而獨於文焉是徵，故視其表，將以探其中；玩其華，將以冀其實。其志正，其氣醇，其論議無所悖，見於辭者雖或未工，不得而棄矣。其外燁然，其中枵然，割裂裝綴，徒事口耳，文非無可觀也，而無所於
translation_en: …to say that literary composition is not what education should put first is permissible; to say that it is inadequate for selecting worthy men is mistaken. Even so, the responsible officials must exercise care in their likes and dislikes. The improvement or deterioration of scholars’ habits, and the flourishing or decline of social customs, invariably depend upon these. A scholar must possess a foundation of loyalty and trustworthiness and clearly understand the distinctions between righteousness and profit, and between kingly and hegemonic rule. Only then can each be of service to the world, according to the measure of his abilities. This, surely, is what His Majesty seeks in the men upon whom he relies. Yet literary composition alone serves as the evidence. Thus we examine its outward appearance to probe what lies within, and contemplate its flowering in the hope of finding its fruit. If a man’s aspirations are upright, his disposition pure, and his arguments free of what is contrary to right principle, then, even if his expression is not yet accomplished, he must not be rejected. If his exterior is resplendent but his interior empty, if he cuts and splices passages and pieces them together, occupying himself merely with what passes from ear to mouth, his writing may indeed have something worth admiring, yet it provides no basis for…

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
徵不得而取矣其有志鄉不謬
而學業未成者則亦不得而與
焉俊等之職蓋將以廣
德意求材實庶幾得駒駼駃騠於牝
牡驪黄之外以資任重致遠之
用謂遂能空其羣也則烏乎敢
諸士子有得於此者其毋以文
===
自多未得於此者尚知不昧於
所求俾究論習俗之變移者不
以病今日之有司則幸矣
翰林院侍讀學士奉訓大夫
汪俊謹序
alt_text:
徵不得而取矣其有忘鄉不謬
而學業未成者則亦不得而與
焉〔俊〕等之職盖将以廣
德意求材實庶幾得騊駼駃騠於牝
牡驪黃之外以資任重致遠之
用謂遂能空其羣也則烏乎敢
諸士子有得於此者其毋以文
===
自多未得於此者尚知不昧於
所求俾究論習俗之變移者不
以病今日之有司則幸矣
翰林院侍　讀學士奉訓大夫
汪俊謹序
punctuated:
徵，不得而取矣。其有志鄉不謬而學業未成者，則亦不得而與焉。俊等之職，蓋將以廣德意，求材實，庶幾得駒駼、駃騠於牝牡驪黄之外，以資任重致遠之用。謂遂能空其羣也，則烏乎敢？諸士子有得於此者，其毋以文自多；未得於此者，尚知不昧於所求。俾究論習俗之變移者，不以病今日之有司，則幸矣。
翰林院侍讀學士、奉訓大夫汪俊謹序。
translation_en:
… substantiate it, and thus they cannot be selected. Those whose aspirations are not misguided but whose learning is still incomplete likewise cannot be admitted. The duty of us examiners—myself, Jun, and my colleagues—is to extend the imperial benevolent intention and seek substantive talent. We hope to find fine steeds such as the jutu and jueti, looking beyond whether they are female or male, black or yellow, so that they may bear heavy burdens and travel far. But how would we dare claim that we could thereby select every outstanding steed from the herd? Those candidates who have succeeded here should not boast of their literary abilities; those who have not succeeded should still understand clearly what is being sought. If those who investigate and discuss changes in prevailing customs do not use them to fault the officials responsible today, we shall count ourselves fortunate.
Preface respectfully written by Wang Jun 汪俊, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy and Grand Master for Instruction.

translation_en:
Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination, the eleventh year of Zhengde (1516)

Proctors

Hu Shao, Grand Master for Excellent Counsel and Prefect of Shuntian Prefecture. His courtesy name was Dasheng; he was from Poyang County, Jiangxi, and was a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the jiachen year.

Zhang Run, Grand Master of Central Compliance and Vice Prefect of Shuntian Prefecture. His courtesy name was Rulin; he was from Linfen County, Shanxi, and was a metropolitan graduate of the renxu year.

Examiners

Wang Jun, Expositor-in-Waiting in the Hanlin Academy and Grand Master for Instruction. His courtesy name was Yizhi; he was from Yiyang County, Jiangxi, and was a metropolitan graduate of the guichou year.

Gu Dingchen, Grand Master for Instruction, Left Admonisher in the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent, and concurrently Reader-in-Waiting in the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Jiuhe; he was from Kunshan County, Zhili, and was a metropolitan graduate of the yichou year.

Associate Examiners

Chen Qi, Instructor in the Confucian School of Taizhou, Yangzhou Prefecture, Zhili. His courtesy name was Zhongyu; he had official household registration in Quanzhou, Guangxi, was originally from Chaling Subprefecture, Huguang, and was a tribute scholar (gongshi) of the renzi year.

Zheng Han, Instructor in the Confucian School of Daizhou, Taiyuan Prefecture, Shanxi. His courtesy name was Liangqing; he was from Longxi County, Fujian, and was a tribute scholar of the jiazi year.

Zhou Gao, Instructor in the Confucian School of Longyou County, Quzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang. His courtesy name was Tingxuan; he was from Guixi County, Jiangxi, and was a tribute scholar of the renzi year.

Ke Xin, Instructor in the Confucian School of Yongxin County, Ji’an Prefecture, Jiangxi. His courtesy name was Ruchong; he was from Nan’an County, Fujian, and was a tribute scholar of the jiazi year.

Zhou Chao, Instructor in the Confucian School of Jishui County, Ji’an Prefecture, Jiangxi. His courtesy name was Wangying; he was from Taicang Subprefecture, Zhili, and was a tribute scholar of the guiyou year.

Tang Jian, Instructor in the Confucian School of Guangchang County, Jianchang Prefecture, Jiangxi. His courtesy name was Jingfan; he was from Lin’an County, Zhejiang, and was a tribute scholar of the yimao year.

Fu Quan, Instructor in the Confucian School of Guantao County, Linqing Subprefecture, Dongchang Prefecture, Shandong. His courtesy name was Gongheng; he had official household registration in the Guilin Central Guard, Guangxi, was originally from Luotian County, Huguang, and was a tribute scholar of the dingmao year.

Ao Yue, Instructor in the Confucian School of Jixi County, Huizhou Prefecture, Zhili. His courtesy name was Bingzhi; he was from Gao’an County, Jiangxi, and was a tribute scholar of the dingmao year.

Yi Zongzhou, Instructor in the Confucian School of Taoyuan County, Huai’an Prefecture, Zhili. His courtesy name was Shiwen; he was from Lingui County, Guangxi, and was a tribute scholar of the dingmao year.

text:
第壹場
四書
舉直錯諸枉能使枉者直
成己仁也成物知也性之德也合内外之
道也故時措之宜也
行有不慊於心則餒矣我故曰告子未嘗
知義以其外之也
易
小往大來吉亨
===
九五渙汗其大號渙王居无咎
慎斯術也以往其无所失矣
神也者妙萬物而為言者也動萬物者莫
疾乎雷撓萬物者莫疾乎風燥萬物者
莫熯乎火說萬物者莫說乎澤潤萬物
者莫潤乎水終萬物始萬物者莫盛乎
艮故水火相逮雷風不相悖山澤通氣
然後能變化既成萬物也

punctuated:
第壹場

四書

舉直錯諸枉，能使枉者直。

成己，仁也；成物，知也。性之德也，合内外之道也，故時措之宜也。

行有不慊於心，則餒矣。我故曰：告子未嘗知義，以其外之也。

易

小往大來，吉亨。

九五：渙汗其大號，渙王居，无咎。

慎斯術也以往，其无所失矣。

神也者，妙萬物而為言者也。動萬物者莫疾乎雷，撓萬物者莫疾乎風，燥萬物者莫熯乎火，說萬物者莫說乎澤，潤萬物者莫潤乎水，終萬物始萬物者莫盛乎艮。故水火相逮，雷風不相悖，山澤通氣，然後能變化，既成萬物也。

書
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

Raise up the upright and place them over the crooked: this can make the crooked upright.

Perfecting oneself is benevolence; perfecting things is wisdom. These are virtues of our nature and the Way that unites the inner and the outer. Thus, whenever they are put into practice, they are fitting.

If one’s conduct leaves the heart dissatisfied, one’s vital energy will starve. Thus I said that Gaozi had never understood righteousness, because he regarded it as external.

Book of Changes

The small departs and the great comes. Auspiciousness and success.

Nine in the fifth place: In dispersion, his great proclamations spread like sweat. He disperses the royal stores. No blame.

Proceed henceforth with due care in this method, and nothing will be lost.

The term “numinous” refers to that which works wondrously in all things. For setting all things in motion, nothing is swifter than thunder; for stirring all things, nothing is swifter than wind; for drying all things, nothing is more parching than fire; for giving joy to all things, nothing is more gladdening than the lake; for moistening all things, nothing is more nourishing than water; for bringing all things to their end and their beginning, nothing surpasses Gen, the Mountain. Thus water and fire reach one another, thunder and wind do not oppose one another, and mountain and lake communicate their vital energies. Only then can change and transformation take place and bring all things to completion.

text:

鬼神無常享享于克誠
予造天役遺大投艱于朕身越予冲人不
卬自恤義爾邦君越爾多士尹氏御事

予欲宣力四方，汝爲。

鬼神無常享，享于克誠。

予造天役，遺大投艱于朕身。越予冲人，不卬自恤。義爾邦君，越爾多士、尹氏、御事，綏予曰：「無毖于恤！不可不成乃寧考圖功。」

昔在殷王中宗，嚴恭寅畏，天命自度，治民祗懼，不敢荒寧。肆中宗之享國七十有五年。

無以我公歸兮，無使我心悲兮！

鶴鳴于九臯，聲聞于野。魚潛在淵，或在于渚。樂彼之園，爰有樹檀，其下維蘀。他山之石，可以爲錯。

帝謂文王：「無然畔援，無然歆羨，誕先登于岸。」

夙夜基命宥密，於緝熈，單厥心！

春秋
translation_en:
“I wish to extend effective service throughout the four quarters; you undertake it.”

“The spirits do not invariably accept offerings; they accept those offered with true sincerity.”

“I undertake Heaven’s work; great responsibilities and arduous tasks have been left to my person. Yet I, a young and inexperienced man, do not grieve for myself. I look to you, rulers of the states, and to you, the many officers, heads of offices, and those conducting affairs, to reassure me, saying: ‘Do not be overly troubled by anxiety! You must complete the work planned by your deceased father.’”

“Formerly, Zhongzong, king of Yin, was solemn, reverent, respectful, and circumspect. He measured himself against Heaven’s mandate. In governing the people he was respectful and apprehensive, not daring to indulge in idleness or ease. Thus Zhongzong enjoyed his rule for seventy-five years.”

Book of Odes

“Do not take our lord home; do not make our hearts sorrowful!”

“A crane cries in the depths of the marshes; its voice is heard across the fields. Fish hide in the deep pool, or sometimes linger by the islets. Delightful is that garden: there stand sandalwood trees, with fallen leaves beneath them. Stones from other mountains can serve as whetstones.”

“The Lord on High said to King Wen: ‘Do not be so wavering; do not be so covetous. Take the lead and ascend the bank.’”

“Day and night he established the mandate in profound stillness. Ah, continuing in brightness, he devoted his whole heart!”

Spring and Autumn Annals

Third Session
Five Policy Questions
Question: A ruler who founds a dynasty must understand the difficulty of preserving its achievements before he can bequeath a dynastic succession that can be carried on, making his arrangements precise and thorough, with nothing omitted. A ruler who preserves those achievements must understand the difficulty of founding the dynasty before he can sustain its fully attained prosperity, guarding it carefully and not daring to let it fall. Founding and preserving thus follow a single Way. The Han dynasty was praised for the grandeur and far-reaching scope of its arrangements, yet scarcely one or two successions had passed before the Rebellion of the Seven Kingdoms occurred. The Tang dynasty was said to possess a complete system of laws and institutions, yet calamities caused by women occurred in successive reigns. Those who discuss these matters consider them the fault of Gao Di and Taizong respectively. Is this so?
We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao, in the legitimacy of his acquisition of the realm and the excellence of the plans he bequeathed, directly continued the Three Dynasties and surpassed the Han and Tang. His achievement may be called perfect in every respect, with nothing further to add. Throughout the hundred and fifty years down to the present, all within the seas has remained peaceful, as though it were a single day. This is assuredly the merit of successive sage emperors who reverently carried on his work, but the efficacy of our Emperor Gao’s founding achievement can also be seen in it. The grandeur of his overall arrangements and the detail of their provisions cannot be exhaustively recounted; nevertheless, might their broad outlines be set forth?
He also once discussed precedents from the Han and Tang with his attendant officials, lamenting with deep feeling that these must be taken earnestly as warnings. You students have studied and practiced these great instructions and should long since have formed some understanding of them in your hearts. Please respectfully set this forth, to assist the reigning emperor in his filial reflections.

Question: Since Yao and Shun, none have surpassed Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu in a ruler’s virtue; among later ages, those who discuss good government look no further than the Han, Tang, and Song. Yet examination of the accounts in the Classics and histories inevitably raises doubts. Yu kept his food and drink meager; why, then, did he have to taste fine wine and find it sweet before renouncing it? Tang did not amass wealth or profit; why, then, did he condemn the circulation of bribes only when offering a prayer? Wen’s “glory reached its height without blemish,” yet he presented a woman to Shou: this seems inconsistent with his cautious reverence. Wu “sought to carry on the virtue of his forebears,” yet received a mastiff as tribute from Lü: was this attention to minor points of conduct? These sages possessed great virtue and brought about flourishing government, yet their recorded actions still contain matters open to question. Why is this?

Then there was the ruler who presided at court in profound silence, as dignified and majestic as a spirit. He may be said to have possessed a solemn bearing; why, then, did the Han imperial enterprise subsequently decline? Another devoted his energies to government and nearly achieved great peace. One who was resolute, decisive, and intelligent seemed capable of great achievements; why did he cause distress among the people and resentment among the soldiers, becoming a profound source of calamity? These several rulers all relied upon their natural endowments and inherited established imperial achievements, yet suffered disgrace both in person and in reputation, inviting the censure of later generations. Our Emperor Taizu Gao and Emperor Taizong Wen established the supreme standard and handed down the imperial succession. Their virtue and glorious achievements truly sufficed to surpass Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu and to stand alongside Yao and Shun. 尤衆所以摠括天下財賦出入之數而
周知其有無多寡以為豐殺增減者也
===
今亦可倣而為之歟夫財匱而民怨民
裕而國昌有國者不可以不慎而錢穀
之大數亦學者所當知也其毋諉曰有
主者
問詩曰詒厥孫謀以燕翼子又曰干祿百
福子孫千億雖古聖賢莫不願望其子
孫之蕃昌而凡頌禱乎人者亦必歸重
於是蓋人情所同而天理之當然也但
常人狃於一時利害乃或肆惡於身而
punctuated:
制之用、軍國之需，古今一也。宋又有郊賚、歲幣、祠祿，今皆無之，宜其蓄積充牣，無所置之。顧乃皇皇焉有匱乏之憂，其必有故矣。昔人言為國有三計，其說可聞歟？今之國計，於是三者何居？有謂事之害財者有三冗，殆何所指？今於是三者孰甚？國計有錄，始見於唐，至宋作者尤眾，所以摠括天下財賦出入之數，而周知其有無多寡，以為豐殺增減者也。今亦可倣而為之歟？夫財匱而民怨，民裕而國昌，有國者不可以不慎，而錢穀之大數亦學者所當知也。其毋諉曰有主者。

問：詩曰：「詒厥孫謀，以燕翼子。」又曰：「干祿百福，子孫千億。」雖古聖賢，莫不願望其子孫之蕃昌，而凡頌禱乎人者，亦必歸重於是。盖人情所同，而天理之當然也。但常人狃於一時利害，乃或肆惡於身而
translation_en:
…the expenditures required by established institutions and the needs of the military and the state are the same in ancient and modern times. The Song also incurred expenses for rewards at the suburban sacrifices, annual tribute payments, and stipends for temple sinecures, none of which exist today. Our reserves should therefore be so abundant that there is nowhere to store them. Yet instead there is anxious concern about shortages. There must surely be a reason for this. People of former times said that there were three plans for managing a state's finances. Can you explain this saying? Where among these three does our present fiscal management belong? It has been said that three kinds of redundancy harm the finances. What precisely does this refer to? Which of these three is most serious today? Records of state finances first appeared in the Tang, and those who compiled them were especially numerous under the Song. Their purpose was to bring together the figures for fiscal receipts and expenditures throughout the realm, to establish a comprehensive understanding of what was available or lacking and in what quantities, and thereby to determine where to expand or curtail, increase or decrease. Could we follow this precedent and compile such records today? When resources are exhausted, the people grow resentful; when the people are prosperous, the state flourishes. Those who govern a state must attend carefully to this, and the overall figures for money and grain are also matters that scholars ought to know. Do not evade the issue by saying that there are officials responsible for it.

Question: The Book of Odes says, “Bequeath plans to your descendants, thereby bringing peace to and protecting your children.” It also says, “Seek emoluments and a hundred blessings, with descendants in their thousands and hundreds of millions.” Even among the sages and worthies of antiquity, none failed to wish for their descendants to multiply and prosper. All who offer others praise and blessings likewise place particular weight upon this. This is surely a feeling common to humanity and accords with heavenly principle. Yet ordinary people, habituated to considering only immediate advantage and disadvantage, sometimes give free rein to their own wrongdoing and…

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
不顧其子孫亦有不達損益之理不覽
止足之分而營營於子孫富貴謀者皆
惑也兹以古人之言行可為勸戒者相
與評之身為相國祿入厚矣而不為子
孫治垣屋位謝太傅賜予渥矣而不為
子孫益産業果何所見乎身親隴畝子
孫將胼手胝足矣乃曰遺之以安性本
公廉子孫常蔬食步行矣乃曰遺之以
厚何以言之歟主母胡懼而遽有穆伯
===
絕嗣之嘆絕嗣果足深懼邪内史胡知
而遽有臧孫有後之稱有後果能前知
邪衣食餘饒臣節可以盡瘁借曰不然
能忘爾私乎田宅便好帝德可謂念功
借曰不然能保厥家乎治獄無寃而自
知其後必興然則過於殘酷者信及於
子孫否也將兵不妄殺而自知其後必
昌然則肆於屠僇者信殃其子孫否也
夫禍福之來以為天道之必然而善惡

孫將趼手胝足矣乃曰遺之以安性本
公廉子孫常蔬食步行矣乃曰遺之以
厚何以言之歟主母胡懼而還有穆伯
===
絶嗣之嘆絶嗣果足深懼邪内史胡知
而還有臧孫有後之稱有後果能前知
邪衣食餘饒臣節可以盡瘁借曰不然
能忘爾私乎田宅便好帝德可謂念功
借曰不然能保厥家乎治獄無冤而自
知其後必興然則過於殘酷者信及於
子孫否也將兵不妄殺而自知其後必
昌然則肆於屠僇者信殃其子孫否也
夫禍福之来以為天道之必然而善惡
punctuated: 不顧其子孫，亦有不達損益之理、不覽止足之分，而營營於子孫富貴謀者，皆惑也。兹以古人之言行可為勸戒者，相與評之。身為相國，祿入厚矣，而不為子孫治垣屋；位謝太傅，賜予渥矣，而不為子孫益産業，果何所見乎？身親隴畝，子孫將胼手胝足矣，乃曰遺之以安；性本公廉，子孫常蔬食步行矣，乃曰遺之以厚，何以言之歟？主母胡懼，而遽有穆伯絕嗣之嘆？絕嗣果足深懼邪？内史胡知，而遽有臧孫有後之稱？有後果能前知邪？衣食餘饒，臣節可以盡瘁，借曰不然，能忘爾私乎？田宅便好，帝德可謂念功，借曰不然，能保厥家乎？治獄無寃，而自知其後必興，然則過於殘酷者，信及於子孫否也？將兵不妄殺，而自知其後必昌，然則肆於屠僇者，信殃其子孫否也？夫禍福之來，以為天道之必然，而善惡
translation_en:
…disregard their descendants. There are also those who fail to understand the principles of loss and gain or recognize the limits at which to stop and be content, yet ceaselessly scheme for their descendants’ wealth and eminence. All are deluded. Let us now discuss together sayings and actions of the ancients that may serve as encouragements and warnings.

One held office as Chancellor of State, with a generous salary, yet did not build walls and houses for his descendants. Another retired from office as Grand Preceptor [?], having received abundant gifts, yet did not increase his descendants’ property. What understanding truly lay behind these actions? One personally worked in the fields, so that his descendants would have callused hands and feet, yet he said that he was bequeathing them peace. Another was by nature public-spirited and incorruptible, so that his descendants regularly ate vegetables and went on foot, yet he said that he was bequeathing them abundance. How can these statements be explained?

What did the mistress of the household fear, that she immediately lamented that Mu Bo would have no descendants? Is the extinction of one’s line truly something to fear so deeply? What did the Interior Scribe know, that he immediately declared that Zang Sun would have descendants? Can the continuation of a line truly be known beforehand?

With food and clothing in abundance, one can exhaust oneself in fulfilling one’s duty as a minister. Supposing otherwise, could you forget your private interests? With conveniently situated fields and fine residences, the emperor’s beneficence may be said to recognize meritorious service. Supposing otherwise, could one preserve one’s household?

One who adjudicated cases without wronging anyone knew that his descendants would surely prosper. Does it follow, then, that the consequences of excessive cruelty truly extend to one’s descendants? One who commanded troops without indiscriminate killing knew that his descendants would surely flourish. Does it follow, then, that those who indulge in slaughter truly bring calamity upon their descendants?

As for the coming of misfortune and good fortune, if we regard it as the inevitable working of the Way of Heaven, yet good and evil…

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之報時有不類以為人事之適然而成
敗之迹又似可徵亦有一定之說可恃
之訓乎諸士子皆將事
君臨民以右其族而世其家者其肆言之以觀
擇術之慎
問戎狄為中國患自古然矣今之桀黠時
出沒於吾邊境而侵寇者盖昔之入主
中夏而吾之所驅逐以還之塞外者也
則防邊之政宜百倍於前代而後可我
===
朝自立國以来虜嘗為患而卒無大憂豈非
立法之善是以維持為萬世之防哉近
歳虜寇往往深入重獲略無創艾而去
比者宣府之警盖不特侵及涇陽候騎
至雍而已豈承平日久舊政多廢而未
舉歟此其為患盖不小也盗賊竊發亦
治世所不免至於前數年之盗流毒幾
遍天下至遣制帥調邊卒以成剿平之
功禍亦亟矣則弭盗之術尤今日所宜

===
朝自立國以來虜嘗為患而卒無大憂豈非
立法之善足以維持為萬世之防我近
歲虜寇往往深入重獲略無創艾而去
比者宣府之警蓋不特侵及涇陽候騎
至雍而已豈承平日久舊政多廢而未
舉歟此其為患蓋不小也盜賊竊發亦
治世所不免至於前數年之盜流毒幾
遍天下至遣制帥調邊卒以成剿平之
功禍亦烈矣則弭盜之術尤今日所宜
punctuated:
之報時有不類；以為人事之適然，而成敗之迹又似可徵。亦有一定之說、可恃之訓乎？諸士子皆將事君臨民，以右其族而世其家者，其肆言之，以觀擇術之慎。
問：戎狄為中國患，自古然矣。今之桀黠，時出沒於吾邊境而侵寇者，盖昔之入主中夏，而吾之所驅逐以還之塞外者也。則防邊之政，宜百倍於前代而後可。我朝自立國以来，虜嘗為患，而卒無大憂，豈非立法之善，是以維持為萬世之防哉？近歳虜寇往往深入，重獲，略無創艾而去。比者宣府之警，盖不特侵及涇陽、候騎至雍而已。豈承平日久，舊政多廢而未舉歟？此其為患，盖不小也。盗賊竊發，亦治世所不免。至於前數年之盗，流毒幾遍天下，至遣制帥、調邊卒，以成剿平之功，禍亦亟矣。則弭盗之術，尤今日所宜
translation_en:
…the recompense for good and evil sometimes fails to correspond to the deeds. If one regards these things as merely the chance workings of human affairs, the traces of success and failure nevertheless seem to offer evidence. Is there, then, a settled explanation, a teaching upon which one can rely? You examination candidates will all serve your sovereign and govern the people, bringing distinction to your clans and perpetuating your families through the generations. Set forth your views fully, so that we may observe your care in choosing the course you follow.
Question: That the Rong and Di have afflicted China has been so since antiquity. The fierce and cunning men who now appear and disappear along our borders, invading and plundering, are those who formerly entered and ruled the Central Lands, and whom we expelled back beyond the frontier. Our measures for defending the borders must therefore be a hundred times stronger than those of former dynasties before they can suffice. Since the founding of our dynasty, the northern foes have caused trouble, yet ultimately there has been no great calamity. Is this not because well-devised institutions have sustained our defenses for ten thousand generations? In recent years, enemy raiders have repeatedly penetrated deep into our territory, taken substantial booty, and departed with scarcely any chastisement to deter them. The recent alarm at Xuanfu surely amounted to more than merely an invasion reaching Jingyang and mounted scouts arriving at Yong. Can it be that, after so many years of peace, many former measures have fallen into disuse and have not been restored? The danger posed by this is certainly no small matter. Outbreaks of banditry are unavoidable even in a well-governed age. But the bandits of several years ago spread their scourge almost throughout the realm, to the point that commanders-in-chief had to be dispatched and frontier troops mobilized to accomplish their suppression. The calamity was indeed severe. Thus, methods of putting an end to banditry especially deserve, at the present time, …

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
加意者夫戎狄為患亦禦之而已然有
謂禦戎無上策當以氣勝之其說亦有
據乎禦之之策不過振國威飭邊備練
士卒實倉廩而已然有謂其本不在乎
威彊其任不在乎邊境其具不在乎兵
食然則竟安在乎所指急先之務亦可
行於今日乎弭盜之術則論盜有三源
者盡之又曰患莫大於招降禍莫深於
窮治然則何施而可此二者當今之所
===
欲急聞也願得良策以裨執政幸毋讓

加意者夫戎狄為患亦禦之而已然有
謂禦戎無上策當以氣勝之其說亦有
據乎禦之之策不過振國威飭邊備練
士卒實倉廪而已然有謂其本不在乎
威彊其任不在乎邊境其具不在乎兵
食然則竟安在乎所指急先之務亦可
行於今日乎弭盜之術則論盜有三源
者蓋之又曰患莫大於招降禍莫深於
窮治然則何施而可此二者當今之所
欲急聞也願得良策以裨執政幸毋讓
punctuated: 加意者。夫戎狄為患，亦禦之而已。然有謂「禦戎無上策，當以氣勝之」，其說亦有據乎？禦之之策，不過振國威、飭邊備、練士卒、實倉廩而已。然有謂「其本不在乎威彊，其任不在乎邊境，其具不在乎兵食」，然則竟安在乎？所指急先之務，亦可行於今日乎？弭盜之術，則論盜有三源者盡之。又曰：「患莫大於招降，禍莫深於窮治。」然則何施而可？此二者，當今之所欲急聞也。願得良策，以裨執政，幸毋讓。
translation_en: …deserve particular attention. When the Rong and Di cause trouble, one need only defend against them. Yet some say, “There is no supreme strategy for defending against the Rong; one should overcome them through force of spirit.” Does this assertion have any basis? Strategies for defense amount to no more than enhancing the state’s prestige, putting frontier defenses in order, training soldiers, and filling granaries. Yet some say, “Its foundation does not lie in military might; responsibility for it does not lie at the frontier; its resources do not lie in troops and provisions.” Where, then, do these actually lie? Can the urgent priorities indicated by this statement also be put into practice today? As for methods of suppressing banditry, the argument that banditry has three sources exhausts the subject. It is also said, “No trouble is greater than inviting surrender; no calamity is deeper than pursuing investigations and punishment to the utmost.” What measures, then, would be appropriate? These two matters are what we urgently wish to hear about at present. We hope to obtain sound strategies to assist those governing. Pray do not hold back.

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
第壹塲
四書
舉直錯諸枉能使枉者直
同考試官教諭敖批舉直錯枉只是一事
直者舉枉者自錯詳味語意自見塲中士子多未達者
此作體認精切而詞亦簡當必勑學士也讀者當自知
之
同考試官教諭周批作此題者毎病於發露
===
仁知太早且或腐穉可厭此作理得而詞順盖傑然者宜
錄以為式
同考試官教諭柯批聖人之言如化工渾然無
迹而以舉業排比之文擬之難矣繩墨不踰而理趣自到
僅見此篇錄之以示作論語義者
考試官左諭德顧批明白雅健可取
考試官侍讀學士汪批詳整可誦
人不苟用而衆因以化聖人之曉門人也盖舉
直而錯枉是不苟於用人矣枉者皆化而為直

punctuated:
第壹塲

四書

「舉直錯諸枉，能使枉者直。」

同考試官教諭敖批：「舉直錯枉，只是一事。直者舉，枉者自錯，詳味語意自見。塲中士子多未達者，此作體認精切，而詞亦簡當，必勑學士也。讀者當自知之。」

同考試官教諭周批：「作此題者，毎病於發露仁知太早，且或腐穉可厭。此作理得而詞順，盖傑然者，宜錄以為式。」

同考試官教諭柯批：「聖人之言，如化工渾然無迹，而以舉業排比之文擬之，難矣。繩墨不踰，而理趣自到，僅見此篇，錄之以示作論語義者。」

考試官左諭德顧批：「明白雅健，可取。」

考試官侍讀學士汪批：「詳整可誦。」

人不苟用，而衆因以化。聖人之曉門人也，盖舉直而錯枉，是不苟於用人矣，枉者皆化而為直
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

“Raise up the upright and place them over the crooked, and you can make the crooked upright.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Ao, Instructor: “Raising up the upright and placing them over the crooked constitute a single act. When the upright are raised up, the crooked naturally fall into their places beneath them; careful consideration of the wording makes this clear. Many candidates in the examination hall have failed to grasp this. This composition demonstrates a precise and penetrating understanding, and its language is concise and apt. Its author must be a diligent scholar [?]. Readers should recognize this for themselves.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhou, Instructor: “Those who write on this topic commonly err by bringing out benevolence and wisdom too early; some are also tiresomely stale and immature. This composition grasps the principle and expresses it fluently. It is surely outstanding and deserves to be recorded as a model.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Ke, Instructor: “The Sage’s words resemble the workings of creation: seamlessly whole, without any trace of artifice. To emulate them in the parallel prose of examination writing is difficult indeed. Only in this essay have I seen the rules observed without transgression while the import of the principle emerges naturally. It is recorded here for those composing essays on the meaning of passages from the Analects.”

Comment by Examiner Gu, Left Admonisher: “Clear, elegant, and vigorous; worthy of selection.”

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting: “Thorough and orderly, worthy of recitation.”

When men are not employed carelessly, the multitude is thereby transformed. In enlightening his disciple, the Sage meant that raising up the upright and placing them over the crooked was precisely to exercise care in employing men; the crooked would all be transformed and become upright …

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
其容已乎聖人荅樊遲問仁知至此盖謂知人
愛人若非一端曰仁與知本無二道君子於人
鑒裁既精於一心之明察識復稽於眾論之審
其選而舉之使服在大僚簡而拔之俾列於庶
位者必皆經德不回侃侃之正人也彊立不反
藹藹之吉士也盖直者必舉而所舉無不直焉
凡委置在下而不齒於衣冠之列遺棄于野而
不預夫爵命之榮者莫非罔其生理蚩蚩之眾
人也拂其常性碌碌之鄙夫也盖所錯皆枉而
===
枉者無不錯焉夫如是則旌别所及黙寓鼓舞
之機好惡所加自有感化之妙莫不曰彼善是
我乃未善彼能是我乃未能我之棄置固其所
也率相砥礪舎舊而新是圖昔之枉者皆化而
為直矣又孰不曰人所知可學而知人所行可
勉而行我之致用猶可為也爭自濯磨去惡而
善是從昔之錯者皆直而可舉矣是則即知人
之知寓愛人之仁仁知之相為用盖如此樊遲
未達聖人得不明言以曉之哉抑嘗因是而思

punctuated: 其容已乎？聖人荅樊遲問仁知，至此盖謂知人、愛人若非一端，曰仁與知本無二道。君子於人，鑒裁既精於一心之明，察識復稽於眾論之審。其選而舉之，使服在大僚，簡而拔之，俾列於庶位者，必皆經德不回、侃侃之正人也，彊立不反、藹藹之吉士也。盖直者必舉，而所舉無不直焉。凡委置在下而不齒於衣冠之列，遺棄于野而不預夫爵命之榮者，莫非罔其生理、蚩蚩之眾人也，拂其常性、碌碌之鄙夫也。盖所錯皆枉，而枉者無不錯焉。夫如是，則旌别所及，黙寓鼓舞之機；好惡所加，自有感化之妙。莫不曰：「彼善是，我乃未善；彼能是，我乃未能。我之棄置，固其所也。」率相砥礪，舎舊而新是圖，昔之枉者皆化而為直矣。又孰不曰：「人所知，可學而知；人所行，可勉而行。我之致用，猶可為也。」爭自濯磨，去惡而善是從，昔之錯者皆直而可舉矣。是則即知人之知，寓愛人之仁，仁知之相為用盖如此。樊遲未達，聖人得不明言以曉之哉？抑嘗因是而思：
translation_en:
…could this possibly be prevented? In answering Fan Chi’s questions about benevolence and wisdom, the Sage here apparently meant that knowing people and loving people might seem to be separate matters, yet benevolence and wisdom fundamentally do not constitute two different ways. In judging people, the gentleman exercises refined discernment through the clarity of his own mind and further checks his assessments against carefully considered public opinion. Those whom he selects and promotes to serve in high office, whom he chooses and advances to take their places in the various posts, must all be upright men, steadfast in virtue without deviation and firm in their integrity; worthy men, resolute without turning back and abundant in goodness. The upright are invariably promoted, and none who are promoted fail to be upright. Those left below, excluded from the ranks of officials, and those abandoned in the countryside, denied the honor of rank and appointment, are all ignorant common men who disregard the principles inherent in their lives, or mediocre, base fellows who violate their constant nature. Thus all who are set aside are crooked, and none who are crooked escape being set aside.

When this is so, the distinctions publicly drawn quietly contain the means of encouragement, while the approval and disapproval expressed possess their own subtle power to transform. Everyone will say: “He is good at this, whereas I am not yet good; he is capable of this, whereas I am not yet capable. It is indeed fitting that I should have been set aside.” They will all encourage one another, abandon their former ways, and seek renewal. Those formerly crooked will all be transformed into upright men. Moreover, who will not say: “What others know, I can come to know through learning; what others practice, I can practice through effort. It is still possible for me to become fit for service.” They will vie to cleanse and refine themselves, abandoning evil and following goodness. Those formerly set aside will all become upright and eligible for promotion. Thus the wisdom that knows people embodies the benevolence that loves them: this is how benevolence and wisdom function through one another. Since Fan Chi had not understood, could the Sage fail to explain explicitly and enlighten him? I have also reflected on this and thought…

民心之從違政治之得失罔不由之舜舉臯陶
湯舉伊尹不仁者遠聖人之治不越乎此而已
漢唐以下用舍不明君子小人迭為勝負而國
之治亂隨之然則人君之舉錯可不慎哉
成己仁也成物知也性之德也合內外之

translation_en:
…Among the affairs of the world, none is greater than appointing and setting aside men. The ascendancy or decline of gentlemen and petty men, the people's allegiance or disaffection, and the successes or failures of government all depend upon this. Shun appointed Gao Yao, and Tang appointed Yi Yin, and those lacking benevolence withdrew. The government of the sages amounted to no more than this. From the Han and Tang onward, appointments and dismissals were not discerning: gentlemen and petty men alternately prevailed, and order or disorder in the state followed accordingly. How, then, could a ruler fail to exercise caution in appointing and setting aside men?

“Completing oneself is benevolence; completing other things is wisdom. These are the virtues of human nature and the Way that unites the inner and the outer. Thus, when put into practice, they are appropriate to the occasion.”

Associate Examiner Yi, Instructor, comments: The passages explaining unity and application according to the occasion are precise and well grounded. The author seems to have devoted effort to personally experiencing benevolence and wisdom. He certainly cannot be regarded as an ordinary examination candidate.

Associate Examiner Zheng, Instructor, comments: The topic is clear enough in itself, but writers become entangled in forced connections and find it exceedingly difficult to proceed. This essay explains it directly on the basis of principle, without the slightest obstruction. It may be said to articulate the Doctrine of the Mean.

Examiner Gu, Left Admonisher, comments: An exquisitely accomplished work.

Examiner Wang, Academician Expositor-in-waiting, comments: The writing conveys the import of principle.

Once what belongs to one's nature has been fully realized within oneself, its exercise naturally extends to every practical application. This is the work of one who strives to become sincere. For there is no undertaking outside the province of one's nature. When benevolence and wisdom are both fully realized and applied to affairs, could anything fail to be appropriate? title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
成已言之私欲淨盡而本心之德湛乎其恒存
天理純全而本然之體昭乎其不昧非仁乎以
成物言之大以成大小以成小曲成而不遺也
立必俱立成不獨成兼濟而無外也非知乎仁
以為體知以為用性分固有合體用而一原者
也仁存諸內知形諸外随地異名合內外而一
道者也夫知而未仁則其公不足以立制事之
本仁而未知則其明不足以妙應物之機仁知
具內外一於是乎施之於一身或左或右與時
===
宜之無不中其適矣施之於天下若大若小以
時措之無不得其當矣無所用而不周無所施
而不利盖沛乎其有餘也處經事而知宜遭變
事而知權盖無乎而不可也誠之者之功用如
此其大此君子所以必誠之為貴歟大抵仁知
兩言之則各一其德而猶未足以致用故曰仁
者見之謂之仁知者見之謂之知君子之道鮮
矣必仁知合一而後大人之事備時措之宜盖
聖人過化存神之用也誠之者至此則與聖人

translation_en: …speaking of perfecting oneself: selfish desires are utterly purged, and the virtue of the original heart remains clear and constant; heavenly principle is wholly pure, and the original constitution shines unobscured. Is this not benevolence? Speaking of perfecting things: the great are perfected according to their greatness, and the small according to their smallness; each is brought to fulfillment in all its particulars, with none neglected. In establishing oneself, one must establish others as well; in attaining fulfillment, one does not attain it alone. One benefits all, excluding none. Is this not wisdom? Benevolence serves as substance, and wisdom as function: what is inherent in our nature unites substance and function in a single source. Benevolence abides within, and wisdom takes form without; their names differ according to their sphere, but they unite the inner and outer in a single Way. If one has wisdom but has not attained benevolence, one’s impartiality is insufficient to establish the foundation for ordering affairs. If one has benevolence but has not attained wisdom, one’s discernment is insufficient to respond with subtle mastery to the workings of things. When benevolence and wisdom are both complete and the inner and outer are one, their application to oneself, whether turning left or right, accords with the circumstances of the time and invariably hits the proper mark. Applied throughout the realm, whether to great matters or small, they are put into practice at the appropriate time, and nothing fails to receive its due. There is no use in which they are not comprehensive, no application in which they are not beneficial: their abundance more than suffices. In handling ordinary affairs, one knows what is fitting; in encountering exceptional circumstances, one knows how to weigh the alternatives. There is thus no situation in which they are inadequate. So great is the efficacy of the person who makes himself sincere! Is this why the gentleman necessarily prizes making himself sincere? Generally speaking, if benevolence and wisdom are treated separately, each constitutes only one virtue and is still insufficient for full practical application. Thus it is said: “The benevolent see it and call it benevolence; the wise see it and call it wisdom. Few possess the Way of the gentleman.” Only after benevolence and wisdom are united are the undertakings of the great man complete. Acting appropriately as circumstances require is the efficacy of the sage, who transforms wherever he passes and exerts a spiritual influence wherever he abides. When the person who makes himself sincere reaches this point, he and the sage…

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
發矣讀者其詳之
行有不慊於心則餒矣我故曰告子未嘗
知義以其外之也

translation_en:
…manifests [?]. Let readers examine this closely.

“If one’s conduct leaves the heart unsatisfied, then the vital force becomes starved. Thus I say: Gaozi never understood righteousness, because he regarded it as external.”

Associate Examiner Tang, Instructor, comments: “Mencius repeatedly refuted the claim that righteousness is external, but its implications become especially clear when tested against the nourishment of the vital force. This composition expounds the matter almost exhaustively—a truly difficult achievement.”

Associate Examiner Zhou, Instructor, comments: “This topic is especially crucial to the chapter on nourishing the vital force. The flaw in Gaozi’s view that righteousness is external collapses of itself, without an attack. This composition offers real illumination. It is an excellent piece; include it.”

Examiner Gu, Left Mentor, comments: “The writing fully elucidates the principle. It merits inclusion.”

Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-waiting, comments: “His words seem to show that he has grasped something.”

From the very reason why the vital force fails to attain fullness, we can understand why righteousness cannot be spoken of as external. The vital force becomes full when nourished and starved when deprived of nourishment; all of this depends on righteousness. How could someone who regards righteousness as external reach this understanding? Mencius’s meaning is that the vast, flowing vital force can arise through the accumulation of righteous deeds, but cannot be acquired through an isolated act of righteousness. Affairs that proceed from within and respond to what is outside differ in myriad ways. If the degree of weight assigned to them is once inappropriate, shame appears in the mere interval of lowering and raising one’s head. Can the heart then feel at ease? Conduct that begins close at hand and manifests itself far away takes many forms. If its measure of greater or lesser extent once departs from what is fitting, regret and self-reproach accumulate in the most hidden recesses. Can the heart then feel satisfied? From…

義如此然則義豈在外哉彼告子者乃曰義外
也非內也是不知而妄言者也彼義之見於事

punctuated:
是氣之至大者，雖曰初無限量也，心無以為之主，而欿乎其小矣；氣之至剛者，雖曰不可屈撓也，心無以為之帥，而索乎其微矣。養氣必主乎義如此，然則義豈在外哉？彼告子者乃曰：「義，外也，非內也。」是不知而妄言者也。彼義之見於事者，或輕或重，若在外矣，而本然之權則由中制，而非外也；義之形於行者，或長或短，若在外矣，而本然之度則由內出，而非外也。以義為外，而不復以集義為事，則盛大之體、流行之用，彼盖有所未窺也。不能養氣，而徒欲不動其心，則冥然罔覺，悍然不顧，彼盖自以為至也。謂之曰「未嘗知義」，信乎其於義有所未達也歟！大抵判心跡於二途者，異端之曲說；合體用而一致者，吾道之大全也。告子外義以求不動其心，盖於佛老之學絕事物以求心者類矣。孟子性善養氣之論，擴前聖所未發，而闢義外之說，尤有功於後學。學者宜致思焉。

易
translation_en:
…as a result, although qi in its supreme vastness is originally without limit, when the mind cannot govern it, it shrinks into smallness; although qi in its supreme firmness cannot be bent or broken, when the mind cannot command it, it dwindles into weakness. Nourishing qi must thus be grounded in righteousness. How, then, could righteousness be external? Yet Gaozi says: “Righteousness is external, not internal.” This is speaking recklessly without understanding. When righteousness manifests itself in affairs, giving greater or lesser weight to things, it may seem external; yet the inherent balance by which they are weighed is controlled from within, not from without. When righteousness takes form in conduct, setting longer or shorter measures, it may seem external; yet its inherent standard issues from within, not from without. If one regards righteousness as external and no longer makes accumulating righteous deeds one's concern, then one has failed to perceive something of qi's abundant substance and freely circulating operation. Unable to nourish qi, yet seeking only to keep his mind unmoved, Gaozi remains benighted and unperceiving, stubbornly heedless, while apparently believing that he has reached the highest attainment. To say that he “has never understood righteousness” is surely to say that there is something about righteousness he has failed to comprehend!

In general, separating the mind and its outward manifestations into two paths is the distorted teaching of heterodoxy; uniting substance and function into a coherent whole is the full scope of our Way. Gaozi treats righteousness as external in seeking to keep his mind unmoved. In this he resembles those in Buddhist and Daoist learning who cut themselves off from affairs and things in order to seek the mind. Mengzi's teachings on the goodness of human nature and the nourishment of qi develop what earlier sages had not expounded; his refutation of the claim that righteousness is external rendered especially great service to later students. Students should give this careful thought.

Book of Changes

九五：渙汗其大號，渙王居，无咎。

同考試官教諭易批：濟渙莫要於此二事，周公詔後世之意，可謂喫緊。此作足以發之，而文亦精潔可愛，蓋深於易者。

同考試官學正鄭批：作易義者，不失之麤鄙，則失之晦泥，殊非本色。晩得此篇，明鬯詳雅，而事理不遺，宜錄以式後學。

考試官左諭德顧批：文有發明。

考試官侍讀學士汪批：詞足以發而不浮，非苟作者。

事合濟渙之宜，占獲補過之善，渙九五爻義也。蓋渙其號令、居積以濟渙，則事合宜而渙可濟矣。過不於是而補乎？爻易聖人之意若曰：渙之九五，陽剛中正，以居尊位，當濟渙之任，有濟渙之具者也。是故時過於豐，而紀綱不能無解弛；物極於豫，而人心不能無乖離，所謂渙也。王者於此何以濟之？必推誠引咎，脩辭命以誥四方
translation_en:
Nine in the fifth place: Disperse his great proclamations as sweat spreads; disperse the king’s stores. No blame.

Comment by Associate Examiner Yi, Instructor: In remedying dispersion, nothing is more essential than these two measures. The Duke of Zhou’s intention in instructing later generations may truly be called urgently pertinent. This essay fully brings it out, and its writing is also refined, spare, and pleasing. Its author clearly has a deep understanding of the Book of Changes.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, Instructor: Those who compose essays on the meaning of the Book of Changes fall either into coarseness or into obscurity and rigidity, wholly departing from the proper character of such writing. Late in the proceedings I obtained this essay: clear and fluent, thorough and elegant, it neglects neither practical affairs nor their principles. It should be recorded as a model for later students.

Comment by Examiner Gu, Left Admonisher: The writing offers illuminating insights.

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Reader: Its language adequately expounds the meaning without becoming superficial. This is no carelessly composed work.

In action, to accord with what is appropriate for remedying dispersion; in divination, to obtain the benefit of correcting faults: this is the meaning of the fifth, yang line of Dispersion. By disseminating proclamations and distributing accumulated stores to remedy dispersion, one acts appropriately, and dispersion can be remedied. Are faults not thereby corrected? The intention of the sage who composed the line texts of the Book of Changes [?] is as though he were saying: The fifth, yang line of Dispersion possesses yang firmness, centrality, and correctness, and occupies the honored position. It bears responsibility for remedying dispersion and possesses the means to do so. Thus, when an age passes beyond abundance, its governing principles and institutional order inevitably grow lax; when circumstances reach the extreme of ease, people’s hearts inevitably become estranged. This is what is called dispersion. How should the king remedy it? He must demonstrate sincerity and take responsibility for faults, carefully framing proclamations to address the four quarters…

text:
安内攘外布號令以新天下言出乎身加乎民
周流磅礴有以浹於民之肌膚令出惟行弗惟
反融液透徹有以切於民之疾苦開張公道而
幽枉畢達也掃除煩苛而風聲丕變也大號非
時所當渙者乎然徒事虚文不可也必敷實德
以拯塗炭之危託諸空言不可也必布大惠以
慰雲霓之望厚歛可懲而倉廩之粟在所必發
悖出可虞而府庫之財在所必散以四海為一
家大賚有不惜也視百姓猶吾子博施有不鄙
===

序足以折釁蘖之萌處置得宜可以消反側之

心為之再安大業繫於苞桑始雖過而善於補
矣於義為无咎焉丕基固於磐石初雖失而不
遠復矣其占得无咎焉吁因一邑之渙以濟天
下之渙周公示占之意可謂深切著明矣抑考

punctuated: 安内攘外，布號令以新天下。言出乎身，加乎民，周流磅礴，有以浹於民之肌膚；令出惟行，弗惟反，融液透徹，有以切於民之疾苦。開張公道，而幽枉畢達也；掃除煩苛，而風聲丕變也。大號非時所當渙者乎？然徒事虚文不可也，必敷實德以拯塗炭之危；託諸空言不可也，必布大惠以慰雲霓之望。厚歛可懲，而倉廩之粟在所必發；悖出可虞，而府庫之財在所必散。以四海為一家，大賚有不惜也；視百姓猶吾子，博施有不鄙也。王居又非義所當渙者乎？夫如是，則施為有序，足以折釁蘖之萌；處置得宜，可以消反側之禍。興滯補弊，而紀綱為之復振；說近来遠，而人心為之再安。大業繫於苞桑，始雖過而善於補矣，於義為无咎焉；丕基固於磐石，初雖失而不遠復矣，其占得无咎焉。吁！因一邑之渙，以濟天下之渙，周公示占之意，可謂深切著明矣。抑考渙之上體，巽也。巽象為風，德為入，有號令之義；其卦為陰，陰主利，有居積之義。故垢以乾遇巽
translation_en:
…bring peace within and repel threats from without, issuing proclamations and commands to renew all under Heaven. Words proceed from the ruler himself and reach the people, circulating everywhere with an expansive force that penetrates their very skin. Once issued, commands must be carried out, not reversed; their influence permeates thoroughly, addressing the people’s sufferings directly. Open the way of public justice, and all concealed grievances will find a hearing; sweep away vexatious and harsh measures, and the prevailing moral climate will be greatly transformed. Are not great proclamations what the times require to be disseminated?

Yet merely attending to empty formalities will not do: one must extend genuine beneficence to rescue the people from dire suffering. Reliance on empty words will not do: one must distribute substantial favors to satisfy their longing, like the longing for clouds and a rainbow that herald rain. Excessive exactions call for correction, and the grain in the granaries must therefore be released. The prospect that wealth will depart through wrongful means gives cause for concern, and the riches in the treasuries must therefore be distributed. Regard all within the four seas as one family, and be unstinting in generous gifts; regard the common people as one’s own children, and be free of meanness in bestowing benefits widely. Are not the royal stores, too, what righteousness requires to be dispersed?

If this is done, actions will be orderly, sufficient to cut off the first shoots of discord; arrangements will be appropriate, capable of averting the calamity of unrest. Revive what has languished and remedy abuses, and the governing order will thereby be restored. Delight those nearby and attract those far away, and the people’s hearts will again be at peace. The great enterprise will be secured as though bound to a clump of mulberry trees: although there were errors at first, they will have been well remedied, and in principle there will be ‘no blame.’ The great foundation will be firm as a massive rock: although there were failings at first, the return to the right way will have come before straying far, and the divination will yield ‘no blame.’ Ah! Through the dispersal of one domain’s stores, the dispersal of all under Heaven is remedied. The Duke of Zhou’s intention in presenting this prognostication may indeed be called profound, pertinent, manifest, and clear.

Moreover, examine the upper trigram of Dispersion (Huan): it is Xun. Xun’s image is wind, and its characteristic is penetration; thus it carries the meaning of proclamations and commands. The trigram is yin, and yin governs material gain; thus it carries the meaning of accumulated stores. Hence, in Encounter (Gou; transcribed as 垢 [?]), Qian meets Xun…

…the Commentary on the Great Image likewise speaks of issuing commands. In the hexagram Jiaren (The Family), Li meets Xun, and the statement for the six in the fourth place likewise speaks of enriching the household. Although the nine in the fifth place occupies the Xun trigram, its capacity enables it to accomplish something. If it can disseminate its proclamations, it will be like the wind spreading over things, and the Way of Heaven will prevail. If it can disperse its accumulated stores, yang will thereby overcome yin, and Heaven’s virtue will be pure. What difficulty of dispersion could then remain unresolved? The meanings drawn from the lines of the Changes [?] each have their proper application. This, too, should be understood by those who contemplate the images and ponder the statements.
“‘Numinous’ is a term describing the wondrous working of the myriad things. For setting the myriad things in motion, nothing is swifter than thunder; for stirring them, nothing is swifter than wind; for drying them, nothing is more parching than fire; for gladdening them, nothing is more gladdening than the marsh; for moistening them, nothing is more moistening than water; for bringing them to their end and giving them their beginning, nothing is more powerful than Gen (Keeping Still). Thus water and fire reach one another, thunder and wind do not oppose one another, and mountain and marsh communicate their vital energies. Only then can transformation and change take place and bring the myriad things to completion.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Yi, Instructor: The study of the diagrams is inherently difficult, yet readers of the Changes carelessly fail to examine it. Thus many plagiarize conventional formulations merely to fill out an essay. This composition says what others cannot say, and its language is also pure and elegant, worthy of attentive appreciation. Its author must have immersed himself in the diagrams and gained an understanding of them.
Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, Instructor: This topic places particular emphasis on the single statement about the numinous wondrously working through the myriad things. This is the profound substance of the study of the Earlier Heaven and Later Heaven diagrams. Could Confucius have omitted Qian and Kun and spoken of the numinous without a reason? Many write without understanding this. For refined and profound attainment, and for clear and exhaustive exposition, nothing equals this…

text:
篇是用錄出

說卦發明至神之無方必詳六子之造化以見
之也夫神妙萬物本無方也造化之見於六子
者孰非神之所為乎說卦聖人之意若曰造化
之迹固可見於六子陰陽之妙尤不外於一神
神也者寓乎氣而不倚於氣超乎物而不離於
物妙應不測變化無方之謂也果何以見之震
===
居東方動萬物而迅其機者雷也巽居東南撓
萬物以速其化者風也離居於南物長以燥火
之所熯也兌居於西物成而遂澤之所說也坎
居正北萬物歸藏皆水之所潤也艮居東北萬
物始終皆艮之所成也後天六子為陰為陽各
專其功即造化之推遷於四時者如此然豈無
所本乎故離位乎東坎位乎西水火二物相逮
為用而不相射焉震位東北巽位西南雷風之
勢交相助益而不相悖焉艮位西北兌位東南

考試官左諭德顧批：理是如此。
考試官侍讀學士汪批：鋪叙瑩净。
《說卦》發明至神之無方，必詳六子之造化以見之也。夫神妙萬物，本無方也。造化之見於六子者，孰非神之所為乎？《說卦》聖人之意若曰：造化之迹，固可見於六子；陰陽之妙，尤不外於一神。神也者，寓乎氣而不倚於氣，超乎物而不離於物，妙應不測、變化無方之謂也。果何以見之？震居東方，動萬物而迅其機者，雷也；巽居東南，撓萬物以速其化者，風也；離居於南，物長以燥，火之所熯也；兌居於西，物成而遂，澤之所說也；坎居正北，萬物歸藏，皆水之所潤也；艮居東北，萬物始終，皆艮之所成也。後天六子，為陰為陽，各專其功，即造化之推遷於四時者如此。然豈無所本乎？故離位乎東，坎位乎西，水火二物相逮為用，而不相射焉；震位東北，巽位西南，雷風之勢交相助益，而不相悖焉；艮位西北，兌位東南
translation_en:
…this essay; hence it has been selected for inclusion.
Examiner Gu, Left Admonisher, comments: “The principle is indeed so.”
Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting, comments: “The exposition is lucid and clean.”
In elucidating how the utmost spiritual efficacy has no fixed direction, the Explanation of the Trigrams (Shuogua) must describe in detail the creative transformations of the six children to make this apparent. Spiritual efficacy works wondrously upon the myriad things and inherently has no fixed direction. Of the creative transformations manifested in the six children, which is not the work of spiritual efficacy? The sage’s meaning in the Explanation of the Trigrams is as if to say: the traces of creation and transformation can indeed be seen in the six children, while the wondrous workings of yin and yang lie entirely within a single spiritual efficacy. What is called spiritual efficacy resides in vital force (qi) without depending upon it, transcends things without departing from them, responds wondrously beyond all fathoming, and transforms without fixed direction.
How, then, can this be seen? Zhen occupies the east: what stirs the myriad things and quickens their incipient activity is thunder. Xun occupies the southeast: what agitates the myriad things to hasten their transformation is wind. Li occupies the south: things grow and become dry through the drying action of fire. Dui occupies the west: things mature and reach fulfillment through the gladdening action of the marsh. Kan occupies due north: the myriad things return to storage, all through the moistening action of water. Gen occupies the northeast: the beginnings and endings of the myriad things are all brought to completion by Gen. The six children in the Later Heaven arrangement, whether yin or yang, each exercise their particular function: such is the progression of creation and transformation through the four seasons. Yet could this be without a foundation?
Thus Li is positioned in the east and Kan in the west: water and fire reach one another in their operation without assailing one another. Zhen is positioned in the northeast and Xun in the southwest: the forces of thunder and wind mutually assist and augment one another without opposing one another. Gen is positioned in the northwest and Dui in the southeast…

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
山澤之氣彼此感通而不相隔焉後天六子一
陰一陽各得其偶即造化之象形於兩間者爾
夫位有對待斯用有流行體有配合斯氣有變
化於是陰變為陽陽化為陰往来不窮以司亭
毒之妙陰極復變陽極復化進退不已以鼓顯
藏之機而凡物之盈於兩間生於四時者大造
而無間曲成而不遺矣然何莫非神之所為也
哉吁神之可見於先天後天卦位者如此宜聖
人發以示人歟抑此章去乾坤而專言六子豈
===
以二老不用歟曰非然也先天圖學所以明造
化之體乾坤陰陽也即天地也六子陰陽之経
緯乎其間者爾陰陽不測之謂神言神則乾坤
在其中矣後天退乾於西北退坤於西南六子
各易其位者所以著造化之用皆出於理勢之
自然爾然致役者母之養也戰者父之成也曰
坤者地則乾為天可知是二老君藏之道亦未
嘗不在焉後天豈出於先天之外哉故曰帝曰
萬物曰神曰八卦曰六子合而言之一陰一陽

punctuated: 山澤之氣彼此感通而不相隔焉。後天六子，一陰一陽，各得其偶，即造化之象形於兩間者爾。夫位有對待，斯用有流行；體有配合，斯氣有變化。於是陰變為陽，陽化為陰，往来不窮，以司亭毒之妙；陰極復變，陽極復化，進退不已，以鼓顯藏之機。而凡物之盈於兩間、生於四時者，大造而無間，曲成而不遺矣。然何莫非神之所為也哉！吁！神之可見於先天後天卦位者如此，宜聖人發以示人歟！抑此章去乾坤而專言六子，豈以二老不用歟？曰：非然也。先天圖學，所以明造化之體。乾坤，陰陽也，即天地也；六子，陰陽之経緯乎其間者爾。「陰陽不測之謂神」，言神則乾坤在其中矣。後天退乾於西北，退坤於西南，六子各易其位者，所以著造化之用，皆出於理勢之自然爾。然致役者，母之養也；戰者，父之成也。曰「坤者地」，則乾為天可知。是二老君藏之道，亦未嘗不在焉。後天豈出於先天之外哉？故曰帝，曰萬物，曰神，曰八卦，曰六子，合而言之，一陰一陽
translation_en:
…The vital energies of mountain and lake communicate and respond to one another without obstruction. In the Later Heaven arrangement, the six children—the six derivative trigrams—each find their partner, one yin and one yang: these are simply the configurations of creative transformation taking form between Heaven and Earth. Where positions stand opposite one another, their functions circulate; where underlying forms are paired, their vital energies undergo transformation. Thus yin changes into yang and yang transforms into yin, their coming and going inexhaustible, governing the subtle work of nurturing all things. Yin at its utmost changes again; yang at its utmost transforms again. Their advance and retreat never cease, driving the workings of manifestation and concealment. Thus all things that fill the space between Heaven and Earth and arise through the four seasons are created on a vast scale without interruption, and brought to fulfillment in every particular without omission. Yet what part of this is not the work of numinous efficacy? Ah! Such is the numinous efficacy visible in the trigram positions of Earlier Heaven and Later Heaven. Surely it was fitting for the sage to expound it and reveal it to others!

But this chapter omits Qian and Kun and speaks exclusively of the six children. Is this because the two elders have no function? The answer is: it is not so. The study of the Earlier Heaven diagram serves to illuminate the underlying substance of creative transformation. Qian and Kun are yin and yang—that is, Heaven and Earth. The six children are simply yin and yang interweaving between them. “That which is unfathomable in yin and yang is called numinous.” To speak of the numinous therefore already includes Qian and Kun. In Later Heaven, Qian withdraws to the northwest and Kun to the southwest, while the six children each change their positions. This serves to reveal the functioning of creative transformation, all arising naturally from principle and the tendencies of things. Yet “bringing service to completion” is the mother's nurturing, and “doing battle” is the father's bringing to fulfillment. When it says, “Kun is Earth,” we can know that Qian is Heaven. Thus the way in which the two elders rule while remaining concealed [?] is also invariably present here. How could Later Heaven lie outside Earlier Heaven? Thus, whether one speaks of the Sovereign, the myriad things, numinous efficacy, the eight trigrams, or the six children, taken together these amount to one yin and one yang…

考試官左諭德顧批：說盡舜命禹之意。

考試官侍讀學士汪批：得旨。

聖君欲有為於天下，必責其任於大臣。盖有為者君之欲，而代之以為者臣之任也。聖君舉所欲而責之大臣，不亦宜哉？帝舜命禹之意，盖謂天下之大，主於一人，而分理於衆職；其承治於上而總治於下者，獨大臣焉耳。彼四方之道里不為近也，吾雖不能身歷，而思欲竭心思以溥其恩澤，使無遠而弗届焉。四方之人民不為少也，吾雖不能家撫，而思欲殫知力以施其政令
translation_en:
…is what is called the Way. Otherwise, how could it be said, “Substance and function have a single source; the manifest and the subtle admit of no separation”?

Book of Documents

“I wish to exert my efforts throughout the four quarters; you shall undertake this.”

Associate Examiner Tang, Instructor, comments: Recent essays on the Book of Documents have often erred through rigidity. Throughout the examination, tedious and excessive writing is tiresome [?]. None surpasses this essay in the completeness and concision of its language and meaning. It may serve as a model.

Associate Examiner Zhou, Instructor, comments: “Exerting efforts” does not refer exclusively to nurturing the people. Those who know to broaden their exposition somewhat, however, also err through superficiality. An essay with principles so clear and language so vigorous as this is scarcely ever seen.

Examiner Gu, Left Admonisher, comments: It fully expounds the meaning of Shun’s charge to Yu.

Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting, comments: It grasps the purport.

When a sage ruler wishes to accomplish something in the world, he must hold his great ministers responsible for the task. For accomplishment is the ruler’s desire, while acting on his behalf is the minister’s responsibility. Is it not fitting that the sage ruler should set forth his wishes and charge his great ministers with fulfilling them? The meaning of Emperor Shun’s charge to Yu was, broadly, this: vast though the realm is, it has one man as its sovereign, while its administration is divided among the various offices. Yet it is the great minister alone who receives direction from above and coordinates government below. The distances across the four quarters are by no means short. Although I cannot travel through them in person, I wish to exhaust my thought and care in extending my beneficence, so that no place is too distant to receive it. The people of the four quarters are by no means few. Although I cannot comfort every household in person, I wish to exhaust my understanding and strength in carrying out my governmental commands…

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
使無微而不逮焉黎民阻饑嘗以命后稷矣而
予之意猶未巳也蠻夷猾夏嘗以託皐陶矣而
予之志猶未慊也予之所欲有如此者非汝禹
為之而孰為乎必也布其四體而振迅以奮庸
使予之所欲溥而未能遂者舉形於設施之間
竭其股肱而邁往以興事使予之所欲施而未
能行者悉見於展錯之列導之而生養遂后稷
分為之而實汝之責也治之而爭奪息皐陶分
為之而實汝之任也吁帝舜所以責成於禹者
===
如此是可以觀君道亦可以觀相道矣嗟夫君
臣一身也君以臣為體臣以君為心故舜以股
肱耳目命禹而所自任者予欲而巳君道逸臣
道勞君道無為臣道有為明此以南面舜之所
以為君明此以北面禹之所以為臣嗚呼此有
虞之治所以為不可及也歟

昔在殷王中宗，嚴恭寅畏，天命自度，治民祗懼，不敢荒寧，肆中宗之享國七十有五年。
translation_en:
…so that none, however humble, should remain beyond their reach. When the common people suffered from hunger, I charged Hou Ji with the task; yet my purpose was still not fulfilled. When the Man and Yi peoples disturbed the central lands, I entrusted the matter to Gao Yao; yet my aspirations were still not satisfied. Such are my desires: if you, Yu, do not carry them out, who will? You must put all four limbs to work, rouse yourself vigorously to accomplish meritorious deeds, and give concrete expression in your measures to all that I have wished to extend universally but have not yet been able to accomplish. Exert yourself as my thighs and arms, press forward to undertake affairs, and bring into effect through your arrangements all that I have wished to implement but have not yet been able to carry out. Guiding the people so that their livelihood and nurture are secured is Hou Ji’s allotted work, but the ultimate responsibility is yours. Governing them so that contention and seizure cease is Gao Yao’s allotted work, but the ultimate charge is yours.

Ah! Such was Emperor Shun’s demand that Yu bring matters to completion. Here one may discern both the way of the ruler and the way of the chief minister. Alas! Ruler and minister form a single body: the ruler takes the minister as his body, and the minister takes the ruler as his mind. Thus Shun charged Yu to serve as his thighs and arms, ears and eyes, while what he reserved for himself was simply “I desire.” The ruler’s way is ease; the minister’s way is toil. The ruler’s way is nonaction; the minister’s way is action. Understanding this and facing south was how Shun acted as ruler; understanding this and facing north was how Yu acted as minister. Ah! Was this not why the government of Youyu could never be equaled?

“Formerly, Zhongzong, king of Yin, was solemn and reverent, respectful and fearful. He measured himself against Heaven’s mandate and governed the people with reverence and apprehension, never daring to indulge in idleness or ease. Thus Zhongzong held the throne for seventy-five years.”

Moreover, in discussing the length of the reign, they give the number twice: would that not make nearly 150 years? This essay is recorded as a model for future students.
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhou, Instructor: Its discussion of reverent apprehension in governing the people does not repeat what it says about reverent awe. This amply demonstrates the writer’s skill.

The argument is that the illustrious kings of Shang maintained reverence and thereby achieved good government, receiving blessings in the fullest measure. Among blessings, none surpasses a long reign. When former kings attained this blessing in its fullest measure, was it ever not rooted in reverence alone? The Duke of Zhou composed “Against Ease” (Wu yi) to instruct King Cheng. At this point, he seems to say: In ancient Yin, sage and worthy rulers arose six or seven times, yet none was more illustrious than Zhongzong. His dignity, humility, and restraint, manifested outwardly, were all reverence. He examined himself by moral principle, solemnly conscious that the Lord on High was looking down upon him. His respect, solemnity, vigilance, and apprehension, preserved inwardly, were all reverence. He disciplined himself by moral principle, clearly conscious that Heaven’s daily scrutiny was present here. When governing the people, he held fast to this disposition without losing it. He considered the hardships of those laboring in the fields as though he experienced them himself, never daring to relax his efforts in the slightest. He kept this disposition vigilant and unremitting. When he heard complaints and curses from the villages, he accepted them calmly, never daring to indulge himself in the slightest. 故享年之數殆不可以一二計也至於七十有
五年而後已焉盖其莊敬日强自獲仁者之壽
配天而出治者如是其延長也高朗令終獨得
天眷之厚撫民而為君者如是其悠遠也一繼
而得高宗亦以克壽聞矣所謂五十有九年者
視此為不逮再繼而得祖甲亦以永年著矣所

故享年之數，殆不可以一二計也，至於七十有五年而後已焉。盖其莊敬日强，自獲仁者之壽，配天而出治者，如是其延長也；高朗令終，獨得天眷之厚，撫民而為君者，如是其悠遠也。一繼而得高宗，亦以克壽聞矣，所謂五十有九年者，視此為不逮；再繼而得祖甲，亦以永年著矣，所謂三十有三年者，倍之而有餘。其福之隆如此，謂非無逸之所致乎？成王盍亦知所慕哉！抑論之，人情莫不好逸欲，而所甚好者生也。以其所甚好，禁其所好，庶幾必信。周公作《無逸》，專以享年永不永為言，其示好惡明矣。成王享國四十餘年，為周令王，豈非周公之功哉？厥後漢昭有過人之明，論者盖謂賢於成王矣，而不免於短折，殆未聞周公之訓也。後之人君宜知所鑒矣。
詩
鶴鳴于九臯，聲聞于野。魚潛在淵，或在于渚。樂彼之園，爰有樹檀，其下維毄。他山之石，可以為錯。
translation_en:
…Thus the years he enjoyed could scarcely be counted merely by ones and twos: they reached seventy-five before coming to an end. Through solemn reverence he grew stronger each day and naturally attained the longevity of the benevolent. Such was the long duration of his rule, governing in accord with Heaven. With lofty discernment he brought his life to a good conclusion and received Heaven’s especially abundant favor. Such was the enduring span of his sovereignty as he cared for the people. A subsequent successor, Gaozong, was also renowned for attaining longevity; yet his stated fifty-nine years fell short of this. A further successor, Zujia, was likewise noted for his length of years; yet Zhongzong’s years exceeded twice his stated thirty-three. His blessings were so abundant: could one say they did not result from avoiding ease? Should King Cheng not also have known what to emulate?
To consider this further: human beings all love ease and the gratification of desire, but what they love most is life. By using what they love most to restrain what they love, one may hope to secure their belief. When the Duke of Zhou composed “Against Ease” (Wu yi), he spoke particularly of whether the years enjoyed were long or short, clearly showing what should be loved and what should be shunned. King Cheng ruled for more than forty years and was an excellent king of Zhou. Was this not the Duke of Zhou’s achievement? Later, Emperor Zhao of Han possessed extraordinary discernment, and commentators indeed judged him superior to King Cheng. Yet he did not escape an early death, perhaps because he had never heard the Duke of Zhou’s admonition. Rulers of later ages should know to take warning from this.
Book of Odes
A crane cries in the deep marshes;
Its voice is heard in the open country.
Fish hide in the depths,
Or are by the islet.
Delightful is that garden:
There stand sandalwood trees,
And beneath them is brushwood [?].
Stones from another mountain
Can serve as whetstones.

The poet draws upon things to admonish his ruler indirectly, finding no single approach sufficient. For principles may be inferred from things, but cannot be sought through one approach alone. The poet draws widely upon things to offer admonition: was he not skilled at conveying counsel? I imagine his meaning to be that the principles of the world appear scattered throughout its myriad affairs, yet all may be sought by turning back to oneself. Among feathered creatures there is the crane. It cries in the remoteness of the nine marshes, yet its voice is heard in the open country. Thus, in secluded solitude, one might think oneself free to be careless; yet ten eyes watch and ten hands point. 日者於他日而或悖有因有革不可畫一而議
也理之無定在也盖如此相彼之園喬焉而有
檀若可樂也其下則有蘀之惡焉今有人焉吾
嘗親愛之矣亦嘗畏敬之矣其可好者固也然
豈無一失之非哉好而不知其惡可乎瞻彼他
山塊焉而有石若可棄也而其材中砥礪之用
===
焉今有人焉吾嘗賤惡之矣亦嘗傲惰之矣其
可惡者固也然而豈無一得之善哉惡而不知
其美可乎鹵此四者引而伸之觸類而長之天
下之理其庶幾乎抑夫子嘗有取於諷諫若此
詩者其得風人之義歟且首之以誠身繼之以
明善則天下之本以立由是施之於人莫大乎
慎好惡而天下之能事畢矣其言盖與大學中
庸相為表裏其知道者之言乎

punctuated:
潜在乎不測之淵，而有時則在于渚焉。是故事有萬殊，理之在於此事者，於他事而或違；有損有益，不可執一而論也。時有萬變，理之在於今日者，於他日而或悖；有因有革，不可畫一而議也。理之無定在也，盖如此。相彼之園，喬焉而有檀，若可樂也，其下則有蘀之惡焉。今有人焉，吾嘗親愛之矣，亦嘗畏敬之矣，其可好者固也，然豈無一失之非哉？好而不知其惡，可乎？瞻彼他山，塊焉而有石，若可棄也，而其材中砥礪之用焉。今有人焉，吾嘗賤惡之矣，亦嘗傲惰之矣，其可惡者固也，然而豈無一得之善哉？惡而不知其美，可乎？鹵此四者，引而伸之，觸類而長之，天下之理，其庶幾乎？抑夫子嘗有取於諷諫，若此詩者，其得風人之義歟？且首之以誠身，繼之以明善，則天下之本以立。由是施之於人，莫大乎慎好惡，而天下之能事畢矣。其言盖與《大學》《中庸》相為表裏，其知道者之言乎？

夙夜基命宥密，於緝熈單厥心。
translation_en:
…it hides in an unfathomable pool, yet at times is found by the islet. Thus affairs differ in countless ways: a principle applicable to one affair may prove at odds with another. There are occasions for diminution and for increase; one cannot insist on a single rule in discussing them. Circumstances undergo countless changes: a principle applicable today may prove unsuitable another day. There are occasions for following precedent and for making changes; one cannot deliberate by an unvarying standard. Such is the way principle has no fixed locus.

Look at that garden: a tall sandalwood tree stands there, seemingly a delight, yet beneath it lies the unsightly fallen bark and foliage. Now suppose there is someone whom I have loved dearly and regarded with reverence. That he deserves affection is granted; yet could he be without even one fault or failing? Can one love him without recognizing his faults? Look at that other mountain: its masses of stone seem fit to discard, yet their substance is suitable for whetting and polishing. Now suppose there is someone whom I have despised and disliked, and treated with arrogance and neglect. That he deserves dislike is granted; yet could he lack even one good quality or sound insight? Can one dislike him without recognizing his merits?

Taking these four instances [?], drawing out their implications and extending them through analogous cases, might one come close to understanding the principles of all under Heaven? Moreover, the Master once expressed approval of indirect remonstrance. Does not a poem such as this capture the intent of the poets who admonish through verse? It begins with making oneself sincere and proceeds to discerning goodness; thereby the foundation of all under Heaven is established. When this is then applied to dealings with others, nothing is more important than exercising care in one's likes and dislikes; with this, all that can be accomplished under Heaven is fulfilled. Its words are surely complementary to the Great Learning and the Doctrine of the Mean. Are these not the words of one who understands the Way?

Day and night he laid the foundations of the mandate, profound and still; ah, continuing in brightness, he devoted his whole heart.

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
同考試官教諭敖批難於守成學者類
能言之未必知所以難詩人能道成王之難而此作發揮
無遺𣃔非口耳文字之學矣
同考試官教諭周批講宥密單厥心處精
切明盡真若詩人頌成王然可録
同考試官教諭柯批頌非聖賢之徒不能作
而是詩尤精敷析甚難若此篇者真非苟作矣
考試官左諭德顧批說出成王心事
考試官侍讀學士汪批能頌成王之所以為成
者
詩人嘆美賢王慎保成命而有其德克紹先業
而盡其心夫夙夜積德以永保天命是能緝熈
前人之業矣賢王之心不於是而盡乎此祀成
王之詩也若謂成王以賢聖之資纘文武之緒
其心以為維我祖考受天命興王業以佑啓我
後人矣寧使自我而廢墜乎是以夙興夜寐慎
積厥德以為承藉寶命之基盖唯日而不足也

===
者
詩人嘆美賢王慎保成命而有其德克紹先業
而盡其心夫夙夜積德以永保天命是能緝熙
前人之業矣賢王之心不於是而盡乎此祀成
王之詩也若謂成王以賢聖之資纘文武之緒
其心以為維我祖考受天命興王業以佑啓我
後人矣寧使自我而廢墜乎是以夙興夜寐續
績厥德以為承藉寶命之基蓋惟日而不足也
punctuated:
同考試官教諭敖批：難於守成，學者類能言之，未必知所以難。詩人能道成王之難，而此作發揮無遺，𣃔非口耳文字之學矣。

同考試官教諭周批：講宥密、單厥心處，精切明盡，真若詩人頌成王然，可録。

同考試官教諭柯批：頌非聖賢之徒不能作，而是詩尤精，敷析甚難。若此篇者，真非苟作矣。

考試官左諭德顧批：說出成王心事。

考試官侍讀學士汪批：能頌成王之所以為成者。

詩人嘆美賢王，慎保成命而有其德，克紹先業而盡其心。夫夙夜積德，以永保天命，是能緝熈前人之業矣。賢王之心，不於是而盡乎？此祀成王之詩也。若謂成王以賢聖之資，纘文武之緒，其心以為：「維我祖考受天命，興王業，以佑啓我後人矣，寧使自我而廢墜乎？」是以夙興夜寐，慎積厥德，以為承藉寶命之基，盖唯日而不足也。
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Ao, Instructor, comments: “Scholars can generally say that preserving an established achievement is difficult, yet they do not necessarily understand why it is difficult. The poet could express the difficulties faced by King Cheng, and this essay expounds them fully, leaving nothing out. This is certainly no mere learning of words passed from ear to mouth and committed to writing.”

Associate Examiner Zhou, Instructor, comments: “The passages explaining ‘broad and profound, still and serene’ and ‘devoted his heart to the utmost’ are precise, pertinent, clear, and exhaustive. It truly seems as though the poet himself were praising King Cheng. It merits selection.”

Associate Examiner Ke, Instructor, comments: “Only followers of the sages and worthies can compose a eulogy. This poem is particularly subtle, and very difficult to expound and analyze. An essay such as this is certainly no careless composition.”

Examiner Gu, Left Admonisher, comments: “It brings out what was in King Cheng’s heart.”

Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-waiting, comments: “It succeeds in praising that by which King Cheng became worthy of the name Cheng, ‘Accomplished.’”

The poet marvels at and praises the worthy king: he carefully safeguarded the mandate already bestowed and possessed the requisite virtue; he successfully continued his predecessors’ undertaking and devoted his heart to the utmost. By accumulating virtue morning and night so as to preserve Heaven’s Mandate forever, he was able to continue and glorify his predecessors’ undertaking. Was it not in this that the worthy king devoted his heart to the utmost? This is a poem for the sacrificial worship of King Cheng. Its meaning is as though King Cheng, endowed with the qualities of a worthy and a sage and succeeding to the legacy of Kings Wen and Wu, thought to himself: “My forebears received Heaven’s Mandate and founded the royal undertaking, thereby protecting us, their descendants, and opening the way for us. Could I allow it to fall into ruin through me?” Thus he rose early and retired late, carefully accumulating virtue to provide a foundation for receiving and sustaining the precious Mandate. Indeed, even the whole day seemed insufficient …

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
日積月累務崇其德以為凝承天休之地盖無
時而或怠也吾見其宏深有容而萬善咸備充
其體段將與天為徒焉靜密不擾而一理粹然
致其精一將與天無間焉於嗟成王有德以基
命如此是能繼前人之耿光而基業為之益隆
明文之昭所謂丕顯者益以顯矣續前人之明
績而統緒為之益振定武之烈所謂丕承者益
以承矣吾知其負荷之誠孚格於陟降之表而
無斁善始克終其心寧有絲毫之不盡乎繼述
===
之善對越於孝享之際而無忝光前裕後其心
寧有錙銖之或歉乎是則基命緝熙固足以單
厥心而皆本於夙夜不康以有其德此成王所
以為周之令主而祭於宗廟所當頌也歟嗟夫
三代守成之君以成王為稱首詩人所頌不過
數言而其踐履之篤畜積之大祈天永命之實
亦略可見自今觀之曰不敢康者即所其無逸
之謂也曰夙夜基命宥密者即皇自敬德之謂
也曰緝熙單厥心者即篤前人成烈之謂也是

之善對越於孝享之際而無忝光前裕後其心
寧有錙銖之或歉乎是則基命緝熈固足以單
厥心而皆本於夙夜不康以有其德此成王所
以爲周之令主而祭於宗廟所當頌也歟嗟夫
三代守成之君以成王爲稱首詩人所頌不過
數言而其踐履之篤畜積之大祈天永命之實
亦略可見自今觀之曰不敢康者即所其無逸
之謂也曰夙夜基命宥密者即皇自敬德之謂
也曰緝熈單厥心者即篤前人成烈之謂也是
punctuated:
日積月累，務崇其德，以為凝承天休之地，盖無時而或怠也。吾見其宏深有容，而萬善咸備，充其體段，將與天為徒焉；靜密不擾，而一理粹然，致其精一，將與天無間焉。於嗟！成王有德以基命如此，是能繼前人之耿光，而基業為之益隆；明文之昭，所謂丕顯者益以顯矣。續前人之明績，而統緒為之益振；定武之烈，所謂丕承者益以承矣。吾知其負荷之誠，孚格於陟降之表而無斁，善始克終，其心寧有絲毫之不盡乎？繼述之善，對越於孝享之際而無忝，光前裕後，其心寧有錙銖之或歉乎？是則基命緝熙，固足以單厥心，而皆本於夙夜不康以有其德。此成王所以為周之令主，而祭於宗廟所當頌也歟！

嗟夫！三代守成之君，以成王為稱首。詩人所頌不過數言，而其踐履之篤、畜積之大、祈天永命之實，亦略可見。自今觀之，曰「不敢康」者，即「所其無逸」之謂也；曰「夙夜基命宥密」者，即「皇自敬德」之謂也；曰「緝熙單厥心」者，即「篤前人成烈」之謂也。是
translation_en:
…Day by day and month by month, he strove to exalt his virtue, making it the foundation for securely receiving Heaven’s blessings; indeed, he was never for a moment remiss. I see how his character was broad, deep, and all-embracing, with every goodness fully present. By bringing his moral stature to its fullness, he would become Heaven’s companion. In stillness and inward composure, undisturbed, the one principle remained pure. By attaining the utmost refinement and singleness of purpose, he would leave no separation between himself and Heaven. Ah! King Cheng possessed virtue and thereby established the Mandate in this way. Thus he could carry forward his predecessors’ brilliant glory, making the dynasty’s foundations still more exalted. By illuminating King Wen’s radiance, he made what was called “greatly manifest” still more manifest. By continuing his predecessors’ illustrious achievements, he further strengthened the dynastic succession. By securing King Wu’s accomplishments, he carried still further what was called “greatly continuing.” I know that his sincerity in shouldering this charge reached, without ceasing, beyond the realm in which the ancestral spirits ascend and descend. Beginning well and bringing matters to completion, could he have failed to exert his heart to the slightest degree? His excellence in inheriting and carrying forward their work was displayed before the ancestors during his filial offerings, bringing them no dishonor. Bringing glory to his forebears and abundance to his descendants, could his heart have fallen short by even the smallest measure? Thus, establishing the Mandate and continuing its brightness were indeed sufficient to give full expression to his heart; yet all this was rooted in his taking no ease, morning or night, so as to possess this virtue. Was this not what made King Cheng an excellent ruler of Zhou, deserving praise when sacrifices were offered in the ancestral temple?

Ah! Among the rulers of the Three Dynasties who preserved their inherited achievements, King Cheng is acclaimed as foremost. The poet praised him in only a few words, yet these allow us some glimpse of the steadfastness of his practice, the greatness of his accumulated virtue, and the substance of his efforts to pray to Heaven for an enduring Mandate. Viewed from the present, “not daring to take ease” means precisely “making freedom from ease one’s abiding place.” “Morning and night establishing the Mandate in magnanimity and inward stillness” means precisely “greatly revering virtue in oneself.” “Continuing the brightness and fully exerting his heart” means precisely “consolidating the completed achievements of his predecessors.” Thus…
