取地不以其道，《春秋》專有所責；歸地不以其道，《春秋》兼有所責。此汶陽之取，其失在魯；汶陽之歸，其失不專於晋也。《春秋》備舉其始終，而罪可見矣。且汶陽之田，久侵於齊，乃魯故物也。于鞌之役，一戰勝齊，於是返魯衛之侵地，而復其故壤。自魯言之，曰：「自我失之，自我得之。」可矣。而《春秋》書「取」以責之，何耶？盖建邦啓土，各有疆理，先
translation_en:
…we see that King Cheng’s fine natural endowment was indeed exceptional. Yet was it not the Duke of Zhou’s achievement to nurture and develop it to fulfillment? Here too we can see how the conduct of a chief minister bears upon the ruler’s virtue.

Spring and Autumn Annals

“Acquired the lands of Wenyang.” 〔Second year of Duke Cheng〕 “In spring, the Marquis of Jin sent Han Chuan to come and say that the lands of Wenyang were to be returned to Qi.” 〔Eighth year of Duke Cheng〕

Comment by Associate Examiner Fu, Instructor: “The strands of these events are disparate and difficult to draw together. This essay sets them out fully and clearly, and its prose is elegant and orderly. Surely the work of an accomplished writer.”

Comment by Examiner Gu, Left Mentor: “A well-controlled composition.”

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting: “The narration is well ordered.”

When land is acquired contrary to the proper Way, the Spring and Autumn Annals directs its blame at one party; when land is returned contrary to the proper Way, the Spring and Autumn Annals assigns blame to more than one party. Thus, in the acquisition of Wenyang, the fault lay with Lu; in the return of Wenyang, the fault did not lie solely with Jin. The Spring and Autumn Annals records the entire course of events, from beginning to end, making the culpability apparent.

Now, the lands of Wenyang had long been occupied by Qi, but they were Lu’s former possession. At the battle of An, Qi was defeated in a single engagement. The lands seized from Lu and Wei were then returned, restoring their former territories. From Lu’s standpoint, it would have been acceptable to say: “We lost them ourselves, and we recovered them ourselves.” Why, then, does the Spring and Autumn Annals record this as “acquired,” thereby censuring Lu? When states were established and territories opened up, each had its defined boundaries—the former…

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
王所以體國而經野也是田也使在邦域之中
則先王所錫先祖所受在諸侯有世守之正固
不可亂矣使得於蠶食之侵則興滅國繼絕世
在天子有懷柔之義亦必有處也顧乃偃然據
之未嘗一請於天王其罪亦豈小哉况魯初未
嘗以德服人乃因人而有之是晋之惠也亦何
足多乎所謂取之不以其道其責固有在矣汶
陽之田獲歸于魯乃晋制命也八年之間齊服
事晋於是使韓穿來言而復歸之于齊自晋言
之曰自我予之自我奪之可矣而春秋書來言
以責之何耶盖信以行義義以成命覇主所以
定與而睦鄰也是舉也使齊無貪得之心則保
境息民足以守國不復請之于晋使穿有諫止
之義則惇信明義足以守覇不輕言之于魯顧
皆悍然不顧以成晋侯二命之失其罪不亦均
乎若魯終不能以禮自强遽聽命而歸之是晋
之鄙也不亦惡乎所謂歸之不以其道其責盖
有所分矣吁一得失之小而義之所該有如此

事晉於是使韓穿来言而復歸之于齊自晉言
===
之曰自我予之自我奪之可矣而春秋書来言
以責之何耶蓋信以行義義以成命霸主所以
定與而睦鄰也是舉也使齊無貪得之心則保
境息民足以守國不復請之于晉使穿有諫止
之義則惇信明義足以守霸不輕言之于魯顧
皆悍然不顧以成晉侯二命之失其罪不亦均
乎若魯終不能以禮自強遽聽命而歸之是晉
之鄙也不亦惡乎所謂歸之不以其道其責蓋
有所分矣吁一得失之小而義之所該有如此
punctuated:
王所以體國而經野也。是田也，使在邦域之中，則先王所錫，先祖所受，在諸侯有世守之正，固不可亂矣；使得於蠶食之侵，則興滅國，繼絕世，在天子有懷柔之義，亦必有處也。顧乃偃然據之，未嘗一請於天王，其罪亦豈小哉？况魯初未嘗以德服人，乃因人而有之，是晋之惠也，亦何足多乎？所謂取之不以其道，其責固有在矣。

汶陽之田獲歸于魯，乃晋制命也。八年之間，齊服事晋，於是使韓穿來言，而復歸之于齊。自晋言之，曰：「自我予之，自我奪之」，可矣。而春秋書「來言」以責之，何耶？盖信以行義，義以成命，覇主所以定與而睦鄰也。是舉也，使齊無貪得之心，則保境息民，足以守國，不復請之于晋；使穿有諫止之義，則惇信明義，足以守覇，不輕言之于魯。顧皆悍然不顧，以成晋侯二命之失，其罪不亦均乎？若魯終不能以禮自强，遽聽命而歸之，是晋之鄙也，不亦惡乎？所謂歸之不以其道，其責盖有所分矣。吁！一得失之小，而義之所該有如此
translation_en:
…the means by which the former kings ordered the realm and demarcated its countryside. As for these lands, if they lay within the state's boundaries, they were what the former kings had bestowed and the ancestors had received. The feudal lords had a rightful duty to preserve them generation after generation, and this certainly could not be violated. If they had been acquired through piecemeal encroachment, then restoring extinguished states and continuing broken lines of succession fell within the Son of Heaven's duty to cherish and conciliate the lords; there must likewise have been a proper way to dispose of them. Yet Lu simply occupied them complacently, without once petitioning the Heavenly King. Could its offense be slight? Moreover, Lu had never brought others into submission through virtue, but obtained these lands through another's agency. This was a favor from Jin: what was there to praise? Thus, when we speak of acquiring them contrary to the proper Way, the blame certainly has its proper object.

The restoration of the lands of Wenyang to Lu was commanded by Jin. Within eight years, Qi submitted to and served Jin, whereupon Jin sent Han Chuan to convey its instructions, and the lands were returned to Qi. From Jin's perspective, it might well say, “I bestowed them; I may take them away.” Yet why does the Spring and Autumn Annals record “came to convey instructions” in order to censure this? Trustworthiness serves to put righteousness into practice, and righteousness gives effect to commands: these are the means by which a hegemon secures his allies and maintains harmony with neighboring states. In this affair, had Qi harbored no greedy desire for gain, it could have protected its borders and given its people repose, thereby preserving its state without petitioning Jin again. Had Chuan possessed the sense of righteousness to remonstrate and prevent the action, he could have upheld trustworthiness and made righteousness manifest, thereby preserving Jin's hegemony without lightly conveying such instructions to Lu. Yet both brazenly disregarded these considerations, bringing to completion the error of the Marquis of Jin's contradictory commands. Were their offenses not equal? As for Lu, it ultimately failed to strengthen itself through ritual propriety and promptly obeyed the command to return the lands. This was to be treated with contempt by Jin: was it not also shameful? Thus, when we speak of returning them contrary to the proper Way, the blame is shared. Ah! So small a matter as a single acquisition and loss, yet the principles of righteousness it encompasses are such…

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
者非聖筆其孰能與於此哉抑汶陽之得失固
皆制於晋矣亦成公不能得其民歟叔孫僑如
嘗帥師圍棘以取汶陽之田棘不服故也夫復
故地而民不服何也魯於是時初稅畝作丘甲
稅役日益重所以不願為之氓歟然則其所以
輙得而復失者殆亦未可專罪晋乎
夏公會齊侯于夾谷公至自夾谷定公十年

即望國會鄰之始終，見聖人化彊於俄頃。夫齊之弱魯而欲肆侮也久矣，夾谷之會，相非孔子，又何以化其彊而成好會之始終也哉？自昔春秋之末，齊魯交惡，魯既悔禍於及平，齊亦降心於盟好，夾谷之會，不其韙歟？柰何齊侯不以脩
translation_en:
…if not for the Sage’s brush, who could have attained such insight? Yet although the acquisition and loss of Wenyang were indeed both controlled by Jin, was it also that Duke Cheng could not win over its people? Shusun Qiaoru once led an army to besiege Ji in order to recover the lands of Wenyang, because Ji would not submit. Why would the people not submit when their former territory was restored? At this time Lu had introduced taxation by the mu and imposed military levies by the qiu. Taxes and service obligations grew heavier by the day: was this why the people were unwilling to become its subjects? If so, perhaps Jin alone cannot be blamed for Lu’s gaining the territory only to lose it again.
“In summer, the duke met the Marquis of Qi at Jiagu. The duke returned from Jiagu.” Tenth year of Duke Ding.
Comment by Associate Examiner Fu, Instructor: “A state is strengthened through virtue, not force: this is the intent of the set topic. This composition adequately develops it, and its language is also seasoned and impassioned. Readers should not judge it by conventional standards.”
Comment by Examiner Gu, Left Mentor: “A mature composition, worthy of selection.”
Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting: “It speaks well of the Sage’s transforming influence.”
From the entire course of an eminent state’s meeting with its neighbor [?], we see how the Sage transformed the forceful in an instant. Qi had long regarded Lu as weak and wished to heap insults upon it. Had Confucius not served as ceremonial assistant at the meeting at Jiagu, how could Qi’s domineering conduct have been transformed, and an amicable meeting brought to completion? In the closing years of the Spring and Autumn period, Qi and Lu were at odds. Lu, regretting the calamities of conflict, had made peace; Qi too had humbled itself to enter a friendly covenant. title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
睦為務而誤聴犁彌之詐謀不以恤憐為心而
肆逞萊夷之俘衆兩君就壇兩相相揖齊人鼓
譟而起將劫魯君而執之其輕蔑鄰交為何如
殊不知魯國雖削而周公之法制猶存魯君雖
弱而孔子則文武兼備具官以從歷階以語使
齊侯愧悔不已麾萊夷而辟之其折服彊力
為何如以至責汶陽之田止野外之享聖人一
言之威而重於三軍如此所過者化不於是而
可驗乎慨夫楚子盟盂宋襄見執齊寔效尤而
===
伏禍機於盛際魯不思患以鑒覆轍於前人夾
谷之會亦曰殆哉向非孔子則先事未必有備
臨事未必能勝以禮而始以亂而終會而見執
何以反行飲至而即安於先君之都乎今則徒
恃夫義理之勇以革其彊暴之心易危為安轉
禍為福成事而歸得以舎爵策勳於先君之廟
焉未幾謝過以質侵疆来歸聖人俄頃之化行於
彊國如此兆足以行不於是而可見邪由是以
知春秋既書公會齊侯于夾谷而必書至自夾

punctuated: 睦為務，而誤聴犁彌之詐謀；不以恤憐為心，而肆逞萊夷之俘衆。兩君就壇，兩相相揖，齊人鼓譟而起，將劫魯君而執之，其輕蔑鄰交為何如！殊不知魯國雖削，而周公之法制猶存；魯君雖弱，而孔子則文武兼備，具官以從，歷階以語，使齊侯愧悔不已，麾萊夷而辟之，其折服彊力為何如！以至責汶陽之田，止野外之享，聖人一言之威而重於三軍如此。所過者化，不於是而可驗乎？慨夫楚子盟盂，宋襄見執，齊寔效尤，而伏禍機於盛際。魯不思患，以鑒覆轍於前人，夾谷之會亦曰殆哉！向非孔子，則先事未必有備，臨事未必能勝，以禮而始，以亂而終，會而見執，何以反行飲至，而即安於先君之都乎？今則徒恃夫義理之勇，以革其彊暴之心，易危為安，轉禍為福，成事而歸，得以舎爵策勳於先君之廟焉。未幾，謝過以質，侵疆来歸，聖人俄頃之化行於彊國如此。兆足以行，不於是而可見邪？由是以知，《春秋》既書公會齊侯于夾谷，而必書至自夾
translation_en:
…making amity his concern, he mistakenly heeded Li Mi’s deceitful scheme; instead of taking compassion to heart, he gave free rein to the captive host of the Lai tribesmen. The two rulers ascended the platform, and their two assisting ministers exchanged bows. The men of Qi rose amid drumming and shouting, intending to seize the ruler of Lu and hold him captive. How contemptuously they treated relations with a neighboring state!

Little did they realize that, although Lu’s territory had diminished, the Duke of Zhou’s laws and institutions still survived; and although its ruler was weak, Confucius possessed both civil and military accomplishments. Accompanying him in an official capacity, Confucius mounted the steps and spoke, making the Marquis of Qi so ashamed and remorseful that he waved the Lai tribesmen away. How thoroughly he subdued brute force! He went on to demand the lands of Wenyang and to halt the banquet in the open countryside. Such was the authority of a single utterance from the sage: it outweighed three armies. Is this not proof that wherever he passed, people were transformed?

Alas, when the Viscount of Chu held the covenant meeting at Yu, Duke Xiang of Song was taken captive. Qi was indeed following that evil precedent, concealing the seeds of disaster amid a splendid occasion. Lu failed to anticipate danger and take warning from its predecessors’ disastrous course. The meeting at Jiagu was truly perilous! Had it not been for Confucius, preparations might not have been made beforehand, nor might the crisis have been overcome when it arose. Beginning with ritual propriety and ending in disorder, with the ruler taken captive at the meeting, how could he have returned to perform the homecoming drinking ceremony and rest secure in his predecessors’ capital?

As it was, Confucius relied solely on the courage born of moral principle to reform their violent and overbearing hearts. He changed danger into safety and turned calamity into good fortune. Their business accomplished, they returned, able to set out the sacrificial cups and record meritorious service in the ancestral temple of the former rulers. Before long, Qi offered a sincere apology [?] and restored the territory it had encroached upon. Such was the transformation that the sage brought about in a powerful state in a mere moment. Is this not evidence that his influence was sufficient to take effect [?]?

From this we understand why the Spring and Autumn Annals, after recording that the duke met the Marquis of Qi at Jiagu, necessarily also recorded that he ‘returned from Jia…’

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
谷者實幸而危之耳嗟夫齊彊魯弱盖周公之
於報政季子之於觀樂已知之矣豈待是乎第
以力則彊者有時而可弱以德則弱者有時而
必彊觀孔子相會夾谷而齊人歸田行乎季孫
而大夫墮城為司宼攝相事七日而誅少正卯
三月而國大治此魯覇王之基而聖人綏来動
和之試也不曰吾其為東周乎盖深有望於魯
而惜也女樂饋而孔子行矣於乎是齊之弱魯
邪魯之自弱邪繼是而後不一再傳而公旦之
===

translation_en:
…Valley”—this wording in fact expresses relief at his safe return while recognizing the danger he had faced. Alas! That Qi was strong and Lu weak was already understood when Zhou Gong received the report on government and when Jizi observed the musical performances. Why would one have had to wait until this occasion? Yet, where force is concerned, the strong may sometimes become weak; where virtue is concerned, the weak will sometimes assuredly become strong. Consider how Confucius assisted at the meeting at Jiagu, and the men of Qi returned the lands; how he put his policies into practice with Jisun, and the grandees demolished their city walls; and how, as Minister of Justice acting as chief minister, he executed Shaozheng Mao within seven days and brought the state into excellent order within three months. These were the foundations upon which Lu could attain hegemony or true kingship, and a demonstration of the sage’s ability to bring people to him by reassuring them and to bring harmony through his actions. Did he not say, “Might I not make an Eastern Zhou?” He had indeed placed profound hopes in Lu and regretted its failings. When the female musicians were presented as a gift, Confucius departed. Alas! Was this Qi weakening Lu, or Lu weakening itself? Thereafter, before even one or two further successions, the ruling house of Gong Dan had declined. How could one lament this enough?

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
天一定而不可易也人知禮制於聖人矣而孰
知其為不易之理哉記者論禮樂至此謂夫禮
之為用也無不該而其為體也有所自彼簠簋
俎豆制度文章禮於是乎有器矣器固聖人之
所為也升降上下周旋裼襲禮於是乎有文矣
文固聖人之所議也親疎之序或引而進之或
推而遠之斟酌乎人情初未嘗有一定之拘貴
賤之等或少之為貴或多之為美變通於時宜
初未嘗有一律之守是所謂禮也然是禮也乃
===
理之不可易者也自其親疎之有序也斬以至
緦喪服異等而九族之情無所憾理之形於親
疎者毫髮可少爽乎自其貴賤之有等也王公
至皂隸儀章異制而上下之分莫敢爭理之形
於貴賤者分寸可少移乎禮有大有小理之所
在大者不可損而小者不可益也禮有顯有微
理之所在顯者不可揜而微者不可大也夫禮
出於理之不可易者如此於是推之四海而皆
準傳之萬世而無弊彼謂作禮以疆世者殆未

…Heaven, is fixed and cannot be altered. People know that ritual was instituted by the sages, but who knows that it embodies unalterable principle? At this point in his discussion of ritual and music, the author of the Record says that ritual embraces everything in its operation, while its essential substance has a source. In the fu and gui grain vessels, the zu offering stands and dou dishes, and their prescribed forms and ornamental patterns, ritual has its implements. These implements were indeed made by the sages. In ascending and descending, moving above and below, turning and circling, and exposing or covering the garment, ritual has its formal expression. These forms were indeed deliberated upon by the sages. In ordering closer and more distant relationships, some are drawn forward and others placed farther away. This weighs human feelings, without ever being constrained by a single fixed rule. In distinguishing the ranks of noble and lowly, sometimes fewer things are esteemed, and sometimes greater numbers are considered splendid. This adapts to what is appropriate to the occasion, without ever adhering to one uniform rule. This is what is called ritual. Yet this ritual is precisely what cannot be altered in principle.
In its ordering of closer and more distant relationships, mourning garments differ in grade, from unhemmed sackcloth to fine hemp; yet the feelings of all nine degrees of kinship are left without dissatisfaction. Could principle, as manifested in these relationships, admit even a hair’s breadth of deviation? In its distinctions between noble and lowly, from kings and dukes down to menial servants, ceremonial forms and insignia differ according to prescribed rules; yet no one dares contest the distinction between superior and inferior. Could principle, as manifested in these ranks, admit even the slightest displacement? Ritual has greater and lesser observances. Where principle resides, the greater cannot be diminished, nor the lesser augmented. Ritual has conspicuous and subtle observances. Where principle resides, the conspicuous cannot be concealed, nor the subtle magnified.
Such is the way ritual proceeds from what cannot be altered in principle. Thus, extended throughout the Four Seas, it provides a standard everywhere; transmitted through ten thousand generations, it remains free of defects. Those who say that ritual was devised to constrain the world have probably never…

Yet the Way is also vessels, and vessels are also the Way; they cannot be regarded as two separate things. Ritual is a vessel; its unalterable principle is the Way. Those who comprehend this surely understand the teaching concerning the Way and vessels. Earlier Confucian scholars said that the Record of Music could not have been written by anyone below Mencius in stature. Is this not indeed credible?
“A wife presides over service to one's parents: dare one fail to respect her? A son continues one's parents' line: dare one fail to respect him? title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
常情言之夫為妻綱妻從我者也奈何敬之殊
不知供衣服薦饋食宗廟之禮有待於備官而
妻固吾親之主也敢慢而不敬乎故必冕而親
迎以極體貌之隆敬妻所以敬吾親耳又孰不
曰父為子綱子我所生也胡為敬之殊不知承
宗祧嗣基業社稷之重必歸於適長而子固吾
親之後也敢忽而不敬乎故必冠于阼階而極
儀章之備敬子所以敬吾親耳夫君子豈特敬
其妻子哉於凡物之接固無不敬而惟敬其身
===
為尤大焉盖親也者吾身之本身也者吾親之
枝一氣相為流通生意未甞間斷身即親也又
敢不敬乎故必謹於言動使德積厥躬以為刑
妻之本慎爾樞機俾道成於已以為翼子之謀
惟恐虧體以辱吾親也輕身以傷吾親也其敬
之大為何如吁能敬其身是能孝其親而於妻
子盖不容於不敬矣行此三者豈不慊乎天下
已哉抑考孔子甞曰使臣以禮曰臨民以莊然
則臣民亦所當敬歟盖君之於臣民相須一體

punctuated: 常情言之，夫為妻綱，妻從我者也，奈何敬之？殊不知供衣服、薦饋食，宗廟之禮有待於備官，而妻固吾親之主也，敢慢而不敬乎？故必冕而親迎，以極體貌之隆。敬妻，所以敬吾親耳。又孰不曰父為子綱，子我所生也，胡為敬之？殊不知承宗祧、嗣基業，社稷之重必歸於適長，而子固吾親之後也，敢忽而不敬乎？故必冠于阼階，而極儀章之備。敬子，所以敬吾親耳。夫君子豈特敬其妻子哉？於凡物之接，固無不敬，而惟敬其身為尤大焉。盖親也者，吾身之本；身也者，吾親之枝。一氣相為流通，生意未甞間斷，身即親也，又敢不敬乎？故必謹於言動，使德積厥躬，以為刑妻之本；慎爾樞機，俾道成於已，以為翼子之謀。惟恐虧體以辱吾親也，輕身以傷吾親也。其敬之大為何如！吁！能敬其身，是能孝其親，而於妻子，盖不容於不敬矣。行此三者，豈不慊乎天下已哉？抑考孔子甞曰：「使臣以禮。」曰：「臨民以莊。」然則臣民亦所當敬歟？盖君之於臣民，相須一體。
translation_en:
…speaking from ordinary human sentiment, the husband is the guiding principle for the wife, and the wife is one who follows me: why should I respect her? Such a view fails to recognize that providing garments and presenting sacrificial food—the rites of the ancestral temple—depend upon a full complement of ritual offices. My wife is indeed the mistress who serves my parents: dare I treat her slightingly and without respect? Thus one must wear the ceremonial cap and personally receive the bride, showing her the utmost ceremonial honor. Respecting my wife is simply the means by which I respect my parents. Again, who does not say that the father is the guiding principle for the son, and that the son is one whom I have begotten: why should I respect him? Such a view fails to recognize that continuing the ancestral sacrifices and inheriting the family’s foundations and patrimony—the weighty responsibility for the altars of soil and grain—must fall to the eldest legitimate son. My son is indeed my parents’ successor: dare I neglect him and withhold respect? Thus one must perform his capping ceremony at the eastern steps, observing the fullest ceremonial forms. Respecting my son is simply the means by which I respect my parents.

Does the gentleman respect only his wife and son? In all his dealings with things, he is invariably respectful; yet respecting his own person is especially important. For my parents are the root of my person, and my person is a branch of my parents. A single vital force flows between us, and the impulse of life has never been interrupted. My person is my parents themselves: how could I dare not respect it? Thus one must be circumspect in speech and action, causing virtue to accumulate in one’s person as the foundation for setting an example to one’s wife; one must carefully attend to the pivots of speech and action, bringing the Way to fulfillment in oneself as the means of aiding one’s son. One fears only that injuring one’s body will disgrace one’s parents, or treating one’s person lightly will wound them. How great is such respect! Ah! To be able to respect one’s own person is to be able to show filial devotion to one’s parents; and toward one’s wife and son, one cannot but show respect. In practicing these three things, would one not satisfy all under Heaven?

Moreover, consider that Confucius once said, “Employ your ministers according to ritual,” and “Preside over the people with dignity.” Then are ministers and people also owed respect? For the ruler, his ministers, and his people depend upon one another and form a single body…

…all the more must he treat them with respect. Thus the Book of Documents emphasizes the foundation of the state, and the Book of Odes praises honored guests: such was the respect the former kings showed their ministers and people. As the age declined into the Spring and Autumn period, ritual instruction ceased to prevail. Rulers demeaned their ministers and oppressed their people, without understanding how to respect them. Consequently, their sentiments and intentions became estranged. Ministers sometimes put their rulers last, and the people sometimes broke free of those above them. In extreme cases, husbands and wives turned against one another, fathers and sons harmed one another, and the proper human relationships nearly ceased to exist. Confucius studied the rites of the Three Dynasties, wishing to illuminate the Kingly Way and rectify people’s hearts; he was especially devoted to the land of his parents. In telling Duke Ai this, he sought first to set the foundation right. Yet the words “show respect in all things” have a broad compass indeed. Those who consult antiquity in governing should take this as their mirror.

有見於斯道之全也，而後可以言天地矣。天地之大也，夫人能言之，而其所以為大者，未易言也。盖自其形而求之，見其為大；自其道而觀之，於是見其所以為大。散於萬而不見其不足，合於一而不見其有餘。迎而察之，莫得其所始；引而致之，莫究其所終。小德川流，大德敦化。嗚呼！此天地之所以為大也歟！嘗試論之：天如是其高也，地如是其厚也，上下之歲年如是其悠且久也。人以藐焉之身，生且死於其間，曰吾知其大，且知其所以為大，不幾於妄乎？噫！是非妄也，彼盖以人而知之也。盍觀諸吾夫子乎？堯□□
translation_en:
…its bounds, yet it is balanced, clear, and penetrating, as though something impelled the writer and would not let him refrain from speaking. Surely he has truly perceived what makes Heaven and Earth great! An excellent scholar! An excellent scholar!
Examiner Gu, Left Mentor of Virtue, comments: The writing is neither difficult nor abstruse, and the reasoning is straightforward and sound. At first it seems quite easy; examine it at leisure, however, and its interwoven structure and connections reveal both form and essential points, while the subtle Way becomes unmistakably apparent beyond the words. This is surely someone deeply versed in learning.
Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting, comments: The argument has firm foundations. In its opening and closing movements and its transformations, it seems impossible to measure by any rule, yet in the end it never departs from the rules. It is surely outstanding among the discourses of our time.
Only after perceiving this Way in its entirety can one speak of Heaven and Earth. Anyone can speak of the greatness of Heaven and Earth, but what makes them great is not easy to explain. If we investigate their form, we see that they are great; if we contemplate their Way, we then see what makes them great. Dispersed among the myriad things, it shows no insufficiency; gathered into one, it shows no excess. Going forth to meet and examine it, none can discover its beginning; tracing it onward, none can fathom its end. Its lesser powers flow like rivers; its greater powers bring about profound transformation. Ah! Is this not what makes Heaven and Earth great?
Let us attempt to discuss it. Heaven is so high; Earth is so thick; the years stretching into the past and future are so remote and enduring. A human being, with so insignificant a body, lives and dies between them. If he says, “I know their greatness, and I also know what makes them great,” does this not approach presumption? Ah! This is no presumption: he knows it through the human. Why not look to our Master, Confucius? Yao [two illegible characters] …

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
也文武也天之有時而地之有方也渾然具於
其一心而散為天下之萬事於是乎有動作禮
義威儀之則於是乎有君臣父子兄弟夫婦朋
友長幼之倫於是乎有易詩書禮樂春秋論語
之文布於一身而達之天下作於一時而垂之
萬世其事備矣雖然聖人於此亦有勞乎子貢
嘗窺而疑之盖將以為多學而識之者也夫子
從而决之曰非也予一以貫之嗚呼此夫子之
所以為聖而聖人之所以為大也歟知聖人之
===
所以為大則知天地之所以為大矣今夫天覆
於上地載於下日月寒暑盈虛代謝於其中而
萬物之洪者纖者動者植者形者色者類聚群
分生生化化不知其何所始而方未已也然豈
物物而雕刻之哉盖有為之者而莫知其所以
為之者矣故自其殊者而觀之高下之形往來
之運流峙之性飛躍之情粲然心目之間者萬
有不齊小德之川流也自其一者而言之天之
所以覆地之所以載日月之所以明寒暑之所

punctuated: 也，文武也，天之有時而地之有方也，渾然具於其一心，而散為天下之萬事。於是乎有動作禮義威儀之則，於是乎有君臣父子兄弟夫婦朋友長幼之倫，於是乎有《易》《詩》《書》《禮》《樂》《春秋》《論語》之文。布於一身而達之天下，作於一時而垂之萬世，其事備矣。雖然，聖人於此亦有勞乎？子貢嘗窺而疑之，盖將以為多學而識之者也。夫子從而决之曰：「非也，予一以貫之。」嗚呼！此夫子之所以為聖，而聖人之所以為大也歟！知聖人之所以為大，則知天地之所以為大矣。今夫天覆於上，地載於下，日月寒暑盈虛代謝於其中，而萬物之洪者、纖者、動者、植者、形者、色者，類聚群分，生生化化，不知其何所始，而方未已也。然豈物物而雕刻之哉？盖有為之者，而莫知其所以為之者矣。故自其殊者而觀之，高下之形，往來之運，流峙之性，飛躍之情，粲然心目之間者，萬有不齊，小德之川流也。自其一者而言之，天之所以覆，地之所以載，日月之所以明，寒暑之所
translation_en:
…and Kings Wen and Wu, Heaven’s seasons and Earth’s regions—all are integrally present within his single mind and unfold into the myriad affairs of the world. Thus there are standards for action, ritual propriety, righteousness, and dignified bearing; thus there are the relationships between ruler and minister, father and son, elder and younger brothers, husband and wife, friends, and seniors and juniors; thus there are the texts of the Book of Changes, Book of Odes, Book of Documents, Book of Rites, Book of Music, Spring and Autumn Annals, and Analects. Embodied in one person and extended throughout the world, brought forth in one age and handed down through ten thousand generations: these achievements are complete. Yet did the sage expend labor upon them? Zigong once glimpsed this and wondered, supposing that the Master was one who learned much and retained it in memory. The Master then resolved his doubt, saying: “No. I draw everything together with a single thread.” Ah! Is this not what makes the Master a sage, and what makes the sage great? To understand what makes the sage great is to understand what makes Heaven and Earth great.

Now Heaven covers above and Earth supports below. Within them, sun and moon, cold and heat wax and wane and succeed one another. The myriad things—large and small, moving and rooted, with their forms and colors—gather by kind and divide into groups, continually generating and transforming. We do not know where this began, and it has yet to cease. Yet could each thing have been individually carved into shape? There is surely that which brings this about, yet none knows how it does so. Thus, viewed in their diversity, the forms of things high and low, the movements of coming and going, the natures of things flowing and standing firm, and the dispositions of creatures flying and leaping—all that appears vividly before mind and eye—differ in myriad ways. This is “the lesser powers flowing like rivers.” Speaking of their unity, that by which Heaven covers, that by which Earth supports, that by which sun and moon shine, that by which cold and heat…

所以為大者如此苟未知天地請觀之聖人苟

聞文章小德之謂歟性與天道大德之謂歟子

translation_en:
…proceed, and the myriad things multiply and flourish: all issue from a single source, admitting not the slightest separation. This is the abundant transforming power of the greater virtue. When the one disperses into the myriad, the Way’s functioning is put into operation; when the myriad unite as one, the Way’s substance is established. Such is what makes Heaven and Earth great. If you do not yet understand Heaven and Earth, observe the sage; if you do not yet understand the sage, observing Heaven and Earth will suffice. Zigong once said: “The Master’s cultural accomplishments can be heard about; his words on human nature and the Way of Heaven cannot be heard.” Do “cultural accomplishments” refer to the lesser virtues? Do “human nature and the Way of Heaven” refer to the greater virtue? Zigong evidently gained some understanding of the transmitted teaching of the single thread running through all things, while Zisi’s composition of the Doctrine of the Mean truly elucidates the ultimate reaches of human nature and the Way. Alas! Its explanation is so detailed, yet students still admire heterodox teachings as lofty. Is what is said to be unavailable to hearing indeed not to be found within words?

Same as above.

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
瑣而放縱不羈所謂泛駕之馬若難控馭而步
驟自是不凡世有九方臯當得之於驪黄牝牡之
外矣
考試官左諭德顧批汪洋恣肆文不拘腐而
理亦暢達場中得此可以為難矣
考試官侍讀學士汪批以顯微之間立說識見
高甚從此肆筆數千言沛然不窮其學力過人遠矣
論曰明大道於顯微之間君子不得已而有言
也道在天地無終窮其在聖人以人而傳亦以
===
人而已以人而明亦以人而晦也聖賢不常生
而斯道可憂也矣子思子贊仲尼而終之以天
地之所以為大一言於乎顯微之間其示人以
斯道之的乎其真為天下萬世有不得已者乎
請推本而論之道果易言邪知者知之過愚者
不及知也道果難言邪百姓日用而不知耳是
道也何道也聖人之道也其即天地之道也其
即聖人天地之所以為大者也人知天地之大
而不知聖人之大知天地之大而不知其所以

論曰：明大道於顯微之間，君子不得已而有言也。道在天地，無終窮；其在聖人，以人而傳，亦以人而已；以人而明，亦以人而晦也。聖賢不常生，而斯道可憂也矣。子思子贊仲尼，而終之以天地之所以為大一言。於乎！顯微之間，其示人以斯道之的乎？其真為天下萬世有不得已者乎？請推本而論之。道果易言邪？知者知之過，愚者不及知也。道果難言邪？百姓日用而不知耳。是道也，何道也？聖人之道也，其即天地之道也，其即聖人天地之所以為大者也。人知天地之大，而不知聖人之大；知天地之大，而不知其所以
translation_en:
…pettiness, giving itself free rein without restraint. It is like the proverbial horse that breaks free of the traces: seemingly hard to control, yet its pace and gait are truly extraordinary. Were there a Jiufang Gao in the world, he would surely recognize its worth beyond considerations of black or yellow coat, mare or stallion.
Examiner Gu, Left Mentor, comments: Vast and freely flowing, the writing is unconfined by stale conventions, while its reasoning is lucid and unimpeded. Finding such a piece in the examination hall is indeed rare.
Examiner Wang, Reader-in-waiting, comments: By grounding his argument in the relation between the manifest and the subtle, the writer displays exceptionally lofty insight. From this starting point, he gives his brush free rein for several thousand words, pouring forth inexhaustibly. His scholarly attainments far surpass those of others.
The discourse reads: In elucidating the great Way between the manifest and the subtle, the gentleman speaks because he cannot do otherwise. Within Heaven and Earth, the Way has neither end nor limit. Among the sages, its transmission depends on people, and so too does its cessation; through people it is made clear, and through people it is obscured. Sages and worthies are not born in every age, and thus there is reason to fear for this Way. Master Zisi, in praising Zhongni, concludes with a statement about what makes Heaven and Earth great. Ah! In speaking of the manifest and the subtle, does he not show people the true object of this Way? Was he not truly compelled to speak for the sake of all under Heaven and the myriad generations to come? Allow me to trace this to its source and discuss it. Is the Way really easy to speak of? The knowing go too far in their understanding, while the foolish fall short of understanding it. Is the Way really difficult to speak of? The common people use it daily, yet simply do not know it. What Way is this? It is the Way of the sages; it is precisely the Way of Heaven and Earth; it is precisely what makes the sages and Heaven and Earth great. People know the greatness of Heaven and Earth but do not know the greatness of the sages. They know the greatness of Heaven and Earth but do not know what makes them so…

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
大猶未知也況聖人乎曰天地果大乎曰四時
之行大矣而行乎其間也日月之明大矣而明
乎其間也萬物之育大矣而覆載乎其間也天
地大也聖人果大乎曰聖人天地覆載中之一
物爾未足以為大也是以物不以道也以物則
聖人物也天地亦物也物莫有大於天地者聖
人固不得而與之準也以道則天地聖人一而
已矣道者何天地所由生以不窮者也鳶魚之
飛躍道乎其一體也夫婦之能知行道乎其一
===
事也率性之謂人物之不可離道乎其為也其
然也而未極聖人天地之全也然則四時之錯
行日月之代明萬物之並育道乎曰四時日月
萬物非道也而其行其明其育者道也其行其
明其育者非道而其錯行代明並育而不害不
悖者道也是道也顯之而不能使之顯也微之
而不能使之微也不離於有無而不可以為有
無也包乎天地之外而未嘗有外也通乎天地
之内而未嘗有内也先乎天地而始而莫知其

translation_en:
…great, one still does not understand them; how much more is this true of the sage? Someone asks, “Are Heaven and Earth truly great?” The reply is: “Great is the movement of the four seasons, yet they move within them. Great is the brightness of the sun and moon, yet they shine within them. Great is the growth of the myriad things, yet they are sheltered and borne within them. Heaven and Earth are great.” “Is the sage truly great?” The reply is: “The sage is merely one thing among all that Heaven shelters and Earth bears, and so cannot be accounted great.” This judges by things, not by the Way. In terms of things, the sage is a thing, and Heaven and Earth are also things. Among things, none is greater than Heaven and Earth, so the sage certainly cannot stand on an equal footing with them. In terms of the Way, however, Heaven, Earth, and the sage are simply one.

What is the Way? It is that through which Heaven and Earth generate life without exhaustion. Are the kite’s flight and the fish’s leap the Way? They are one embodiment of it. Is what ordinary husbands and wives can know and practice the Way? It is one instance of it. What is meant by following one’s nature, and what people and things cannot depart from—is this the Way? These are its workings and the manner of its being, but they do not exhaust the wholeness of the sage and of Heaven and Earth.

Then are the successive movements of the four seasons, the alternating light of the sun and moon, and the concurrent growth of the myriad things the Way? The reply is: “The four seasons, the sun and moon, and the myriad things are not the Way; that through which they move, shine, and grow is the Way. Their moving, shining, and growing are not the Way; that through which they move in succession, shine in alternation, and grow together without harming or conflicting with one another is the Way.”

This Way cannot be made manifest by treating it as manifest, nor can it be made hidden by treating it as hidden. It is inseparable from being and nonbeing, yet cannot be regarded as either being or nonbeing. It encompasses what lies outside Heaven and Earth, yet has never had an outside; it pervades what lies within Heaven and Earth, yet has never had an inside. It begins before Heaven and Earth, yet no one knows its …

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
先也後乎天地而終而莫知其後也易而無體
也神而無方也一而無二也自其一而散之以
為萬萬而斂之復歸於一一固一也萬亦一也
一在於萬萬物各一道也萬統於一萬物同一
道也故曰小德川流大德敦化天地之所以為
大也以道觀天地天地小也道不外乎天地而
凡天地間者皆道故曰顯微之間也道無終窮
而四時日月萬物相與無終窮信乎天地之為
大也其在聖人則夫居鄉黨在宗廟朝廷言動
===
威儀衣服飲食之則皆是道也安老懷少信友
得天下英才而教育之皆是道也行於魯厄於
陳蔡周流於齊楚宋衞之郊而必聞其政者皆
是道也其得邦家而行夏時乗殷輅服周冕樂
則韶舞立斯立綏斯來動斯和者皆是道也其
祖述堯舜憲章文武上律天時下襲水土以至
刪詩書定禮樂贊周易脩春秋者莫非是道也
故曰如天地之無不持載無不覆幬如四時之
錯行如日月之代明而本之則不外乎聖人之

punctuated:
先也，後乎天地而終，而莫知其後也。易而無體也，神而無方也，一而無二也。自其一而散之以為萬，萬而斂之復歸於一。一固一也，萬亦一也。一在於萬，萬物各一道也；萬統於一，萬物同一道也。故曰：「小德川流，大德敦化。」天地之所以為大也。以道觀天地，天地小也。道不外乎天地，而凡天地間者皆道，故曰：「顯微之間也。」道無終窮，而四時日月萬物相與無終窮，信乎天地之為大也。

其在聖人，則夫居鄉黨，在宗廟朝廷，言動威儀衣服飲食之則，皆是道也。安老懷少信友，得天下英才而教育之，皆是道也。行於魯，厄於陳蔡，周流於齊楚宋衞之郊，而必聞其政者，皆是道也。其得邦家而行夏時，乗殷輅，服周冕，樂則韶舞，立斯立，綏斯來，動斯和者，皆是道也。其祖述堯舜，憲章文武，上律天時，下襲水土，以至刪詩書，定禮樂，贊周易，脩春秋者，莫非是道也。故曰：「如天地之無不持載，無不覆幬；如四時之錯行，如日月之代明。」而本之，則不外乎聖人之
translation_en:
…what precedes it. It ends after Heaven and Earth, yet none knows what follows it. It changes without a fixed form; it is numinous without a fixed direction; it is one, without a second. From its unity it disperses into the myriad things; gathered back from the myriad things, it returns to unity. The one is indeed one, but the myriad are also one. The one is present in the myriad: each thing has its own Way. The myriad are united in the one: all things share the same Way. Hence it is said, “The lesser powers flow like rivers; the great power brings forth transformations in abundance.” This is what makes Heaven and Earth great. Viewed from the Way, Heaven and Earth are small. The Way does not lie outside Heaven and Earth, and everything between Heaven and Earth is the Way. Hence the saying, “Between the manifest and the hidden.” The Way has no end or limit, and the four seasons, the sun and moon, and the myriad things together likewise have no end or limit. Great indeed are Heaven and Earth!

As embodied in the sage, the rules governing his speech and action, dignified bearing, clothing, and food and drink, whether in his home community, the ancestral temple, or the court, are all this Way. Giving peace to the aged, cherishing the young, being trustworthy toward friends, and obtaining the finest talents under Heaven and educating them—all are this Way. His activity in Lu, his distress in Chen and Cai, his travels through the outskirts of Qi, Chu, Song, and Wei, and his invariably learning about their government—all are this Way. Were he to obtain a state to govern, his following the Xia calendar, riding in the Yin carriage, wearing the Zhou ceremonial cap, and choosing the Shao dance for music; his establishing the people so that they stand firm, bringing them peace so that they come to him, and stirring them so that they live in harmony—all are this Way. His transmitting the tradition of Yao and Shun, taking Kings Wen and Wu as his models, following the seasons of Heaven above and conforming to the waters and lands below, and even his editing the Book of Odes and Book of Documents, settling rites and music, elucidating the Changes of Zhou, and compiling the Spring and Autumn Annals—none of these is other than this Way. Hence it is said, “Like Heaven and Earth, which sustain and bear everything, cover and shelter everything; like the four seasons in their alternating course, and like the sun and moon shining in succession.” Yet traced to its root, it does not go beyond the sage’s…

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
一心也所謂吾道一以貫之是也自志學以至
從心自灑掃應對以至精義入神自明善誠身
以至經綸大經立大本知化育皆一之所為也
是道也即天地之大德敦化而小德川流者也
於乎此聖人之所以為大也孔子嘗曰知我者
其天乎曰天何言哉聖人固以大而自居矣其
曰予欲無言下學而上達則所謂顯微之間者
也窮高極遠而不知其止者荒於無而非道也
知者之過也物而不化者滯於有而非道也愚
===
者之不及也下此則日用而不知矣聖賢所以
必明是道而傳之者為吾人計也其亦為天地
計也是故堯以是傳之舜舜以是傳之禹湯文
武周公孔子而孔子則集大成者耳孔子傳之
曾子曾子傳之子思子思感世道之降知聖賢
之生不常不得已而筆之於書也自孟子以迄
于今孔氏之徒世守而傳之四時之常行日月
之常明萬物之常育而斯道賴以不墜人之為
人而不入於夷狄禽獸者謂非子思之功而誰

punctuated:
一心也。所謂「吾道一以貫之」是也。自志學以至從心，自灑掃應對以至精義入神，自明善誠身以至經綸大經、立大本、知化育，皆一之所為也。是道也，即天地之大德敦化而小德川流者也。於乎！此聖人之所以為大也。孔子嘗曰：「知我者，其天乎！」曰：「天何言哉！」聖人固以大而自居矣。其曰「予欲無言」、「下學而上達」，則所謂顯微之間者也。窮高極遠而不知其止者，荒於無而非道也，知者之過也；物而不化者，滯於有而非道也，愚者之不及也。下此，則日用而不知矣。
聖賢所以必明是道而傳之者，為吾人計也，其亦為天地計也。是故堯以是傳之舜，舜以是傳之禹、湯、文、武、周公、孔子，而孔子則集大成者耳。孔子傳之曾子，曾子傳之子思。子思感世道之降，知聖賢之生不常，不得已而筆之於書也。自孟子以迄于今，孔氏之徒世守而傳之。四時之常行，日月之常明，萬物之常育，而斯道賴以不墜。人之為人而不入於夷狄禽獸者，謂非子思之功而誰
translation_en:
…the single mind of the sage. This is what is meant by “My Way is threaded together by one principle.” From setting his heart upon learning to following his heart’s desires; from sprinkling and sweeping, answering and responding, to refining meaning and entering the realm of the numinous; from understanding goodness and making himself sincere to ordering the great norms, establishing the great foundation, and knowing the processes of transformation and nurture—all are the workings of this unity. This Way is precisely that by which Heaven and Earth transform abundantly through their great virtue, while their lesser virtues flow like streams. Ah! This is what makes the sage great. Kongzi once said, “Is it not Heaven that knows me?” He also said, “What does Heaven say?” The sage indeed regarded himself as possessing such greatness. His sayings “I wish to say nothing” and “I learn what is below and attain understanding of what is above” concern what is called the relation between the manifest and the subtle. To pursue the utmost heights and farthest reaches without knowing where to stop is to lose oneself in nothingness, and is not the Way: this is the excess of the knowing. To be bound to things without transformation is to be mired in being, and is not the Way: this is the shortcoming of the foolish. Below these are those who use it daily without knowing it.
The sages and worthies insisted on making this Way clear and transmitting it out of concern for us; they did so also out of concern for Heaven and Earth. Thus Yao transmitted it to Shun, and Shun transmitted it onward to Yu, Tang, Wen, Wu, Zhougong, and Kongzi; Kongzi brought it all together in its fullest achievement. Kongzi transmitted it to Zengzi, and Zengzi transmitted it to Zisi. Moved by the decline of the moral order, and knowing that sages and worthies are born only rarely, Zisi felt compelled to commit it to writing. From Mengzi down to the present, followers of Kongzi have preserved and transmitted it from generation to generation. The four seasons continue their regular course, the sun and moon continue to shine, and the myriad things continue to grow; through this transmission, the Way is kept from falling away. That human beings remain human and do not sink to the level of the Yi and Di peoples or of birds and beasts—if this is not Zisi’s achievement, then whose …

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄

punctuated: 綏猷允迪於先王，造士不遺於僻壤。甫及投戈之暇，遂弘鼓篋之休。士類傾心，巖阿生色。茲蓋伏遇英毅性成，聰明天啓，大孝寔同乎虞帝，丕烈克配於周王。遠惟藝祖開基，本於揖遜；近體高皇垂統，尤事表章。家有塾，黨有庠，謂教典必端於蒙士；興於詩，立於禮，庶德風肆被於成人。顧慚講授之迂，乃荷恩綸之寵。竊惟白鹿洞書院者，廢興凡幾，文獻足徵。在有唐，初維李渤隱居；迄五季，遂為廬山國學。入我昭代，益闡儒風，啟我前脩，每收治效。偕嵩陽、嶽麓、睢陽三院，並著聲稱。歷太平興國、咸平
translation_en:
…In Your peaceful governance, You faithfully follow the former kings; in nurturing scholars, You overlook no remote region. No sooner was there respite from laying down arms than You extended the blessings of learning, symbolized by beating the drum and opening book chests. Scholars turn wholeheartedly toward You, and even secluded mountain valleys gain new lustre. This is because we humbly encounter in Your Majesty one whose heroic resolution is innate and whose intelligence Heaven has awakened. Your great filial devotion truly equals that of the Emperor of Yu, and Your magnificent achievements match those of the king of Zhou. Looking far back, You recall how the Founding Ancestor established his foundations through ceremonial deference and abdication; looking nearer, You emulate Emperor Gao, who handed down the imperial succession and devoted particular attention to honouring and promoting learning. With a school in every residential community and an academy in every district, You hold that educational institutions must begin with untutored scholars; through being inspired by the Odes and established in ritual, You hope that the influence of virtue will spread widely among mature men. Yet, ashamed of the pedantry of our teaching, we have nevertheless received the honour of Your gracious decree.

We humbly consider that Bailudong Academy has undergone repeated decline and revival, amply attested by writings and worthy men. Under the Tang, it was initially the secluded residence of Li Bo; by the Five Dynasties, it had become the State School of Lushan. Under our illustrious dynasty, it further spread the Confucian tradition and inspired our worthy predecessors, repeatedly yielding benefits for governance. Together with the three academies of Songyang, Yuelu, and Suiyang, it enjoyed a distinguished reputation. During the Taiping Xingguo and Xianping reign periods…

褒錫頃罹兵燹之禍鞠為草莽之墟殘甓斷
碑每興嗟於往迹齋居廩食已寖復於

聖主之懷俯納儒臣之請謂有屋廬而無
勅額詎為經久之圖有生徒而無

寵冠門墻人爭覩為快焉喧傳衢道自兹煩

恩重於丘山
奎翰宸章翥鳳光回於雲漢榮並
先朝之飛白制踰遂古之汗青天祿校讎輝
分太乙藜火石渠臨決陋洗汲冢竹書炳
炳乎龜書馬圖皇皇乎天經地緯山若增
而高也
寵冠門墻人爭覩為快焉喧傳衢道自茲煩
覉神而呵護可以免風雨之漂揺〔臣等忝〕
竊師儒覩沾敎育敢不珍藏什襲瞻拜敬
punctuated: 兩朝再蒙褒錫。頃罹兵燹之禍，鞠為草莽之墟。殘甓斷碑，每興嗟於往迹；齋居廩食，已寖復於明時。仰厪聖主之懷，俯納儒臣之請，謂有屋廬而無勅額，詎為經久之圖；有生徒而無賜書，未稱褒嘉之意。一時載給，衆美洊臻。鈎鈴啓東壁之藏，琬琰搨西雍之本。琅函縹帙汗牛，恩重於丘山；奎翰宸章翥鳳，光回於雲漢。榮並先朝之飛白，制喻邃古之汗青。天禄校讎，輝分太乙藜火；石渠臨决，陋洗汲冢竹書。炳炳乎龜書馬圖，皇皇乎天經地緯。山若增而高也，寵冠門墻；人爭覩為快焉，喧傳衢道。自兹煩鬼神而呵護，可以免風雨之漂摇。臣等忝竊師儒，親沾教育，敢不珍藏什襲，瞻拜敬
translation_en:
…under the two reigns, it again received commendations and gifts. Recently it suffered the calamity of war and was reduced entirely to a wilderness of weeds. Broken bricks and shattered steles continually prompted sighs over its past; lodging for scholars and provisions from the granary have now gradually been restored in this enlightened age. It has graciously engaged the concern of our sage sovereign, who has condescended to accept the petition of his Confucian ministers. He considered that buildings without an imperially bestowed name plaque could hardly constitute a lasting provision, while students without imperially bestowed books did not adequately fulfill his intention to commend and encourage them. Both were now supplied together, and manifold blessings arrived in succession.

The hooks and bells [?] opened the collections of the Eastern Wall, the celestial library; fine jade tablets bore rubbings of exemplars from the western imperial academy. Precious book cases and pale-blue wrappers enclosed volumes enough to make oxen sweat beneath their weight: imperial grace weighed more heavily than hills and mountains. Imperial calligraphy and compositions, radiant as the literary constellation Kui, soared like phoenixes, their brilliance circling through the Milky Way. Their glory equaled the “flying-white” calligraphy of the former reign; the imperial compositions illuminated the histories of remote antiquity [?]. Collation in the Tianlu library shared the radiance of Taiyi’s burning goosefoot staff; judgments delivered in person at the Shiqu library swept away the crudeness of the bamboo texts from the tomb at Ji. How brilliant, like the writing borne by the tortoise and the diagram borne by the horse! How majestic, like the warp of Heaven and the weft of Earth!

The mountain seems to have gained in height, so supreme is the favor bestowed upon this seat of learning. People vie for the pleasure of seeing these gifts, and excited reports fill the streets. Henceforth even spirits will be called upon to guard them, and they may escape the buffeting of wind and rain. We, your servants, unworthily occupy the positions of teachers and scholars and have personally benefited from your instruction. How could we fail to treasure these gifts, wrapping them in many layers, and gaze upon them and bow in reverence…

…with reverence. Reciting by day and reflecting by night, we shall devote ourselves fully to contemplating and probing the learning of the sages, practice righteousness and attain the Way, hoping thereby to embellish Your Majesty’s imperial designs. We humbly wish that, serving as ruler and as teacher, you may promulgate the words of the August Ultimate as enduring norms and instructions; that, attaining renown and longevity, you may manifest the virtue celebrated in “Great Happiness” (Jia le), without error or forgetfulness. May you personally inherit the succession of the Way transmitted through the hundred kings and inaugurate lasting peace for ten thousand generations. Gazing toward Heaven and looking up to Your Sagely Majesty, we, your servants, cannot contain our intense joy and devotion. We respectfully submit this memorial to express our thanks for Your Majesty’s hearing.

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
聖祖立國貽謀為萬世慮至深且遠
列聖敬承如一日故海內晏然無事而不知
帝力之何有子能敷析而昌言之殆得於
涵育之深者歟
同考試官學正鄭批能誦
昭代之制之
訓略無遺者其究心於當世之故也久矣
考試官左諭德顧批三場俱優而五策英
議橫發皆有根據識見真老於世故者恨不能盡錄也
===
魁選若此可以為
國家得人賀

凡五策沛然議論慷慨馳騁今古溢出問目塲屋得此
為之喜躍不已策多可刻姑出此以例其餘擢冠多士可
以報
上矣
有天下之度然後能成天下之大功有萬
世之慮然後能建萬世之長策此我

translation_en:
…sagely founder established the state and bequeathed his plans, thinking profoundly and far ahead for ten thousand generations. The successive sage emperors have reverently carried them forward with unwavering constancy. Thus all within the seas enjoys peace, free from trouble, unaware of what the emperor’s power contributes. You have expounded this fully and spoken eloquently about it: surely this comes from the profound nurture you have received?

Associate Examiner Zheng, an Instructor, comments: “He can recite the institutions and instructions [?] of our illustrious dynasty with scarcely an omission. He must have long devoted his attention to the affairs of the present age.”

Examiner Gu, Left Admonisher, comments: “Excellent in all three sessions, he offers brilliant arguments in all five policy essays, each well grounded. His discernment truly shows seasoned understanding of worldly affairs. I regret that we cannot print them all. With such a candidate selected to head the list, we may congratulate the state on obtaining a worthy man.”

Examiner Wang, a Reader-in-waiting, comments: “After reading his work for the first two sessions, I already knew that his talent and spirit were extraordinary. His five policy essays flow abundantly; his arguments are spirited and forceful, ranging freely over past and present and extending beyond the questions posed. Finding such work in the examination hall fills me with irrepressible delight. Many of his policy essays deserve publication; for now, we print this one as a sample of the others. By placing him first among the candidates, we can repay His Majesty.”

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
太祖高皇帝所以功加于時德垂後裔動而世
爲天下道行而世爲天下法言而世爲天
下則有非漢祖唐宗所能彷彿其萬一者
也三代而降漢唐爲盛漢稱規模宏遠其
懲秦孤立大封同姓封三庶孽分天下半
則七國之釁實高帝啓之也唐號法制備
具而晋陽啓祚王明給封閨門之間多有
慙德則武韋之變乃太宗之身教也洪惟
我
===
太祖高皇帝用夏變夷繼天出治經綸妙用出
於一心文臣武將受其成筭若外戚不預
政
宗藩不治民兵戎大權歸之
朝廷有事則
命將出征事旋則束身歸第其規模大畧亦
可覩矣至於文章制度之詳見於職掌會
典諸書官領其事事歸於職上下相承內
外相制煥乎其可述也故百五十年間海

translation_en:
…why our Emperor Taizu Gao brought benefits to his age through his achievements and bequeathed his virtue to posterity: his movements served as a guide for all under Heaven for generations, his conduct as their model, and his words as their standard. In these things, the founding emperor of Han and Taizong of Tang could not approach even a ten-thousandth of his greatness.

After the Three Dynasties, Han and Tang were the most flourishing. Han was praised for the breadth and foresight of its grand design. Taking warning from Qin’s isolation, it extensively enfeoffed members of the imperial clan, granting fiefs to three sons of secondary consorts and dividing among them half the empire. Thus, it was Emperor Gao himself who sowed the seeds of the Rebellion of the Seven Kingdoms. Tang was reputed to possess a complete system of laws and institutions. Yet, when its imperial fortunes began at Jinyang, royal enfeoffments were granted [?, the wording here is garbled], and within the imperial household there was much shameful conduct. Thus, the upheavals involving Wu and Wei followed the example set by Taizong himself.

We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao transformed the barbarians through Chinese civilization and, succeeding to Heaven’s mandate, established his government. The masterful ordering of affairs issued from his mind alone; civil officials and military commanders received his fully formed plans. Imperial in-laws took no part in government; imperial princes did not govern the people; supreme military authority rested with the court. When trouble arose, commanders were ordered out on campaign; when the undertaking was concluded, they returned submissively to their residences. From these arrangements, the broad outlines of his grand design can be discerned.

The details of ceremonial forms and institutions appear in such books as Duties of Offices (Zhizhang) and Collected Statutes (Huidian). Officials undertook their respective affairs, and each affair fell within the duties of an office. Superiors and subordinates supported one another, while authorities at the capital and outside it checked one another. How splendid these arrangements are to recount! title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
内晏然相安於無事愚以為非有天下之
度者不能成此功也又嘗與侍臣商確今
古且謂漢無外戚閹寺之權唐無藩鎮夷
狄之禍國何能滅朕觀往古深用為戒其
曰不惑聲色嚴宫闈之禁貴賤有體恩不
掩義則所以戒女寵也其曰不牽私愛惟
賢是用苟干政典裁以至公則所以待外
戚也其曰閹寺便習職在掃除供給使令
不假兵柄則所以御近習也其曰上下相
===

移則所以防權臣也財歸有司兵必待符
而調則藩鎮無跋扈之憂脩武備謹邊防
來則禦之去不窮追則夷狄無侵暴之虞
凡古今治亂興亡之故皆决於此數言使
漢唐季世之君與聞乎此則至今存可也

列聖相承恪守一道所以基
punctuated:
内晏然，相安於無事。愚以為非有天下之度者，不能成此功也。又嘗與侍臣商確今古，且謂：「漢無外戚閹寺之權，唐無藩鎮夷狄之禍，國何能滅？朕觀往古，深用為戒。」其曰「不惑聲色，嚴宫闈之禁，貴賤有體，恩不掩義」，則所以戒女寵也；其曰「不牽私愛，惟賢是用，苟干政典，裁以至公」，則所以待外戚也；其曰「閹寺便習，職在掃除，供給使令，不假兵柄」，則所以御近習也；其曰「上下相維，大小相制，防耳目之壅蔽，謹威福之下移」，則所以防權臣也。財歸有司，兵必待符而調，則藩鎮無跋扈之憂；脩武備，謹邊防，來則禦之，去不窮追，則夷狄無侵暴之虞。凡古今治亂興亡之故，皆决於此數言。使漢唐季世之君與聞乎此，則至今存可也。愚故以為非有萬世之慮者，不能建此策也。
列聖相承，恪守一道，所以基
translation_en:
…within the realm all was peaceful, and people lived together in undisturbed tranquillity. In my humble view, only someone whose breadth of vision encompassed all under Heaven could have accomplished this. He also once discussed past and present with his attendant ministers, saying: “Had the Han been free of the power of imperial in-laws and eunuchs, and the Tang free of the calamities caused by regional military commands and foreign peoples, how could those dynasties have perished? I examine the past and take its lessons deeply to heart.” His words, “Do not be beguiled by music and beauty; strictly enforce the prohibitions of the inner palace; maintain proper distinctions between high and low; do not let affection override righteousness,” provided a safeguard against the influence of favored women. His words, “Do not be swayed by private affection; employ only the worthy; if anyone interferes with the established order of government, judge the matter with complete impartiality,” prescribed how to treat imperial in-laws. His words, “Eunuchs are familiar with personal service; their duties lie in sweeping and cleaning, supplying necessities, and carrying out commands; do not entrust them with military authority,” prescribed how to control intimate attendants. His words, “Let superiors and subordinates sustain one another, and greater and lesser authorities check one another; guard against the obstruction of the ruler’s eyes and ears, and take care that the power to punish and reward does not pass down to subordinates,” provided a safeguard against overmighty ministers. When finances are entrusted to the responsible offices, and troops are mobilized only upon receipt of a tally, there need be no fear of insubordination by regional military commands. When military preparedness is maintained and frontier defenses are carefully guarded, when invaders are resisted upon arrival but not pursued relentlessly upon withdrawal, there need be no fear of invasion and violence by foreign peoples. All the causes of order and disorder, rise and fall, past and present, hinge upon these few statements. Had the rulers of the final years of the Han and Tang been able to hear them, their dynasties might have survived to this day. Thus, in my humble view, only someone whose foresight extended through ten thousand generations could have established this policy.
The successive sage emperors have inherited the throne and scrupulously upheld this single Way, thereby laying the foundation …

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
大命而垂鴻休者其淵源所自深且遠矣易
曰首出庶物萬國咸寧詩曰訏謨定命遠猶辰告聖
人作之我
高皇帝有焉詩曰不愆不忘率由舊章又曰永
言孝思孝思維則願以為億萬世之
神孫獻
第二問
同考試官教諭敖批究心於古帝王我
===
祖宗心學之微條答甚詳而詞氣簡勁誦之知為佳士
同考試官教諭周批我
祖宗務學正心以為
聖子神孫萬世之法真與古帝王同一揆書生盖鮮知之此策敷答無遺
而文亦可錄且初二場皆稱葩經士子莫之先矣
同考試官教諭柯批該博古
今貫穿經史文氣沛乎有餘决非初學可到
考試官左諭德顧批得主司發策之旨而
其言明白剴切刻之不為無補

曰首出庶物萬國咸寧詩曰莫莫大猷聖
人作之我
高皇帝有焉詩曰不愆不忘率由舊章又曰永
言孝思孝思維則顧以爲億萬世之

第二問
同考試官教諭敖　批〔究心於古帝王我〕
祖宗心學之微條荅甚詳而詞氣簡勁誦之知爲佳士
===
同考試官教諭周　批〔我〕
祖宗務學正心以爲
聖子神孫萬世之法真與古帝王同一揆書生盖鮮知之此策敷荅無遺
而文亦可錄且初二場皆稱葩經士子莫之先矣
同考試官教諭柯　批〔該博古〕
今貫穿經史文氣沛乎有餘决非初學可到
考試官左諭德顧　批〔得主司發策之旨而〕
其言明白剴切刻之不爲無補
punctuated:
大命而垂鴻休者，其淵源所自深且遠矣。《易》曰：「首出庶物，萬國咸寧。」《詩》曰：「訏謨定命，遠猶辰告。」聖人作之，我高皇帝有焉。《詩》曰：「不愆不忘，率由舊章。」又曰：「永言孝思，孝思維則。」願以為億萬世之神孫獻。
第二問
同考試官教諭敖批：究心於古帝王、我祖宗心學之微，條答甚詳，而詞氣簡勁，誦之知為佳士。
同考試官教諭周批：我祖宗務學正心，以為聖子神孫萬世之法，真與古帝王同一揆。書生盖鮮知之。此策敷答無遺，而文亦可錄。且初二場皆稱葩經士子，莫之先矣。
同考試官教諭柯批：該博古今，貫穿經史，文氣沛乎有餘，决非初學可到。
考試官左諭德顧批：得主司發策之旨，而其言明白剴切，刻之不為無補。
translation_en:
…the great Mandate and bequeathed abundant blessings: their origins are deep and far-reaching indeed. The Book of Changes says, “He emerges foremost among all beings, and the myriad states are all at peace.” The Book of Odes says, “Great counsels establish the Mandate; far-reaching plans are announced at the proper time.” A sage initiates it: our Emperor Gao exemplified this. The Book of Odes says, “Neither erring nor forgetting, follow the established statutes.” It also says, “Ever cherish filial thoughts; filial thoughts are the model.” I wish to offer these words to his divine descendants for countless generations.
Second Question
Comment by Associate Examiner Ao, Instructor: He has carefully investigated the subtleties of the learning of the mind practiced by the ancient emperors and kings and by our dynastic ancestors. His answers to the individual points are very detailed, while his language is concise and forceful. Reading it aloud, one knows him to be an outstanding scholar.
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhou, Instructor: Our dynastic ancestors devoted themselves to learning and rectifying the mind, thereby providing an enduring model for their sage sons and divine descendants. They truly followed the same principles as the ancient emperors and kings. Few scholars, however, understand this. This policy essay develops its answers without omission, and its writing also merits inclusion. Moreover, his work in both the first and second sessions was commendable; among candidates specializing in the Book of Odes, none surpasses him.
Comment by Associate Examiner Ke, Instructor: His knowledge ranges broadly across past and present and draws together the Classics and histories. His writing overflows with vigor. This is certainly beyond the reach of a beginner.
Comment by Examiner Gu, Left Mentor: He has grasped the intent behind the chief examiner’s policy question, and his words are clear, pertinent, and earnest. Publishing it in print will certainly be of some benefit.

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官侍讀學士汪批善敷陳末寓忠愛之
意足占所蘊
人君欲治天下正其心而已矣欲正其心
務於學而已矣夫君心天下之大本也天
下之治忽係於心心之邪正本於學上古
帝王曁我
祖宗心學淵微先後一揆是以天下善治而道
德功烈垂休無窮漢唐宋諸君不知務學
以正其心是以事功卑汚名譽不終而卒
===
詒後世非笑於乎可不鑒哉請因執事之
問而陳之自古及今聖治之善莫過於唐
虞而君德之盛亦莫過於堯舜禹湯文武
善法堯舜者也是故克勤於邦克儉於家
禹豈湎於旨酒者乎防微杜漸曰為後世
慮宜爾也以義制事以禮制心湯豈黷於
苞苴者乎省愆思咎曰遇災而懼宜爾也
樂天知命不顯維德也獻女釋囚閔夭之
徒自獻耳文王何歁乎建極錫福無競維

徒自獻耳文王何歉乎建極錫福無競維
punctuated:
考試官侍讀學士汪批：善敷陳，末寓忠愛之意，足占所蘊。
人君欲治天下，正其心而已矣；欲正其心，務於學而已矣。夫君心，天下之大本也。天下之治忽係於心，心之邪正本於學。上古帝王曁我祖宗，心學淵微，先後一揆。是以天下善治，而道德功烈垂休無窮。漢唐宋諸君不知務學以正其心，是以事功卑汚，名譽不終，而卒詒後世非笑。於乎，可不鑒哉？請因執事之問而陳之。自古及今，聖治之善莫過於唐虞，而君德之盛亦莫過於堯舜。禹湯文武，善法堯舜者也。是故克勤於邦，克儉於家，禹豈湎於旨酒者乎？防微杜漸，曰為後世慮，宜爾也。以義制事，以禮制心，湯豈黷於苞苴者乎？省愆思咎，曰遇災而懼，宜爾也。樂天知命，不顯維德也。獻女釋囚，閔夭之徒自獻耳，文王何歁乎？建極錫福，無競維
translation_en:
Examiner Wang, Academician Expositor-in-waiting, comments: “The exposition is skillful. Its conclusion conveys loyal devotion, sufficient to reveal what the writer holds within.”
If a ruler wishes to govern All-under-Heaven, he need only rectify his mind; if he wishes to rectify his mind, he need only apply himself to learning. The ruler’s mind is the great foundation of All-under-Heaven. Order and disorder throughout the realm depend upon his mind; whether his mind is deviant or upright depends upon his learning. The ancient emperors and kings, together with our imperial ancestors, possessed profound and subtle learning of the mind, following the same standard across the ages. Thus All-under-Heaven was well governed, and their moral virtue and glorious achievements bequeathed blessings without end. The rulers of the Han, Tang, and Song did not understand that they must apply themselves to learning to rectify their minds. Consequently, their achievements were base, their reputations did not endure, and they ultimately incurred the ridicule of later generations. Alas, should we not take warning? Allow me to expound upon this in response to your question.
From antiquity to the present, no sagely government has surpassed that of Tang and Yu, nor has any ruler’s virtue surpassed that of Yao and Shun. Yu, Tang, King Wen, and King Wu excelled in taking Yao and Shun as their models. Thus, “diligent in affairs of state and frugal in his household”—could Yu have been one to indulge in fine wine? He guarded against the slightest beginnings of wrongdoing and checked their growth; to say that he was concerned for later generations is fitting. “Regulating affairs through righteousness and regulating the mind through ritual propriety”—could Tang have sullied himself with bribes? He examined his faults and reflected upon his errors; to say that he felt fear when calamity struck is fitting. Rejoicing in Heaven and understanding its mandate: “How illustrious was his virtue!” As for presenting a woman to secure a prisoner’s release, it was Min Yao [?] and his companions who made the offering on their own; how was King Wen deceitful? Establishing the supreme standard and bestowing blessings: “Unrivalled was his…”

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
烈也厎貢厥獒西旅自貢耳武王奚累乎
之數聖人者學已至矣而憂勤之念不息
心已正矣而操存之功不忘觀其執厥中
而敷文命也顧天命而脩人紀也危平易
傾之道演於易也敬怠義欲之戒受於丹
書也德業之盛與天無極有由然哉漢唐
宋諸君不知法堯舜者也是故成帝外雖
尊嚴而內則湛於酒色陽阿禍水莫止披
香博士之唾漢業之遂衰宜也玄宗初雖
===
勵精而未幾溺於嬖幸華清麗質久垂桞
城胡孽之涎唐祚之不移幸也明帝尊師
重傅正坐自講似矣而迎佛書於天竺以
汙中夏文明之統右文者固若是乎憲宗
銳意勤政削平僭叛得矣而餌丹藥於方
士以速近習慘烈之變願治者固若是乎
瓊林之財大盈之積如民之膏血何不免
引虎軀而入室也德宗之聰明安在哉寶
籙之侈靡艮嶽之竒麗如國之膏肓何矧

之數聖人者學已至矣而憂勤之念不息
心已正矣而操存之功不忘觀其執厥中
而敷文命也顧天命而脩人紀也危平易

===
勵精而末甚溺於嬖幸華清驪質久謳柳
城胡孽之誕唐祚之不移幸也明帝尊師
重傳正坐自講似矣而迎佛書於天竺以
汙中夏文明之統右文者固若是乎憲宗

籙之侈靡艮嶽之奇麗如國之膏肓何翊
punctuated: 烈也。厎貢厥獒，西旅自貢耳，武王奚累乎？之數聖人者，學已至矣，而憂勤之念不息；心已正矣，而操存之功不忘。觀其執厥中而敷文命也，顧天命而脩人紀也，危平易傾之道演於《易》也，敬怠義欲之戒受於《丹書》也，德業之盛，與天無極，有由然哉！漢唐宋諸君，不知法堯舜者也。是故成帝外雖尊嚴，而內則湛於酒色，陽阿禍水，莫止披香博士之唾，漢業之遂衰宜也。玄宗初雖勵精，而未幾溺於嬖幸，華清麗質，久垂桞城胡孽之涎，唐祚之不移幸也。明帝尊師重傅，正坐自講，似矣，而迎佛書於天竺，以汙中夏文明之統，右文者固若是乎？憲宗銳意勤政，削平僭叛，得矣，而餌丹藥於方士，以速近習慘烈之變，願治者固若是乎？瓊林之財，大盈之積，如民之膏血何？不免引虎軀而入室也，德宗之聰明安在哉？寶籙之侈靡，艮嶽之竒麗，如國之膏肓何？矧
translation_en:
…were his mighty achievements. As for the presentation of that mastiff, the western Lü offered it of their own accord: what fault could attach to King Wu? These several sages had already attained the highest learning, yet their concern and diligence never ceased; their hearts were already rectified, yet they never neglected the work of holding fast to and preserving them. Consider how they held to the mean and spread civil instruction, attended to Heaven’s mandate and cultivated human relationships; how the principle that apprehension brings security while complacency brings downfall was expounded in the Book of Changes; and how admonitions concerning reverence and indolence, righteousness and desire, were received from the Cinnabar Writing. There was indeed a reason why the fullness of their virtue and achievements was as boundless as Heaven!

The various rulers of the Han, Tang, and Song did not know how to emulate Yao and Shun. Thus Emperor Cheng, though outwardly dignified, inwardly wallowed in wine and sex. The “calamitous waters” of Yang’a could not escape the spittle of the Erudite of the Pixiang Hall [?]; it was fitting that the Han’s imperial enterprise should consequently decline. Xuanzong initially applied himself diligently, but before long became immersed in his favorites. The beauty at Huaqing had long made the barbarian villain from Liucheng drool; it was fortunate that the Tang did not lose the throne. Emperor Ming honored teachers and esteemed tutors, sitting upright and personally lecturing: this seemed proper. Yet he brought Buddhist scriptures from Tianzhu, thereby defiling the succession of civilized learning in the Central Lands. Is this really how one honors culture? Xianzong resolutely applied himself to government and subdued usurpers and rebels: this was commendable. Yet he consumed elixirs supplied by masters of esoteric arts, thereby hastening a brutal catastrophe at the hands of his intimate attendants. Is this really how one aspires to good government?

What did the wealth of the Qionglin Treasury and the stores of the Daying Treasury mean for the people’s lifeblood? He could not avoid drawing a tiger into his own chamber. Where was Dezong’s intelligence? What did the extravagance of Baolu and the extraordinary splendor of Genyue do to remedy the state’s mortal sickness? How much more so…

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
復决藩籬以媚盜也徽宗之技能奚用哉
之數君者氣質用事而不知所以務於學
情欲為主而不知所以正其心故倏而明
倏而昏倏而彊倏而懦用君子則治任小
人則亂崇正道則為中國惑邪說則為夷
狄身名俱辱而詒笑後世無足怪矣洪惟

translation_en:
…and further breached the protective barriers to curry favor with bandits. Of what use were Emperor Huizong’s talents and accomplishments? These several rulers [?] let their temperamental dispositions govern their actions and did not know how to apply themselves to learning; they let their passions and desires take command and did not know how to rectify their hearts. Thus they were suddenly discerning, suddenly benighted; suddenly strong, suddenly weak. When they employed exemplary men, there was order; when they entrusted affairs to petty men, there was disorder. When they honored the correct Way, theirs was the civilized Central Realm; when deluded by heterodox teachings, they became barbarians. That both their persons and their reputations suffered disgrace, making them objects of ridicule for later generations, is hardly surprising.
We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao founded the realm, and Emperor Taizong Wen brought peace to the state. Their standards and plans surpassed those of Yu and King Wen; their achievements and renown exceeded those of Tang and King Wu. The successive sage emperors continued their work, bringing ever greater glory to that inheritance. Truly, this has been a moment of cosmic renewal, when completion gives way to a new beginning. What you, honored examiners, call the methods of self-cultivation and the essentials of steadfast adherence—establishing the supreme standard for those who follow and bequeathing a ruling tradition to posterity—surely cannot lie outside diligent learning through which to rectify the heart?
I have heard that, in the intervals between attending to government, our imperial ancestors would regularly take their places in an informal palace hall and summon Confucian officials to discuss the principles of the Classics and refine their understanding of the Way of governance. Even deep within the palace, sometimes as late as the second watch of the night, they would still examine ancient writings, investigate the subtle teachings of the sages and worthies, and scrutinize the successes and failures of earlier dynasties as lessons. 老、方術、聚斂、土木，凡漢唐宋諸君所為，非惟不發之於事，抑亦不萌之於心。
太祖嘗曰：「人君一心，治化之本。存諸中者無堯舜之心，欲施於政者有堯舜之治，不可得也。」
太宗嘗曰：「人君誠不可有所好樂。一有好樂，泥而不反，則慾必勝理。若心能靜虛，事来則應，事去如明鏡止水，自然純是天理。朕每退朝，未嘗不思管束此心為切要。」大哉，王言乎！是即危微精一之旨，而脩己安百姓、致中和位天地育萬物之道也。非深體篤行，實嘗用力於是，其能言之親切如此乎？心學淵源，父子授受，是以道德功烈直追堯舜而並駕焉。於乎休哉！今，天子聖學緝熈，正心圖治，所以光前而啓後者，無容喙矣。愚則以為欲法堯舜，但法
translation_en:
…Daoism, esoteric arts, extracting wealth, and building projects—all those things pursued by the rulers of the Han, Tang, and Song—were neither put into practice nor even allowed to take root in their minds.
Taizu once said: “The ruler’s heart is the foundation of governance and moral transformation. If what he harbors within is not the heart of Yao and Shun, yet he wishes to achieve the governance of Yao and Shun in his administration, this cannot be attained.”
Taizong once said: “A ruler truly must not have particular pleasures or preferences. Once he has such preferences and becomes mired in them without turning back, desire will inevitably overcome principle. If his heart can remain still and empty, responding when affairs arise and, when they pass, resembling a bright mirror or still water, it will naturally consist wholly of heavenly principle. Whenever I withdraw from court, I never fail to reflect that keeping this heart under control is the essential task.” How great are these royal words! This is precisely the purport of the teaching that the human heart is precarious and the heart of the Way subtle, requiring refinement and singleness of purpose. It is also the Way of cultivating oneself to bring peace to the common people, and of attaining equilibrium and harmony so that Heaven and Earth take their proper places and all things flourish. Had he not deeply apprehended this, earnestly practiced it, and actually devoted effort to it, could he have spoken of it with such intimate understanding? This learning of the heart had a profound source, transmitted from father to son. Thus their virtue and glorious achievements directly followed those of Yao and Shun and stood alongside them. Ah, how splendid!
Now the Son of Heaven continually illuminates his sagely learning, rectifies his heart, and strives for good government. As for how he brings glory to his predecessors and opens the way for his successors, there is nothing for me to add. In my humble view, however, whoever wishes to emulate Yao and Shun need only emulate…

理財，財以聚眾，眾以守邦，此百王不易之常道也。執事發策，有及於財用，殆非口談玄理、錢穀為迂者矣。敢不攄所聞見以對？
今夫天下之土地，古猶今也；其財用，古猶今也。若以宋言之，北遼西夏割據中土，其視今日一統之盛，蓋甚劣矣。而其經費之大者，有歲幣，有郊賚，又有祠祿，皆今日之所無者。地過於昔，而用減焉，是宜今日之財，陳腐不可勝食，貫朽不可勝用。而上下之間，猶皇皇以匱乏為憂，此誠所未喻也。傳曰：「生之者眾，食之者寡，為之者疾，用之者舒，則財恒足矣。」今日之所以不足者，毋乃與斯言戾乎？

translation_en:
…to regulate wealth; wealth serves to gather the people, and the people serve to defend the state. This is the constant Way, unchanged through a hundred reigns. Your examination question touches upon public finances: surely you are not among those who speak only of abstruse principles and regard matters of money and grain as beneath their concern. How could I fail to set forth what I have heard and observed in reply?
The land under Heaven was much the same in antiquity as it is today; so too were its financial resources and expenditures. Take the Song dynasty: the Liao in the north and the Xia in the west occupied portions of the central lands. Compared with the flourishing unity of the realm today, its circumstances were decidedly inferior. Yet its major expenditures included annual payments to neighboring states, rewards bestowed at the suburban sacrifices, and stipends for temple sinecures—all expenses that do not exist today. Our territory exceeds that of the past, while our expenditures are smaller. Accordingly, today's wealth ought to consist of grain so abundant that it spoils before it can all be eaten, and cash so plentiful that its strings rot before it can all be spent. Yet high and low alike remain anxiously concerned about shortages. This I truly cannot understand. The Commentary says: “If those who produce are many and those who consume are few, if production is swift and expenditure slow, wealth will always suffice.” Might today's insufficiency arise precisely because we act contrary to these words?
There are three approaches to providing for a state, as Su Shi explained. To maintain reserves sufficient for nine years, ordinarily left untouched, is to plan for ten thousand generations. For one year's revenue barely to meet one year's expenditure is to plan only for the moment. As for the lowest approach, which lacks foresight altogether, it sets revenue according to expenditure: whenever resources fail to meet expenses, still more is extracted. Though all under Heaven is tranquil and free from great calamities, it resorts entirely to the policies of a declining…

不終月之計也今之國計肉食者謀之非

世苟且之政，不知有急則將何以加之？此不終月之計也。今之國計，肉食者謀之，非藿食者之所知也。然竊見夫入粟鬻爵之令、徵逋預借之法，亦往往見之行矣，得不有近於所謂苟且之政乎？害財有三冗，則論者多言之：朝多倖位，事有剰員，此吏之冗也；養之數世，徒坐食以病農，用之一旦，或不足以禦敵，此兵之冗也；或好興作，或倖邉功，或濫賞予，或佞神佛，此費之冗也。

今日之冗，廟堂方議之，非草茅之所敢預也。竊見諸司有定員，而武功之賞大濫；軍士多失伍，而食粮之籍日增。其他不急之務、無名之費，盖未暇悉數也。則於是三冗者，得無仝乎？唐李吉甫為《元和國計錄》，丁謂因之為《景德會計錄》，林特作於祥符，田况作於皇祐，韓絳作於熈寧，蘇轍作於元祐，所以總括天下財賦出入之數，而周知其有無多寡
translation_en:
…the makeshift policies of a declining age, without knowing what further measures could be taken if an emergency arose. This is a plan that will not last out a month. As for the state's finances today, those who eat meat deliberate upon them; they are beyond the knowledge of those who subsist on bean leaves. Yet I have privately observed that orders granting rank in exchange for grain and selling titles, and measures for collecting tax arrears and borrowing against future revenues, are repeatedly put into practice. Do these not approach what are called makeshift policies? Commentators have often spoken of the three forms of excess that damage the finances. At court, many hold posts through favoritism, and offices have superfluous personnel: this is excess in officialdom. Soldiers are maintained for generations, merely consuming provisions without working and burdening the farmers; yet when suddenly called upon, they may prove incapable of resisting the enemy: this is excess in the military. Some delight in construction projects, some seek lucky gains through frontier exploits, some bestow rewards indiscriminately, and some lavish devotion upon gods and Buddhas: this is excess in expenditure.

The court is now deliberating upon today's excesses; such matters are not for an untutored subject outside official life to presume to intervene in. Yet I have privately observed that, although the various offices have fixed staffing quotas, appointments awarded for military merit are grossly excessive. Many soldiers have left their units, yet the rolls of those drawing grain rations grow daily. As for other nonessential undertakings and expenditures without justification, there has scarcely been time to enumerate them all. Are these not the same as those three forms of excess? Li Jifu of the Tang compiled the Record of State Finances of the Yuanhe Era. Following his example, Ding Wei compiled the Fiscal Accounts of the Jingde Era. Lin Te compiled such a work during the Xiangfu era, Tian Kuang during Huangyou, Han Jiang during Xining, and Su Zhe during Yuanyou. These works brought together the figures for revenue and expenditure in money and grain throughout the realm, providing comprehensive knowledge of what was available and what was lacking, and of the amounts involved…

考試官侍讀學士汪批：善於擇術，故能答之詳
translation_en:
…thereby providing a basis for increasing or reducing allocations. The responsible officials could thus understand the past while administering the present, and determine state expenditure through annual accounting. If we now truly followed these examples, examining the successive sage emperors’ reigns down to the present day—how much revenue came in each year, how much was spent each year, which expenditures were greatest, and which economies should take priority—all would surely become clear to the mind’s eye, without any need to seek elsewhere. In the Rites of Zhou, the Controller-General of Accounts cross-checks daily accounts to assess each day’s accomplishments, uses monthly summaries to assess each month’s accomplishments, and uses annual accounts to assess each year’s accomplishments. In this way he gains comprehensive knowledge of administration throughout the realm and advises the king and the Grand Steward on dismissals and appointments. Alas! How could this undertaking be delayed or treated as insignificant?

Fourth Question

君子為善有心於徼福乎曰非也小人為
惡有心於蹈禍乎曰亦非也善者福之基
也惡者禍之媒也善不與福期而福自集
惡不與禍期而禍自至此理之必然也故
君子非私其子孫而詒之以為善之福小

者主張於其間耳是以古之哲人慎於擇

之謀而為子孫千百世計者誠有見乎此
也執事發此策詢多士將因其言以察其
心術之微耳請試陳之子孫之於人大矣
統緒基業吾受之於先祖者孰承而傳之

translation_en:
…His other policy essays are equally good and merit acceptance.

When a gentleman does good, does he intend to seek blessings? The answer is no. When a petty man does evil, does he intend to incur disaster? The answer is likewise no. Goodness is the foundation of blessings; evil is the means by which disaster comes. Goodness makes no appointment with blessings, yet blessings gather of themselves; evil makes no appointment with disaster, yet disaster arrives of itself. This is the inevitable working of principle. Thus, it is not out of partiality toward his descendants that the gentleman bequeaths to them the blessings of doing good; nor is it out of hatred for his descendants that the petty man afflicts them with the disasters of doing evil. Rather, the paths they pursue differ, and the outcomes they encounter diverge. Something that acts without anyone causing it to act governs what happens between the two. Thus the wise men of antiquity were careful in choosing their course of conduct. They did not yield to immediate considerations but constantly considered what would follow their deaths; they planned not merely for the morning and evening, but for their descendants over hundreds and thousands of generations. Truly, they perceived this principle.

You, honored examiners, have posed this policy question to the assembled candidates in order to discern, through their words, the subtleties of their minds and intentions. Allow me to attempt an explanation. Descendants are of great importance to a person! Who will inherit and transmit the lineage and patrimony that we have received from our ancestors? The answer is our descendants. Thus, among the wise and foolish alike, past and present, who has not thought of his descendants? It is only in how they plan for them that they differ.

Xiao He rose to the position of Chancellor of State, yet did not build walls and houses for his descendants. He said: “If later generations are worthy, let them emulate my frugality; if they are unworthy, let there be nothing for powerful families to seize.” Was Xiao He truly wise? Then his…

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
言可以鑒矣䟽廣懸車太傅不為子孫益
産業曰賢而多財則損其志愚而多財則
益其過廣果賢邪則其言可以省矣刺史
問龐德公何以遺子孫曰人皆遺之以危
吾獨遺之以安雖所遺不同未為無所遺
也夫以耕稼為安則遺子孫以官祿者非
危乎故人請楊伯起為子孫開産業曰使
後世稱為清白吏子孫以此遺之不亦厚
乎夫以清白為厚則遺子孫以貨賄者非
===
薄乎母績而勸以自安公甫文伯之孝也
奚至於絶嗣賢母之以身教其言固如此
爾君違不忘諫之以德臧哀伯之忠也奚
必於有後賢臣之自天佑其理固如此爾
王業偏安於鼎足是豈大丈夫之志哉其
曰鞠躬盡瘁又奚暇私家衣食之謀即此
以觀管樂之比盖自道焉爾兵權頓釋於
杯酒夫亦保全功臣之道哉雖曰成功不
居顧得世享田宅之利由是以知韓彭之

punctuated:
言可以鑒矣。䟽廣懸車太傅，不為子孫益産業，曰：「賢而多財，則損其志；愚而多財，則益其過。」廣果賢邪？則其言可以省矣。刺史問龐德公何以遺子孫，曰：「人皆遺之以危，吾獨遺之以安。雖所遺不同，未為無所遺也。」夫以耕稼為安，則遺子孫以官祿者，非危乎？故人請楊伯起為子孫開産業，曰：「使後世稱為清白吏子孫，以此遺之，不亦厚乎？」夫以清白為厚，則遺子孫以貨賄者，非薄乎？

母績而勸以自安，公甫文伯之孝也，奚至於絶嗣？賢母之以身教，其言固如此爾。君違不忘，諫之以德，臧哀伯之忠也，奚必於有後？賢臣之自天佑，其理固如此爾。

王業偏安於鼎足，是豈大丈夫之志哉？其曰「鞠躬盡瘁」，又奚暇私家衣食之謀？即此以觀，管樂之比，盖自道焉爾。兵權頓釋於杯酒，夫亦保全功臣之道哉！雖曰成功不居，顧得世享田宅之利。由是以知韓彭之
translation_en:
…his words may serve as a warning. Shu Guang retired from his post as Grand Tutor and did not enlarge his descendants’ property. He said: “If they are worthy yet have abundant wealth, it will impair their aspirations; if they are foolish yet have abundant wealth, it will increase their faults.” Was Guang indeed worthy? Then his words give us cause for reflection. A Regional Inspector asked Pang Degong what he would leave his descendants. He replied: “Others all leave them danger; I alone leave them security. Though what we leave differs, it cannot be said that I leave them nothing.” If farming constitutes security, then is leaving descendants official positions and emoluments not dangerous? An old friend asked Yang Boqi to establish an estate for his descendants. He replied: “Let later generations call them the descendants of an incorruptible official. Is leaving them this not a generous legacy?” If incorruptibility constitutes generosity, then is leaving descendants wealth and valuables not a meager legacy?

When his mother was spinning, Gongfu Wenbo urged her to take her ease: this was his filial devotion. Why should it have led to the extinction of his line? A worthy mother teaches by her own example; this was indeed the tenor of her words. When his ruler erred, Zang Aibo did not forget his duty [?], but remonstrated with him on grounds of virtue: this was his loyalty. Why must he necessarily have descendants? That a worthy minister receives Heaven’s protection is indeed the principle involved [?].

For the royal enterprise to rest content with holding one region in a balance of three powers—could this be the aspiration of a great man? When he spoke of “bending every effort until utterly exhausted,” what leisure could he have had to plan for his own household’s food and clothing? Seen in this light, his comparison of himself with Guan Zhong and Yue Yi was surely an expression of his own aspirations. To relinquish military command at once over a cup of wine—was this not also a way to preserve meritorious ministers unharmed? Though they might be said to have withdrawn after achieving success, they nevertheless secured the benefits of fields and residences for generations. text:
