能繼則垣屋何必多治産業何必廣營筐
篋衣食之豐誰無是心使積而未必能守
則故人之饋胡不郤於暮夜聖主之恵胡
不仁其宗族夫君子為善亦性之而已小
punctuated: 禍乃自取焉爾。于公為縣小吏，治獄無冤，而奕世貴顯；殘民如周興、来俊臣者，寧免於赤族乎？鄧禹身為大將，未嘗妄殺，而闔門貴盛；殺降如白起、李廣者，寧免於覆宗乎？於乎！天道神靈，日監在下，惡盈好謙，賞善罰惡，毫髮不差。但教子孫以忠孝勤儉，毋導之以非道之為；寧令子孫清白久長，毋累之以非義之得。吾不計利鈍，寧肯罔上以便其私圖？吾不苟富貴，寧忍殺人以為己地？功德及於民，則世祿世官，豈必危道？名實加於上，則爾昌爾熾，决非空言。勞以向義，則耕可也，績可也，孰非裕後之謀？仕苟為道，則兵可也，刑可也，孰非陰德之地？阡陌甲第之廣，誰無是心？使創而未必能繼，則垣屋何必多治，産業何必廣筦？筐篋衣食之豐，誰無是心？使積而未必能守，則故人之饋胡不卻於暮夜，聖主之惠胡不仁其宗族？夫君子為善，亦性之而已。小
translation_en:
…calamity was thus of their own making. Lord Yu served as a minor county functionary, deciding criminal cases without injustice, and successive generations of his descendants attained rank and distinction. Could men who cruelly oppressed the people, such as Zhou Xing and Lai Junchen, escape the extermination of their clans? Deng Yu was a great general who never killed wantonly, and his entire household enjoyed eminence and prosperity. Could those who killed surrendered men, such as Bai Qi and Li Guang, escape the ruin of their lineages?

Alas! The numinous Way of Heaven watches daily over those below. It abhors arrogance and favors humility, rewards goodness and punishes evil, without the slightest error. Teach your descendants only loyalty, filial piety, diligence, and frugality; do not guide them into conduct contrary to the Way. Rather let your descendants remain upright and endure for generations; do not burden them with unjust gains. If I do not reckon success or failure, would I willingly deceive my sovereign to further my private designs? If I do not seek wealth and rank by improper means, could I bear to kill others to secure my own position?

When meritorious and virtuous deeds benefit the people, hereditary stipends and offices need hardly be a perilous course. When reputation and actual achievement reach the sovereign, the promise that “you shall flourish and prosper” is certainly no empty saying. If labor is directed toward righteousness, farming is acceptable, and spinning is acceptable: which is not a means of providing abundantly for posterity? If service in office truly accords with the Way, military affairs are acceptable, and penal affairs are acceptable: which does not offer scope for hidden virtue?

Who does not desire extensive fields and grand residences? Yet if what one establishes cannot necessarily be carried on, why build so many walls and houses, and why manage such extensive estates? Who does not desire chests and baskets amply stocked with clothing and food? Yet if what one accumulates cannot necessarily be preserved, why not refuse an old acquaintance’s gift offered late at night? Why not use the sage sovereign’s bounty to show kindness to one’s lineage?

The gentleman does good simply by following his nature. As for the petty…

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
人雖愚獨無是心哉彼任情縱欲固以牽
挽推拒於趨利避害之場不能自主矣又
見夫為善者偶得无妄之禍為惡者或享
非分之福則以天道寥遠未足憑據由是
作姦效尤肆無忌憚亡身喪家率由於此
善乎蘇軾之言曰盜跖之壽孔顏之厄此
天之未定者也善惡之報至於子孫而定
也久矣胡寅亦曰人之為善與惡天未必
逐逐然而禍福之也理存感應如寒暑雨
暘之消息自不可誣故人亦自脩而已人
能力於自脩而天有不定者乎脩之何如
曰立德行義久操而不渝積功累仁世濟
而無斁仰不愧於天俯不愧於吾心上不
負君父下不負生民中亦不負其所學如
此而其子孫不昌以永吾未之信也孔子
曰積善之家必有餘慶此又君子所持以
為善而不移者愚也服膺斯訓久矣敢就
正於有道執事其幸教之

遂遂然而禍福之也理存感應如寒暑雨
===

能力於自脩而天有不定者乎脩之何如
曰立德行義久操而不渝積功累仁世濟
而無斁仰不愧於天俯不愧於吾心上不
負君父下不負生民中亦不負其所學如
此而其子孫不昌以承吾未之信也孔子
曰積善之家必有餘慶此又君子所恃以

punctuated:
人雖愚，獨無是心哉？彼任情縱欲，固以牽挽推拒於趨利避害之場，不能自主矣。又見夫為善者偶得无妄之禍，為惡者或享非分之福，則以天道寥遠，未足憑據。由是作姦效尤，肆無忌憚，亡身喪家，率由於此。
善乎蘇軾之言曰：「盜跖之壽，孔顏之厄，此天之未定者也。善惡之報，至於子孫而定也久矣。」胡寅亦曰：「人之為善與惡，天未必逐逐然而禍福之也。理存感應，如寒暑雨暘之消息，自不可誣，故人亦自脩而已。」人能力於自脩，而天有不定者乎？脩之何如？曰：立德行義，久操而不渝；積功累仁，世濟而無斁。仰不愧於天，俯不愧於吾心；上不負君父，下不負生民，中亦不負其所學。如此而其子孫不昌以永，吾未之信也。
孔子曰：「積善之家，必有餘慶。」此又君子所持以為善而不移者。愚也服膺斯訓久矣，敢就正於有道，執事其幸教之。
translation_en:
…though petty men are foolish, can they alone lack this disposition? Giving free rein to their feelings and desires, they are pulled and pushed about in the pursuit of advantage and avoidance of harm, unable to govern themselves. Moreover, when they see that those who do good sometimes suffer undeserved calamities, while those who do evil sometimes enjoy blessings beyond their due, they conclude that Heaven’s Way is remote and offers no reliable basis for conduct. Thus they commit wrongdoing and imitate bad examples, acting without restraint or scruple. Their own ruin and the destruction of their households generally arise from this.
How well Su Shi put it: “The longevity of Robber Zhi and the adversity of Confucius and Yan Hui are instances in which Heaven’s judgment is not yet settled. That recompense for good and evil becomes settled in one’s descendants has long been so.” Hu Yin likewise said: “When people do good or evil, Heaven does not necessarily pursue each deed and bring calamity or blessing upon them. The principle of stimulus and response exists, like the waxing and waning of cold and heat, rain and sunshine, and cannot be denied. Thus people need only cultivate themselves.” If people exert themselves in self-cultivation, can Heaven’s judgment remain unsettled? How should one cultivate oneself? I say: establish virtue and practice righteousness, maintaining this resolve without wavering over time; accumulate meritorious deeds and acts of benevolence, carrying them on from generation to generation without wearying. Looking upward, have nothing to be ashamed of before Heaven; looking inward, have nothing to be ashamed of in one’s own heart. Above, fail neither sovereign nor father; below, fail neither the people nor their needs; and in oneself, do not betray what one has learned. I cannot believe that the descendants of someone who acts thus would fail to prosper enduringly.
Confucius said: “A household that accumulates goodness is sure to have blessings left over.” This, too, is what the gentleman holds fast to as he does good without wavering. I, in my ignorance, have long taken this teaching to heart. I venture to seek correction from one who possesses the Way; may you, honored sir, graciously instruct me.

translation_en:
Fifth Question

Comment by Associate Examiner Yi, Instructor: The five policy essays in this script each run to several thousand words. All are well grounded, and their treatment of current affairs and worldly circumstances is systematic and exhaustive. Here is a talent fit for service to the world, deserving fame for more than extensive learning alone. I respectfully admire him—indeed I do!

Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, Instructor: Taken together, his compositions from the three sessions amply demonstrate learning encompassing both underlying principles and practical application. The five policy essays are especially striking and outstanding. My only regret is that we cannot reproduce them all.

Comment by Examiner Gu, Left Mentor: These five policy essays fully express his deeply felt concerns and impassioned convictions, yet all are precise and exceptionally penetrating. These are no mere compositions pieced together from borrowed scraps. In his everyday life, he must long have kept the affairs of All-under-Heaven at heart. Outstanding talents like you are truly rare in the examination hall.

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting: This young man speaks of worldly affairs with passionate indignation, showing something of the spirit of Jia Yi. Moreover, his literary power surpasses that of others, allowing his writing to follow wherever his thoughts lead. Considered alongside the preceding scripts, none can be ranked above or below the others. Such spirit among scholars foretells a flourishing age.

There are grave warnings for the Central Kingdom and hidden anxieties even in an age of good government. The Central Kingdom and the non-Chinese peoples tend to rise and decline in opposition to one another, while the security of the common people is difficult to ensure. The incipient causes of order and disorder often lie concealed within one another, beyond perception. Gentlemen who establish good government and safeguard the realm must indeed attend to this. Allow me to set forth my views in response to your illuminating question.

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
戎狄之患自古有之至元遂入主中國則
夷狄之極盛而中國之極衰也我
太祖起而逐之塞外復帝王所自立之中國華
夷之辨冠屨截然此中國之方盛而夷狄
之就衰也然彼以餘黎遺孽誕紀其緒而
與吾邊境鄰則吾之所以嚴為之備而預
為之防者固宜百倍於前代而後可今邊
關亭障萬里相屬可謂盛矣虜嘗竊入而
卒無大憂豈非
===
祖宗之法至精至密有以維持綱紀為不拔之
基哉近年以來虜寇犯邊往往深入腹裏
所過赤地無遺略無懲創而去識者蓋久
憂之近日宣府之警羽檄交馳
朝野動色豨突鳥逝莫之誰何其為患蓋未
可量也盜賊之起治世有所不免以近歲
言之盜起近畿而中原為之殘破盜起楚
蜀而環境為之繹騷至遣制帥動邊卒調
夷兵以成勦平之功然凋殘之餘生理未

translation_en:
The threat posed by the Rong and Di has existed since antiquity. By the Yuan dynasty, they had come to rule China: this marked the utmost ascendancy of the barbarians and the utmost decline of China. Our Taizu arose and drove them beyond the frontier, restoring the China in which emperors and kings had established their rule. The distinction between Chinese and barbarians was as sharply drawn as that between caps and shoes. China was then rising to strength, while the barbarians were declining. Yet, with their surviving people and remnant offspring, they perpetuated their line [?] and remained adjacent to our frontier. Our preparations against them must therefore be stringent, and our precautions taken in advance; only measures a hundredfold greater than those of previous dynasties would suffice. Today, frontier passes, watchposts, and defensive works extend in an unbroken chain for ten thousand li. These may indeed be called formidable. The enemy has sometimes slipped in, yet ultimately caused no great calamity. Is this not because the institutions of our imperial ancestors were supremely refined and comprehensive, sustaining the governing order and providing an unshakable foundation? In recent years, enemy raiders have violated the frontier and repeatedly penetrated deep into the interior, leaving everything in their path utterly desolate and departing virtually unpunished. Those who understand affairs have long been troubled by this. With the recent alarm at Xuanfu, urgent military dispatches sped back and forth, and consternation spread through court and country alike. The enemy charged like wild boars and vanished like birds, with no one able to challenge them. The harm they may cause is surely beyond reckoning.

Even an age of good government cannot always avoid outbreaks of banditry. To speak of recent years: bandits arose near the capital, and the Central Plain was devastated; bandits arose in Chu and Shu, and the surrounding territories were thrown into turmoil [?]. Matters reached the point of dispatching commanders, mobilizing frontier troops, and transferring tribal soldiers to accomplish their suppression and pacification. title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
復公私之積猶可哀痛而水旱之不時饑
饉之荐臻其為患亦未可量也夫禦戎無
上策論者曰當以氣勝之中國為陽夷狄
為陰君子道長小人道消則陽氣勝而陰
不能奸故二帝三王之世而夷狄之患無
甚君子道消小人道長則陰氣勝而陽不
能立故秦漢而下而夷狄之患始滋夫豈
無據之虛談哉宋儒朱熹告其君曰古先
聖王所以制馭夷狄之道其本不在乎威
===
彊而在乎德業其任不在乎邊境而在乎
朝廷其具不在乎兵食而在乎紀綱所謂上
策盖不出此數言而必以開納諫諍黜遠
佞邪杜塞倖門安固邦本四者為急先之
務此萬世不易之論也豈特可行於今日
而已乎若夫盜源之說盖曰衣食不足盜
之源也政賦不均盜之源也教化不脩盜
之源也一源慢則探囊發篋而為盜矣二
源慢則執兵刃刼良民而為盜矣三源慢

復，公私之積猶可哀痛，而水旱之不時，饑饉之荐臻，其為患亦未可量也。
夫禦戎無上策，論者曰：「當以氣勝之。」中國為陽，夷狄為陰。君子道長，小人道消，則陽氣勝而陰不能奸，故二帝三王之世，而夷狄之患無甚；君子道消，小人道長，則陰氣勝而陽不能立，故秦漢而下，而夷狄之患始滋。夫豈無據之虛談哉？宋儒朱熹告其君曰：「古先聖王所以制馭夷狄之道，其本不在乎威彊，而在乎德業；其任不在乎邊境，而在乎朝廷；其具不在乎兵食，而在乎紀綱。」所謂上策，盖不出此數言，而必以開納諫諍、黜遠佞邪、杜塞倖門、安固邦本四者為急先之務。此萬世不易之論也，豈特可行於今日而已乎？
若夫盜源之說，盖曰：「衣食不足，盜之源也；政賦不均，盜之源也；教化不脩，盜之源也。一源慢，則探囊發篋而為盜矣；二源慢，則執兵刃刼良民而為盜矣；三源慢
translation_en:
…have yet to recover, and the condition of public and private reserves remains grievous. With floods and droughts arriving out of season and famines repeatedly occurring, the harm they cause is likewise beyond measure.
As for resisting the northern peoples, there is no supreme strategy. Some commentators say, “One should overcome them through qi.” The Central Kingdom represents yang; the foreign peoples represent yin. When the way of noble men advances and the way of petty men recedes, yang qi prevails and yin cannot encroach. Thus, in the age of the Two Emperors and Three Kings, troubles caused by foreign peoples were not severe. When the way of noble men recedes and the way of petty men advances, yin qi prevails and yang cannot stand firm. Thus, from the Qin and Han onward, troubles caused by foreign peoples began to multiply. Can this really be dismissed as empty talk without foundation? The Song Confucian scholar Zhu Xi told his ruler: “The means by which the sage kings of antiquity controlled and governed foreign peoples rested fundamentally upon virtuous achievements, rather than military might; responsibility lay with the court, rather than the frontier; and the instruments were governing principles and discipline, rather than troops and provisions.” What is called the supreme strategy surely amounts to no more than these few words. Four tasks must take urgent priority: welcoming and accepting remonstrance, dismissing and distancing oneself from deceitful flatterers and the wicked, closing the avenues of unmerited favor, and securing the foundations of the state. This is a judgment that will remain unchanged for ten thousand generations. Could it be applicable only today?
As for the explanation of the sources of banditry, it says: “Insufficient food and clothing are a source of banditry; inequitable administration and taxation are a source of banditry; neglect of moral instruction is a source of banditry. If one source is neglected, people become thieves who reach into bags and break open chests. If two sources are neglected, they become robbers who take up weapons and plunder law-abiding people. If three sources are neglected…”

text:
則攻城邑略百姓而為盜矣豐世無盜者
足也治世無賊者均也化世無亂者順也
求其源而止之何盜之患若俟其起而平
之窮治則有不戢自焚之禍招降則有養
虎遺患之憂誠未見其一可也斯二患者
當今之急務也愚也不敏於邊防廢弛之
因軍士怨憤之情生民愁苦之狀官吏侵
漁之弊誠欲發憤痛哭一為執事陳之而
未暇悉數也伏望
===
朝廷於本原之地深加之意任老成為腹心
用臺諫為耳目
邦國大計安危所係必付之公論而勿參以
一髮之私則所以彊本折衝安內攘外之
道不期月而粲然可備舉矣芻蕘之言俾
得上達以備
采擇之萬一執事之賜也謹對

朝廷於本原之地深加之意任老成爲腹心
用臺諫爲耳目

道不期月而粲然可備舉矣芻蕘之言俾

采擇之萬一執事之賜也謹對
punctuated:
則攻城邑、略百姓而為盜矣。豐世無盜者，足也；治世無賊者，均也；化世無亂者，順也。求其源而止之，何盜之患？若俟其起而平之，窮治則有不戢自焚之禍，招降則有養虎遺患之憂，誠未見其一可也。斯二患者，當今之急務也。愚也不敏，於邊防廢弛之因、軍士怨憤之情、生民愁苦之狀、官吏侵漁之弊，誠欲發憤痛哭，一為執事陳之，而未暇悉數也。
伏望朝廷於本原之地深加之意，任老成為腹心，用臺諫為耳目。邦國大計，安危所係，必付之公論，而勿參以一髮之私，則所以彊本折衝、安內攘外之道，不期月而粲然可備舉矣。芻蕘之言，俾得上達，以備采擇之萬一，執事之賜也。謹對。
translation_en:
…then they attack cities and towns and plunder the common people, becoming bandits. That prosperous ages have no bandits is due to sufficiency; that well-governed ages have no malefactors is due to equity; that morally transformed ages have no disorder is due to willing obedience. If we seek out the sources and stop them, what trouble need we fear from bandits? If instead we wait for them to rise and then suppress them, pursuing suppression to the utmost risks the calamity of failing to put away weapons and thereby burning ourselves; inviting their surrender raises the fear of rearing tigers and leaving trouble for the future. Truly, I cannot see that either course is acceptable. These two troubles are urgent matters of the present day. Dull-witted though I am, I truly wish to give vent to my indignation and weep bitterly, laying before you in turn the causes of neglected frontier defenses, the soldiers’ resentment and anger, the common people’s misery and distress, and the abuses of predatory officials. Yet I have not had time to enumerate them all.
I humbly hope that the court will give profound attention to these foundations, entrusting mature and experienced men with service as its closest confidants and employing censorial and remonstrance officials as its eyes and ears. Great plans of state, upon which security or peril depends, must be entrusted to public deliberation, without the intrusion of even a hair’s breadth of private interest. Then the means of strengthening the foundations and repelling aggression, securing the realm within and warding off threats from without, can all be clearly put into effect before a full year has passed. If these words of a humble woodcutter may reach the throne, so that even one part in ten thousand might be selected for adoption, it will be owing to your favor. Respectfully submitted in reply.

順天府鄉試錄後序

正德十一年秋八月，上命臣俊、臣鼎臣主北畿試事。事竣，錄成，鼎臣當序其後。

竊惟古者迪士，材成而後進，論材授官，謹好尚，明考課，以先後之，故士知自重而有立。我國家學校之教、科目之法，最為近古。邇者，士號明經，習為文，發解無餘事。朝取第，暮篋書，不復省覽者眾矣。仕習於法理簿書，不復知學；學矣，而徒攻於詞章，務枝葉，失本根，中無所主，就世之趨而靡焉。古之成材者固若是
translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination

In autumn, in the eighth month of the eleventh year of Zhengde [1516], His Majesty commanded your servants Jun and Dingchen to preside over the examination in the Northern Metropolitan Region. Once the examination was concluded and its record compiled, it fell to me, Dingchen, to write its postface.

I humbly reflect that in antiquity, scholars were guided and advanced only after their abilities had matured. Their abilities were assessed and offices conferred accordingly; care was taken over what was esteemed, and performance evaluations were made clear, so as to determine their relative precedence. Thus scholars knew to respect themselves and establish a firm footing. Our dynasty’s instruction in schools and system of examinations come closest to those of antiquity. Recently, however, scholars profess to understand the Classics and practice composing examination essays, concerning themselves with nothing beyond passing the Provincial Examination. Many obtain their degree in the morning and pack away their books that evening, never again to examine or read them. Once in office, they become practiced in legal principles and paperwork and no longer know to pursue learning. Even when they do study, they devote themselves merely to literary composition, attending to branches and leaves while losing the roots. With no guiding principle within, they bend to the prevailing tendencies of the age. Were those whose abilities matured in antiquity really like this …

乎？下此，决禮義之閑，困富貴之馳，類則士，途則科目，志行則夫氓也。是誠有負於經術迪士之初意矣。夫六經皆聖賢經綸之迹，其道極于天地，通于神明。學者誦其言而通其意，已非常人，况以是淑其身心、蓄德脩業者哉！
甞聞先朝名臣，往往朴茂堅特，若無他技能，而道德功業無愧於古。其所成立，偉然一代之望，豈當時務實學、尚質行，所謂材成而後進者歟？夫亦有以振厲作興之，而不能自已也。《詩》曰：「思皇多士
translation_en:
…was it so? Below this level are those who breach the bounds of ritual propriety and righteousness and become ensnared in the pursuit of wealth and rank. In their category they are scholars, and their avenue of advancement is the examinations, yet in aspiration and conduct they are common fellows [?]. This truly betrays the original intention of guiding scholars through classical learning. The Six Classics all preserve traces of how the sages and worthies ordered the world. Their Way reaches throughout Heaven and Earth and communicates with the spirits. Those who recite their words and comprehend their meaning are already no ordinary people; how much more so those who use them to refine body and mind, accumulate virtue, and cultivate their undertakings!
I have heard that eminent ministers of former reigns were often sincere, substantial, steadfast, and resolute, seemingly possessing no other particular skills, yet in moral character and achievement they stood without shame before the ancients. Through what they accomplished, they stood magnificently as figures to whom their whole age looked up. Was this because people then pursued substantive learning and esteemed sound conduct—the principle of advancing men only after their abilities had matured? There were also means of rousing and inspiring them, so that they could not cease their efforts. The Book of Odes says: “Admirable are the many scholars…

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
生此王國今兹百年禮樂之餘
畿甸俊造之選所謂其人夫豈少
哉矧登名是錄者類能上下古
今敷析理事醞齊以成文察人
以言藹然鹿鳴之賓豈復有如
前所云者哉必是之云者誠過
計而厚望焉耳諸士子其仰思
===
聖天子所以賓興我者之意不啻於
吏治君子之用世不在於浮華
益務績學砥行夷考老成典刑
泝而上之以求聖賢六經之道
進將舉所實有諸已者措之以
弼成采薇天保之治則主司之
心始慰而諸士子所自立亦偉

益務績學砥行夷考老成典刑

punctuated: 生此王國。」今兹百年禮樂之餘，畿甸俊造之選，所謂其人，夫豈少哉？矧登名是錄者，類能上下古今，敷析理事，醞齊以成文。察人以言，藹然鹿鳴之賓，豈復有如前所云者哉？必是之云者，誠過計而厚望焉耳。諸士子其仰思聖天子所以賓興我者之意，不啻於吏治。君子之用世，不在於浮華。益務績學砥行，夷考老成典刑，泝而上之，以求聖賢六經之道。進將舉所實有諸已者措之，以弼成采薇天保之治，則主司之心始慰，而諸士子所自立亦偉
translation_en:
…“born in this royal realm.” Now, after a hundred years of rites and music, could there be few such men among the outstanding talents selected from the metropolitan region? Moreover, those whose names appear in this record can generally range through past and present, expound and analyze principles and affairs, and blend them harmoniously into compositions. Judging the men by their words, they are an illustrious company of guests worthy of the ode “The Deer Call.” Could any of them still be as described above? If we insist on speaking thus, it is only from excessive concern and high expectations for them.

You scholars should reverently consider the sage Son of Heaven’s intention in honoring and advancing us as guests: it extends beyond official administration alone. The gentleman’s service to the world does not depend on superficial brilliance. Apply yourselves still more to accumulating learning and tempering your conduct; carefully examine the exemplary models of mature and accomplished men, and trace these back to their sources to seek the Way of the sages and worthies in the Six Classics. When you advance to office, put into practice what you truly possess within yourselves, thereby helping to achieve the good governance celebrated in “Gathering Vetch” and “Heaven Protects.” Only then will the hearts of those presiding over the examination be satisfied, and what you scholars establish for yourselves will also be magnificent…

者亦將感且奮而不能已焉又

punctuated:
矣。臣等祗奉明詔，既夙夜殫厥心力，期以免不明之責。因念夫南畿及諸省所薦士，皆將登名天府，後先效用，而令甲科試、朝覲之典相繼舉行。是固人材進退□□機，而祖宗作□振厲天下之微意也。示好惡，明賞罰，公黜陟，多士目擊於觀光之餘，長善遏惡以成其材者，亦將感且奮而不能已焉。又何假於言哉？是為序。
奉訓大夫、左春坊左諭德兼翰林院侍讀顧鼎臣謹序。
translation_en:
…indeed. We, your servants, have reverently obeyed the illustrious edict, exhausting our mental and physical energies day and night in the hope of escaping reproach for a lack of discernment. We further reflect that the men recommended by the Southern Metropolitan Region and the various provinces will all have their names entered in the registers of the imperial court and, sooner or later, render service. The examinations prescribed by statute [?] and the ceremonies of court audience are held in succession. These are indeed a crucial occasion for the advancement and retirement of talented men [two characters illegible], and embody the subtle intention of the imperial ancestors to rouse [?] and invigorate all under Heaven. By displaying approval and disapproval, making rewards and punishments clear, and administering demotions and promotions impartially, these proceedings allow the assembled scholars to witness such things while beholding the glory of the realm. Those who cultivate their strengths and restrain their faults so as to develop their abilities will also be moved and stirred to an enthusiasm they cannot contain. What further need is there for words? This serves as the preface.
Respectfully composed by Gu Dingchen, Grand Master for Instruction, Left Admonisher of the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent, and concurrently Reader-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy.

translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination

Of all the tribute presented from throughout the realm, none is greater than the presentation of worthy men. Holding an examination once every three years is the established regulation. The autumn of the bingzi year of Zhengde [1516] was indeed the appointed time. The officials of Shuntian Prefecture petitioned in accordance with precedent, and His Majesty commanded his servants Jun, Academician Expositor-in-waiting, and Dingchen, Left Admonisher, to go and preside over the examination. The Associate Examiners were Qi and Han, school instructors (xuezheng), and Gao, Xin, Chao, Jian, Quan, Yue, and Zongzhou, county school instructors (jiaoyu). The officials overseeing the examination were the censors Lei and Yong; the Proctors were Shao, Prefect, and Run, Vice Prefect. These officials, together with all those serving inside and outside the examination compound, were carefully selected and took their assigned places. At that time, nearly three thousand men presented themselves for examination, bringing their literary skills. After examining them in three sessions, they selected one hundred and thirty…

translation_en:
…five men [completing the total of 135], and twenty-one of their finest compositions were also recorded for presentation to the throne, as prescribed.
I, Jun, consider that the state nurtures scholars in its schools and selects them through the examinations so that their talents may be put to use in the world. Some doubt whether literary composition suffices to identify worthy scholars. I have heard that those of old who excelled at judging horses examined their teeth, their cheeks, their eyes, their thighs, or their coats and manes. Their methods differed, each observing a particular sign in the horse; yet the height of its joints, the ease of its gait, the strength or weakness of its constitution, and the extent of its abilities could none escape their scrutiny. This was neither supernatural insight nor good fortune: it followed the inherent principles of such things. As an indication of a scholar’s qualities, nothing surpasses literary composition, which arises in his heart and issues from his mouth. To say that literary composition is not what education …

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之所先可也謂不足以得士過
矣雖然有司之好惡不可以不
慎也士習之升降風俗之隆替
恒必由之夫士必有忠信之質
而又明於義利王霸之辨然後
隨其材之大小皆足以有用於
世
===
上之所資而求者盖在此也而獨於
文焉是徵故視其表將以探其
中玩其華將以冀其實其志正
其氣醇其論議無所悖見於辭
者雖或未工不得而棄矣其外
燁然其中枵然割裂裝綴徒事
口耳文非無可觀也而無所於

上之所資而求者蓋在此也而獨於
文焉是徵故視其表將以探其
中玩其華將以蕺其實其志正

口耳文非無可觀也而無所於

之所先，可也；謂不足以得士，過矣。雖然，有司之好惡不可以不慎也。士習之升降，風俗之隆替，恒必由之。夫士必有忠信之質，而又明於義利王霸之辨，然後隨其材之大小，皆足以有用於世。
上之所資而求者，盖在此也，而獨於文焉是徵。故視其表，將以探其中；玩其華，將以冀其實。其志正，其氣醇，其論議無所悖，見於辭者雖或未工，不得而棄矣。其外燁然，其中枵然，割裂裝綴，徒事口耳，文非無可觀也，而無所於
translation_en:
…to say that it is not what education should put first is acceptable; to say that it is insufficient for identifying worthy men is mistaken. Even so, the responsible officials must exercise care in their likes and dislikes. The improvement or decline of scholars’ habits, and the flourishing or decay of social customs, invariably depend upon them. Scholars must possess loyalty and trustworthiness as their essential character, and must also understand the distinctions between righteousness and profit, and between kingly rule and hegemonic rule. Only then can all be of service to the world, according to the measure of their abilities.
This, surely, is what His Majesty seeks in the men upon whom he relies; yet writing alone is taken as its evidence. Thus we examine their outward expression to probe what lies within, and contemplate their literary flowers in the hope of finding substantial fruit. If their intentions are upright, their moral temper pure, and their arguments free of anything contrary to right principles, then even if their expression is not yet accomplished, they must not be rejected. Others are dazzling outwardly but empty within: they cut and piece together passages, embellishing and stitching them into compositions, occupied merely with what they hear and repeat. Their writing is not without things worth admiring, yet it offers nothing by which to…

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
徵不得而取矣其有志嚮不謬
而學業未成者則亦不得而與
焉俊等之職蓋將以廣
德意求材實庶幾得駉騋駃騠於牝
牡驪黃之外以資任重致遠之
用謂遂能空其羣也則烏乎敢
諸士子有得於此者其毋以文
===
自多未得於此者尚知不昧於
所求俾究論習俗之變移者不
以病今日之有司則幸矣
翰林院侍讀學士奉訓大夫
汪俊謹序

===
諸士子有得於此者其毋以文
自多未得於此者尚知不跱於
所求俾究論習俗之變移者不
以病今日之有司則幸矣
翰林院侍　讀學士奉訓大夫
汪俊謹序
punctuated:
徵，不得而取矣。其有志嚮不謬而學業未成者，則亦不得而與焉。俊等之職，蓋將以廣德意，求材實，庶幾得駉騋駃騠於牝牡驪黃之外，以資任重致遠之用。謂遂能空其羣也，則烏乎敢？諸士子有得於此者，其毋以文自多；未得於此者，尚知不昧於所求。俾究論習俗之變移者，不以病今日之有司，則幸矣。
翰林院侍讀學士、奉訓大夫汪俊謹序。
translation_en:
…to substantiate it, they cannot be selected. Those whose aspirations are sound but whose learning is not yet accomplished likewise cannot be admitted. The duty of myself, Jun, and my colleagues is to extend the imperial benevolent intent and seek genuine talent. We hope to find sturdy, tall, and swift steeds, looking beyond whether they are female or male, black or yellow, so that they may serve to bear heavy burdens and travel far. Yet how would we dare claim that we can select all the finest horses, leaving none in the herd? Those candidates who have grasped this should not pride themselves on their literary accomplishments; those who have not should at least understand clearly what we seek. If those who investigate and discuss changes in prevailing scholarly habits thereby refrain from finding fault with the officials responsible today, we shall count ourselves fortunate.
Preface respectfully written by Wang Jun, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy and Grand Master for Instruction.

Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination, Eleventh Year of Zhengde (1516)

Proctors

Hu Shao, Grand Master for Court Counsel and Prefect of Shuntian Prefecture. His courtesy name was Dasheng; he was from Poyang County, Jiangxi, and was a metropolitan graduate (jinshi) of the jiachen year.

Zhang Run, Grand Master of Central Accord and Prefectural Vice Administrator of Shuntian Prefecture. His courtesy name was Rulin; he was from Linfen County, Shanxi, and was a metropolitan graduate of the renxu year.

Examiners

Wang Jun, Academician Expositor of the Hanlin Academy and Grand Master for Instruction. His courtesy name was Yizhi; he was from Yiyang County, Jiangxi, and was a metropolitan graduate of the guichou year.

Gu Dingchen, Grand Master for Instruction, Left Admonisher in the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent, and concurrently Expositor of the Hanlin Academy. His courtesy name was Jiuhe; he was from Kunshan County, Zhili, and was a metropolitan graduate of the yichou year.

Associate Examiners

Chen Qi, Instructor in the Confucian School of Taizhou, Yangzhou Prefecture, Zhili. His courtesy name was Zhongyu; he held official household registration in Quanzhou, Guangxi, was originally from Chaling Subprefecture, Huguang, and was a tribute scholar (gongshi) of the renzi year.

Zheng Han, Instructor in the Confucian School of Daizhou, Taiyuan Prefecture, Shanxi. His courtesy name was Liangqing; he was from Longxi County, Fujian, and was a tribute scholar of the jiazi year.

Zhou Gao, Instructor in the Confucian School of Longyou County, Quzhou Prefecture, Zhejiang. His courtesy name was Tingxuan; he was from Guixi County, Jiangxi, and was a tribute scholar of the renzi year.

Ke Xin, Instructor in the Confucian School of Yongxin County, Ji'an Prefecture, Jiangxi. His courtesy name was Ruchong; he was from Nan'an County, Fujian, and was a tribute scholar of the jiazi year.

Zhou Chao, Instructor in the Confucian School of Jishui County, Ji'an Prefecture, Jiangxi. His courtesy name was Wangying; he was from Taicang Subprefecture, Zhili, and was a tribute scholar of the guiyou year.

Tang Jian, Instructor in the Confucian School of Guangchang County, Jianchang Prefecture, Jiangxi. His courtesy name was Jingfan; he was from Lin'an County, Zhejiang, and was a tribute scholar of the yimao year.

Fu Quan, Instructor in the Confucian School of Guantao County, Linqing Subprefecture, Dongchang Prefecture, Shandong. His courtesy name was Gongheng; he held official household registration in Guilin Central Guard, Guangxi, was originally from Luotian County, Huguang, and was a tribute scholar of the dingmao year.

Ao Yue, Instructor in the Confucian School of Jixi County, Huizhou Prefecture, Zhili. His courtesy name was Bingzhi; he was from Gao'an County, Jiangxi, and was a tribute scholar of the dingmao year.

Yi Zongzhou, Instructor in the Confucian School of Taoyuan County, Huai'an Prefecture, Zhili. His courtesy name was Shiwen; he was from Lingui County, Guangxi, and was a tribute scholar of the dingmao year.

text:

舉直錯諸枉能使枉者直
成己仁也成物知也性之德也合内外之
道也故時措之宜也
行有不慊於心則餒矣我故曰告子未嘗
知義以其外之也
易
小往大來吉亨
===
九五渙汗其大號渙王居无咎
慎斯術也以往其无所失矣
神也者妙萬物而爲言者也動萬物者莫
疾乎雷撓萬物者莫疾乎風燥萬物者
莫熯乎火說萬物者莫說乎澤潤萬物

然後能變化既成萬物也

punctuated:
第壹塲

四書

舉直錯諸枉，能使枉者直。

成己，仁也；成物，知也。性之德也，合内外之道也，故時措之宜也。

行有不慊於心，則餒矣。我故曰：告子未嘗知義，以其外之也。

易

小往大來，吉亨。

九五：渙汗其大號，渙王居，无咎。

慎斯術也以往，其无所失矣。

神也者，妙萬物而爲言者也。動萬物者莫疾乎雷，撓萬物者莫疾乎風，燥萬物者莫熯乎火，說萬物者莫說乎澤，潤萬物者莫潤乎水，終萬物始萬物者莫盛乎艮。故水火相逮，雷風不相悖，山澤通氣，然後能變化，既成萬物也。

書
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

Raise up the upright and place them above the crooked, and you can make the crooked upright.

Perfecting oneself is benevolence; perfecting other things is wisdom. These are virtues of our nature and the Way that unites the inner and the outer. Thus, their application accords with what is appropriate to the time.

If one’s conduct leaves the heart dissatisfied, then one becomes starved of vital force. Thus I said: Gaozi has never understood righteousness, because he regards it as external.

Book of Changes

The small departs and the great arrives. Auspiciousness and success.

Nine in the fifth place: In dispersal, his great proclamations issue forth like sweat; he disperses the king’s accumulated stores. No blame.

Proceed cautiously with this method, and there will be no failure.

The term “spiritual” refers to the wondrous working of the myriad things. For stirring the myriad things, nothing is swifter than thunder; for agitating them, nothing is swifter than wind; for drying them, nothing is more parching than fire; for delighting them, nothing is more pleasing than the marsh; for moistening them, nothing is more moistening than water; for bringing them to their end and giving them their beginning, nothing surpasses Gen, the Mountain. Thus water and fire reach one another, thunder and wind do not oppose one another, and mountain and marsh communicate their vital energies. Only then can transformation and change occur and bring the myriad things to completion.

予欲宣力四方，汝爲。

鬼神無常享，享于克誠。

予造天役，遺大投艱于朕身。越予冲人，不卬自恤。義爾邦君，越爾多士、尹氏、御事，綏予曰：「無毖于恤，不可不成乃寧考圖功。」

昔在殷王中宗，嚴恭寅畏，天命自度，治民祗懼，不敢荒寧。肆中宗之享國七十有五年。

無以我公歸兮，無使我心悲兮！

鶴鳴于九皐，聲聞于野。魚潛在淵，或在于渚。樂彼之園，爰有樹檀，其下維毄。他山之石，可以爲錯。

帝謂文王：「無然畔援，無然歆羨，誕先登于岸。」

夙夜基命宥密，於緝熈單厥心！

春秋
translation_en:
“I wish to extend effective service throughout the four quarters; you shall undertake it.”

“Spirits do not invariably accept offerings; they accept those of people capable of sincerity.”

“I have undertaken Heaven’s service; great responsibilities and arduous tasks have been laid upon my person. Yet I, a young man, do not concern myself with my own welfare. It is fitting that you, lords of the states, together with you many officers, heads of offices, and those conducting affairs, should reassure me, saying: ‘Do not be overly anxious amid your cares. You must complete the work planned by your departed father.’”

“In former times, Zhongzong, king of Yin, was solemn, reverent, respectful, and fearful. He measured himself against Heaven’s mandate and governed the people with reverent apprehension, never daring to indulge in idleness or ease. Thus Zhongzong reigned for seventy-five years.”

Book of Odes

“Do not take our lord away home! Do not make my heart sorrowful!”

“A crane cries in the depths of the marshes; its voice is heard in the open country. Fish hide in the deep pool, or linger by the islets. Delightful is that garden, where sandalwood trees grow, with other growth beneath them [?]. Stones from another mountain may serve as whetstones.”

“The Lord on High said to King Wen: ‘Do not waver or seek support elsewhere; do not be covetous or envious. Be the first to ascend the bank.’”

“Morning and night, he laid the foundations of the mandate with magnanimity and quiet care. Ah, continuing and expanding its brilliance, he devoted his whole heart to it!”

Spring and Autumn Annals

柔會宋公、陳侯、蔡叔，盟于折。公會宋公于夫鍾。冬十有二月，公會宋公于闞。俱桓公十一年。公會宋公于虛。冬十有一月，公會宋公于龜。十有二月，及鄭師伐宋。丁未，戰于宋。俱桓公十二年。
夏，齊侯、陳侯、鄭伯遇于垂。莊公四年。晋侯執曹伯，歸于京師。成公十五年。己未，衛侯出奔齊。襄公十四年。吳子使札来聘。襄公二十九年。
取汶陽田。成公二年。春，晋侯使韓穿来言，汶陽之田歸之于齊。成公八年。
夏，公會齊侯于夾谷。公至自夾谷。定公十年。
禮記
是故七介以相見也，不然則已蹙；三辭三讓而至，不然則已蹙。
進則揖之，退則揚之，然後玉鏘鳴也。
禮也者，理之不可易者也。
妻也者，親之主也，敢不敬與？子也者，親之
translation_en:
Rou met with the Duke of Song, the Marquis of Chen, and Shu of Cai, and they concluded a covenant at Zhe. The duke met with the Duke of Song at Fuzhong. In winter, in the twelfth month, the duke met with the Duke of Song at Kan. These entries are all from the eleventh year of Duke Huan. The duke met with the Duke of Song at Xu. In winter, in the eleventh month, the duke met with the Duke of Song at Gui. In the twelfth month, our forces joined the army of Zheng in attacking Song. On the dingwei day, they fought in Song. These entries are all from the twelfth year of Duke Huan.
In summer, the Marquis of Qi, the Marquis of Chen, and the Earl of Zheng met at Chui. Fourth year of Duke Zhuang. The Marquis of Jin seized the Earl of Cao and brought him back to the royal capital. Fifteenth year of Duke Cheng. On the jiwei day, the Marquis of Wei fled to Qi. Fourteenth year of Duke Xiang. The Viscount of Wu sent Zha on a diplomatic visit to our state. Third Session
Policy Questions 〔Five questions〕
Question: Only after understanding the difficulty of preserving an established dynasty can a founding ruler bequeath a line of rule that can be continued, making arrangements so meticulous that nothing is overlooked. Only after understanding the difficulty of founding a dynasty can a ruler who inherits it sustain its full prosperity, guarding it carefully and not daring to let it decline. Thus founding and preserving follow a single Way. The Han was praised for the breadth and foresight of its founding arrangements, yet scarcely one or two successions had passed before the Rebellion of the Seven Kingdoms arose. The Tang was said to possess a complete system of laws and institutions, yet within two generations it suffered calamity brought about by a woman. Commentators regard these as the faults of Gao Di and Taizong respectively. Is this so?
We reverently reflect that our Taizu, the Gao Emperor, acquired the realm with such legitimacy and devised such excellent plans for his successors that he carried forward the legacy of the Three Dynasties and surpassed the Han and Tang. His achievement may be called perfect in every respect, beyond further improvement. Throughout the hundred and fifty years down to the present, all within the seas has remained peaceful, as though it were a single day. This is certainly the achievement of the successive sage emperors in reverently continuing his work, but the efficacy of our Gao Emperor’s founding labors is also apparent. The grandeur of his overall arrangements and the detail of their particular provisions cannot be exhaustively recounted; could you nevertheless give an outline of them? He also once discussed precedents from the Han and Tang with his attendant officials, lamenting earnestly that they should serve as profound warnings: favored women, eunuchs, imperial relatives by marriage, powerful ministers, regional military commands, and non-Chinese peoples. …guard against them. How abundant are these sagely counsels! Truly they are a mirror for all ages. You candidates have studied and practiced these great instructions, and surely have long been deeply moved by them. Please respectfully set forth your views, to support the filial thoughts of His Majesty upon the throne.

Question: Since Yao and Shun, no rulers have surpassed Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu in virtue; and when later generations discuss good government, they look no further than the Han, Tang, and Song. Yet examination of the accounts in the classics and histories leaves certain matters open to doubt. Yu kept his food and drink plain; why, then, did he renounce fine wine only after tasting its sweetness? Tang did not accumulate wealth or profit; why, then, did he condemn the circulation of bribes only when offering a prayer? Wen was described as one whose “glorious influence reached everywhere without fault,” yet he presented a daughter to Shou: this hardly seems the reverent caution of one who was “careful at heart.” Wu “sought to carry forward the virtue of his forebears,” yet received a mastiff as tribute from Lü: was this attentiveness to minor points of conduct? These sages possessed great virtue and brought about flourishing government. Why, then, do their deeds still contain matters susceptible to criticism?

Consider, too, the ruler who presided at court in profound silence, as majestic as a deity. He might be said to have possessed an august bearing; why, then, did the Han imperial enterprise decline? Another devoted himself diligently to government and nearly achieved great peace. He might be said to have enjoyed a reputation for illustrious virtue; why, then, did the Tang dynasty nearly fall? The ruler who honored the aged in the Biyong ceremonial academy and sat upright to lecture in person—was he not a sovereign who esteemed learning? Why was his faith in the Way insufficiently firm, bringing calamity upon the Central Kingdom? 終，以生近習之變？則果聰明者，若大有為，何以使民愁兵怨，而深為厲階？機巧多技能者，殆天縱之，何以致天異人妖，而終蹈夷禍？之數君者，皆挾異資，纘成業，而身名俱辱，取譏於後世，何哉？我太祖高皇帝、太宗文皇帝立極垂統，道德功烈真足以超軼禹湯文武，而並駕堯舜矣。豈天質之美，固出於尋常萬萬邪？抑亦有脩為之方、持守之要，可以為聖子神孫萬世法程而不可越者？諸士子生長畿甸，必嘗仰窺一二矣。其敬陳之，將轉而聞之於上。

…carry through to the end, thereby bringing about an upheaval among his intimate attendants? The ruler who was resolute and intelligent [?] seemed capable of great achievements; why did he cause distress among the people and resentment among the soldiers, becoming a grave source of calamity? The ruler whose ingenuity and many skills seemed almost Heaven-bestowed—why did he bring about celestial anomalies and human monstrosities, and ultimately suffer the calamity of destruction? These several rulers all possessed exceptional endowments and succeeded to established imperial enterprises. Why, then, were both their persons and their reputations disgraced, inviting the reproach of later generations?

Our Emperor Taizu Gao and Emperor Taizong Wen established the supreme standard and handed down the imperial succession. Their moral virtue and glorious achievements truly sufficed to surpass Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu, and to stand alongside Yao and Shun. Was the excellence of their natural endowments indeed countless times greater than that of ordinary men? Or were there also methods of self-cultivation and essential principles of steadfast observance that could serve as inviolable models for their sage sons and divine grandsons through ten thousand generations? punctuated:
制之用、軍國之需，古今一也。宋又有郊賚、歲幣、祠祿，今皆無之，宜其蓄積充牣，無所置之。顧乃皇皇焉有匱乏之憂，其必有故矣。昔人言為國有三計，其說可聞歟？今之國計，於是三者何居？有謂事之害財者有三冗，殆何所指？今於是三者孰甚？國計有錄，始見於唐，至宋作者尤眾，所以揔括天下財賦出入之數，而周知其有無多寡，以為豐殺增減者也。今亦可倣而為之歟？夫財匱而民怨，民裕而國昌，有國者不可以不慎，而錢穀之大數亦學者所當知也。其毋諉曰有主者！

問：詩曰：「詒厥孫謀，以燕翼子。」又曰：「干祿百福，子孫千億。」雖古聖賢，莫不願望其子孫之蕃昌，而凡頌禱乎人者，亦必歸重於是，蓋人情所同而天理之當然也。但常人狃於一時利害，乃或肆惡於身而
translation_en:
…expenditures prescribed by established institutions and the requirements of military and civil government are the same in ancient and modern times. The Song also had rewards distributed on the occasion of the suburban sacrifices, annual payments to foreign states, and stipends attached to temple sinecures. None of these exists today. Our accumulated reserves ought therefore to be so abundant that there is nowhere to store them. Yet instead there is anxious concern over shortages. There must surely be a reason for this. Men of former times said that governing a state involved three kinds of fiscal planning. Can you explain this saying? To which of these three does present-day state fiscal planning belong? It has been said that there are three forms of redundancy in public affairs that harm the finances. What exactly does this refer to? Which of these three is most serious today? Records of state finances first appeared under the Tang, and those who compiled them were especially numerous under the Song. Their purpose was to bring together the figures for revenue and expenditure throughout the realm, providing comprehensive knowledge of what was available or lacking, and in what quantities, as a basis for expanding or curtailing allocations and increasing or reducing expenditures. Could we now follow their example and compile such records? When resources are depleted, the people resent it; when the people are prosperous, the state flourishes. Those who govern a state must attend carefully to this. The overall figures for money and grain are also something scholars ought to know. Do not evade the matter by saying that there are officials responsible for it!

Question: The Book of Odes says: “He bequeathed plans to his descendants, thereby giving peace and aid to his children.” It also says: “Seek emoluments and a hundred blessings, with descendants in their thousands and hundreds of millions.” Even among the sages and worthies of antiquity, none failed to wish for their descendants to multiply and prosper. All who offer praise and prayers for others likewise place particular emphasis on this. It is indeed a sentiment shared by all people and accords with heavenly principle. Yet ordinary people, preoccupied with immediate advantage and harm, sometimes give free rein to their own wrongdoing and…

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
不顧其子孫亦有不達損益之理不覽
止足之分而營營於子孫富貴謀者皆
惑也茲以古人之言行可為勸戒者相
與評之身為相國祿入厚矣而不為子
孫治垣屋位謝太傅賜予渥矣而不為
子孫益產業果何所見乎身親隴畝子
孫將胼手胝足矣乃曰遺之以安性本
公廉子孫常蔬食步行矣乃曰遺之以
厚何以言之歟主母胡懼而遽有穆伯
===
絕嗣之嘆絕嗣果足深懼邪內史胡知
而遽有臧孫有後之稱有後果能前知
邪衣食餘饒臣節可以盡瘁借曰不然
能忘爾私乎田宅便好帝德可謂念功
借曰不然能保厥家乎治獄無寃而自
知其後必興然則過於殘酷者信及於
子孫否也將兵不妄殺而自知其後必
昌然則肆於屠僇者信殃其子孫否也
夫禍福之來以為天道之必然而善惡

===

知其後必興然則過於殘酷者信及於

昌然則肆於屠僇者信映其子孫否也
夫禍福之來以為天道之必然而善惡
punctuated: 不顧其子孫，亦有不達損益之理、不覽止足之分，而營營於子孫富貴謀者，皆惑也。茲以古人之言行可為勸戒者，相與評之。身為相國，祿入厚矣，而不為子孫治垣屋；位謝太傅，賜予渥矣，而不為子孫益產業，果何所見乎？身親隴畝，子孫將胼手胝足矣，乃曰遺之以安；性本公廉，子孫常蔬食步行矣，乃曰遺之以厚，何以言之歟？主母胡懼，而遽有穆伯絕嗣之嘆？絕嗣果足深懼邪？內史胡知，而遽有臧孫有後之稱？有後果能前知邪？衣食餘饒，臣節可以盡瘁，借曰不然，能忘爾私乎？田宅便好，帝德可謂念功，借曰不然，能保厥家乎？治獄無寃，而自知其後必興，然則過於殘酷者，信及於子孫否也？將兵不妄殺，而自知其後必昌，然則肆於屠僇者，信殃其子孫否也？夫禍福之來，以為天道之必然，而善惡
translation_en:
…without regard for their descendants. There are also those who do not understand the principles of loss and gain or recognize the proper bounds of knowing when to stop and be content, but busily scheme to secure wealth and rank for their descendants. All these people are deluded. Let us now discuss sayings and deeds of the ancients that may serve as encouragements and warnings.

One held office as Chancellor of State and received a generous salary, yet did not build houses for his descendants. Xie held office as Grand Mentor [?] and received abundant imperial gifts, yet did not enlarge his descendants’ property. What understanding lay behind their actions? One personally worked in the fields, so that his descendants would have callused hands and feet, yet he said he was bequeathing them peace. Another was by nature impartial and incorruptible, so that his descendants regularly ate vegetables and traveled on foot, yet he said he was bequeathing them abundance. How can these statements be explained?

What did the mother of the household [?] fear, that she suddenly lamented that Mu Bo’s line would die out? Is the extinction of one’s line indeed something greatly to fear? What did the Interior Scribe know, that he suddenly declared that Zangsun would have descendants? Can the continuation of a line really be known in advance?

With food and clothing in abundance, a minister can devote himself utterly to his duty. Supposing this were not so, could you forget your private interests? In providing comfortable fields and dwellings, the emperor’s benevolence may be said to remember meritorious service. Supposing this were not so, could one preserve one’s household?

A man who decided legal cases without injustice knew that his descendants would surely flourish. Does it follow that the consequences of excessive cruelty truly extend to one’s descendants? A man who commanded troops without indiscriminate killing knew that his descendants would surely prosper. Does it follow that those who indulge in slaughter truly bring calamity upon their descendants?

As for the coming of calamity and good fortune, one may regard it as the inevitable working of the Way of Heaven, yet good and evil…

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之報時有不類以為人事之適然而成
敗之迹又似可徴亦有一定之說可恃
之訓乎諸士子皆将事
君臨民以右其族而世其家者其肆言之以觀
擇術之慎
問戎狄為中國患自古然矣今之桀黠時
出沒於吾邊境而侵寇者盖昔之入主
中夏而吾之所驅逐以還之塞外者也
則防邊之政宜百倍於前代而後可我
===
朝自立國以来虜嘗為患而卒無大憂豈非
立法之善足以維持為萬世之防哉近
歳虜寇往往深入重獲略無創艾而去
比者宣府之警盖不特侵及涇陽候騎
至雍而已豈承平日久舊政多廢而未
舉歟此其為患盖不小也盜賊竊發亦
治世所不免至於前數年之盜流毒幾
遍天下至遣制帥調邊卒以成勦平之
功禍亦亟矣則弭盜之術尤今日所宜

朝自立國以來虜嘗爲患而卒無大憂豈非
立法之善足以維持爲萬世之防哉近
歲虜寇往往深入重獲略無創艾而去
比者宣府之警蓋不特侵及涇陽候騎
至雍而已豈承平日久舊政多廢而未
舉歟此其爲患蓋不小也盜賊竊發亦
治世所不免至於前數年之盜流毒幾
遍天下至遣制師調邊卒以成剿平之
功禍亦亟矣則弭盜之術尤今日所宜
punctuated:
之報，時有不類；以為人事之適然，而成敗之迹又似可徴。亦有一定之說、可恃之訓乎？諸士子皆将事君臨民，以右其族而世其家者，其肆言之，以觀擇術之慎。

問：戎狄為中國患，自古然矣。今之桀黠，時出沒於吾邊境而侵寇者，盖昔之入主中夏，而吾之所驅逐以還之塞外者也。則防邊之政，宜百倍於前代而後可。我朝自立國以来，虜嘗為患，而卒無大憂，豈非立法之善，足以維持，為萬世之防哉？近歳虜寇往往深入，重獲，略無創艾而去。比者宣府之警，盖不特侵及涇陽、候騎至雍而已。豈承平日久，舊政多廢而未舉歟？此其為患，盖不小也。盜賊竊發，亦治世所不免。至於前數年之盜，流毒幾遍天下，至遣制帥、調邊卒，以成勦平之功，禍亦亟矣。則弭盜之術，尤今日所宜
translation_en:
…yet the recompense for good and evil sometimes fails to correspond to the deeds. If one considers these outcomes mere contingencies of human affairs, the traces of success and failure nevertheless seem to offer evidence. Is there, then, a settled explanation or a teaching on which one can rely? You candidates will all serve the ruler and govern the people, thereby supporting your clans and perpetuating your families through the generations. Set forth your views fully, so that we may observe the care with which you choose your course of action.

Question: That the Rong and Di have troubled China has been so since antiquity. The fierce and cunning men who now appear intermittently along our frontiers to invade and plunder are, indeed, those who formerly entered and ruled the Central Lands, whom we expelled and drove back beyond the frontier. Our policies for frontier defense must therefore surpass those of earlier dynasties a hundredfold before they can be adequate. Since our dynasty was founded, these barbarians have caused trouble, yet ultimately no great calamity has ensued. Is this not because the excellence of our established institutions has sufficed to sustain us and provide a defense for ten thousand generations?

In recent years, barbarian raiders have repeatedly penetrated deep into our territory, taken substantial booty, and departed virtually unscathed and undeterred. The recent alarm at Xuanfu surely amounted to more than merely an invasion reaching Jingyang and mounted scouts arriving at Yong. Could it be that, after a long period of peace, many former measures have fallen into disuse and have not been restored? The danger this poses is certainly no small matter.

Outbreaks of banditry are unavoidable even in a well-governed age. Yet the bandits of the past few years spread their devastation almost throughout the realm, to the point that commanders-in-chief had to be dispatched and frontier troops mobilized to accomplish their suppression and pacification. The calamity was indeed grave. Thus, methods of putting an end to banditry are especially what today ought to…

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
加意者夫戎狄為患亦禦之而已然有
謂禦戎無上策當以氣勝之其說亦有
據乎禦之之策不過振國威飭邊備練
士卒實倉廩而已然有謂其本不在乎
威疆其任不在乎邊境其具不在乎兵
食然則竟安在乎所指急先之務亦可
行於今日乎弭盜之術則論盜有三源
者盡之又曰患莫大於招降禍莫深於
窮治然則何施而可此二者當今之所
===
欲急聞也願得良策以裨執政幸毋讓

punctuated: 加意者。夫戎狄為患，亦禦之而已。然有謂「禦戎無上策，當以氣勝之」，其說亦有據乎？禦之之策，不過振國威、飭邊備、練士卒、實倉廩而已。然有謂「其本不在乎威疆，其任不在乎邊境，其具不在乎兵食」，然則竟安在乎？所指急先之務，亦可行於今日乎？弭盜之術，則論盜有三源者盡之。又曰：「患莫大於招降，禍莫深於窮治。」然則何施而可？此二者，當今之所欲急聞也。願得良策，以裨執政，幸毋讓。
translation_en: …to which particular attention should be given. When the Rong and Di cause trouble, one need only defend against them. Yet some say, “There is no supreme strategy for resisting the Rong; one must overcome them through spirit.” Does this assertion have any basis? Strategies for resisting them amount to no more than asserting the state’s might, putting frontier defenses in order, training the troops, and filling the granaries. Yet some say, “Its foundation does not lie in might and territory; responsibility for it does not lie at the frontier; its means do not lie in troops and provisions.” Where, then, do these actually lie? Can the urgent priorities indicated by this saying also be put into practice today? As for methods of suppressing banditry, the argument that banditry has three sources treats the matter exhaustively. It is also said, “No danger is greater than inviting surrender; no calamity is more profound than pursuing investigations to the utmost.” What measures, then, would be appropriate? These two matters are what we urgently wish to hear about at present. We hope to obtain sound strategies to assist those governing; please do not hold back.

punctuated:
第壹場

四書

舉直錯諸枉，能使枉者直。

同考試官教諭敖批：舉直錯枉，只是一事。直者舉，枉者自錯，詳味語意自見。場中士子多未達者，此作體認精切，而詞亦簡當，必勤學士也。讀者當自知之。

同考試官教諭周批：作此題者，每病於發露仁知太早，且或膚稺可厭。此作理得而詞順，蓋傑然者，宜錄以為式。

同考試官教諭柯批：聖人之言，如化工渾然無迹，而以舉業排比之文擬之，難矣。繩墨不踰，而理趣自到，僅見此篇。錄之以示作《論語》義者。

考試官左諭德顧批：明白雅健，可取。

考試官侍讀學士汪批：詳整可誦。

人不苟用，而衆因以化。聖人之曉門人也，蓋舉直而錯枉，是不苟於用人矣。枉者皆化而為直，
translation_en:
First Session

Four Books

“Promote the upright and set the crooked aside: this can make the crooked upright.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Ao, Instructor: Promoting the upright and setting the crooked aside are a single act. When the upright are promoted, the crooked are naturally set aside. Carefully savor the wording, and its meaning becomes apparent. Many candidates in the examination hall failed to grasp this. This composition shows precise and penetrating understanding, and its language is concise and apt. Its author must be a diligent student. Readers should recognize this for themselves.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhou, Instructor: Those who write on this topic commonly make the mistake of bringing benevolence and wisdom into view too early; some are also tiresomely superficial and immature. This composition grasps the principle and expresses it fluently. It is outstanding and should be recorded as a model.

Comment by Associate Examiner Ke, Instructor: The sage’s words are like nature’s creative workings, seamless and leaving no trace of artifice. It is difficult to emulate them through the parallel constructions of examination prose. Only in this piece have I seen the prescribed rules observed while the import of the principle emerges naturally. It is recorded here for those composing expositions on the Analects.

Comment by Examiner Gu, Left Admonisher: Clear, elegant, and vigorous; worthy of acceptance.

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting: Thorough and well ordered; worthy of recitation.

When men are not employed indiscriminately, the multitude is thereby transformed. In enlightening his disciples, the sage meant that promoting the upright and setting the crooked aside constitutes care in employing men. The crooked are all transformed and become upright…

text:
其容已乎聖人荅樊遲問仁知至此盖謂知人
愛人若非一端曰仁與知本無二道君子於人
鑒裁既精於一心之明察識復稽於衆論之審
其選而舉之使服在大僚簡而拔之俾列於庶
位者必皆經德不回侃侃之正人也彊立不反
藹藹之吉士也盖直者必舉而所舉無不直焉
凡委置在下而不齒於衣冠之列遺棄于野而
不預夫爵命之榮者莫非罔其生理蚩蚩之衆
人也拂其常性碌碌之鄙夫也盖所錯皆枉而
===
枉者無不錯焉夫如是則旌別所及黙寓鼓舞
之機好惡所加自有感化之妙莫不曰彼善是
我乃未善彼能是我乃未能我之棄置固其所
也率相砥礪舎舊而新是圖昔之枉者皆化而
為直矣又孰不曰人所知可學而知人所行可
勉而行我之致用猶可為也爭自濯磨去惡而
善是從昔之錯者皆直而可舉矣是則即知人
之知寓愛人之仁仁知之相為用盖如此樊遲
未達聖人得不明言以曉之哉抑嘗因是而思

translation_en:
…how could this fail to happen? At this point in the Sage’s reply to Fan Chi’s questions about benevolence and wisdom, his meaning was that discerning people and loving people might seem to be separate matters, yet benevolence and wisdom fundamentally do not constitute two different ways. In judging people, the gentleman exercises refined discernment through the clarity of his own mind, and further tests his understanding against the considered judgments of others. Those whom he selects and promotes to serve in high office, and chooses and advances to occupy the various posts, must all be upright men who steadfastly uphold virtue without deviation and speak with forthright assurance, worthy men of gracious bearing who stand firm without turning back. Thus the upright are invariably promoted, and none of those promoted is other than upright. Those left in lowly circumstances, excluded from the ranks of officials, and abandoned in the countryside without sharing in the honor of rank and appointment are all undiscerning ordinary men who disregard the principles of their inborn nature, or mediocre, petty men who act against their constant nature. Thus all those set aside are crooked, and none of the crooked escapes being set aside.

When this is so, the very act of distinguishing people’s merits silently contains the means to stir them to exertion; the expression of approval and disapproval naturally possesses the subtle power to transform them. They all say: “He is good at this, while I am not yet good at it; he can do this, while I cannot yet do it. It is only fitting that I have been set aside.” Together they encourage and sharpen one another, abandoning their former ways and seeking renewal, until those formerly crooked are all transformed into the upright. And who would not also say: “What others know, I can learn to know; what others practice, I can exert myself to practice. It is still possible for me to become useful in service.” They vie to cleanse and polish themselves, abandoning evil and following goodness, until those formerly set aside are all upright and fit for promotion. Thus the wisdom that discerns people embodies the benevolence that loves them: this is how benevolence and wisdom work through one another. Since Fan Chi had not understood, how could the Sage fail to explain this plainly to enlighten him? Yet, prompted by this, I have also reflected that…

…Among the affairs of the realm, none is more consequential than promoting some men and setting others aside. The ascendancy or decline of gentlemen and petty men, the allegiance or disaffection of the people, and the successes or failures of government all arise from this. Shun promoted Gao Yao, and Tang promoted Yi Yin, and those lacking benevolence withdrew. The government of the sages amounted to no more than this. From the Han and Tang onward, rulers failed to distinguish clearly whom to employ and whom to reject. Gentlemen and petty men alternately prevailed, and order or disorder in the state followed accordingly. Can a ruler, then, afford to be incautious in promoting men and setting them aside?
“Perfecting oneself is benevolence; perfecting things is wisdom. These are virtues of human nature, the Way that unites the internal and the external. Hence, when put into practice as circumstances require, they are fitting.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Yi, Instructor: The passages explaining unity and timely application are precise and well grounded. The author seems to have devoted effort to experiencing and embodying benevolence and wisdom. He certainly cannot be regarded as an ordinary examination candidate.
Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, School Director: The topic itself is clear, but writers become entangled in forced connections and find themselves painfully constrained. This essay speaks directly on the basis of principle, without the slightest obstruction; it may be said to expound the Doctrine of the Mean.
Comment by Examiner Gu, Left Admonisher: A work of exquisite subtlety.
Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting: The essay has coherence and depth of principle.
Once what belongs to one's nature is fully realized within oneself, its exercise naturally extends throughout one's practical activity. This is the work of one who strives to become sincere. For there is no affair outside the bounds of one's inherent nature. When benevolence and wisdom are both fully realized and applied to affairs, could anything fail to be fitting? text:
成已言之私欲淨盡而本心之德湛乎其恒存
天理純全而本然之體昭乎其不昧非仁乎以
成物言之大以成大小以成小曲成而不遺也
立必俱立成不獨成兼濟而無外也非知乎仁
以為體知以為用性分固有合體用而一原者
也仁存諸內知形諸外隨地異名合內外而一
道者也夫知而未仁則其公不足以立制事之
本仁而未知則其明不足以妙應物之機仁知
具內外一於是乎施之於一身或左或右與時
===
宜之無不中其適矣施之於天下若大若小以
時措之無不得其當矣無所用而不周無所施
而不利盖沛乎其有餘也處經事而知宜遭變
事而知權盖無乎而不可也誠之者之功用如
此其大此君子所以必誠之為貴歟大抵仁知

者見之謂之仁知者見之謂之知君子之道鮮
矣必仁知合一而後大人之事備時措之宜盖
聖人過化存神之用也誠之者至此則與聖人

translation_en:
…speaking of perfecting oneself, selfish desires are utterly purged, and the virtue of the original mind abides constantly in its limpid purity; heavenly principle is wholly pure, and the mind’s original substance shines undimmed. Is this not benevolence? Speaking of perfecting things, the great are perfected according to their greatness and the small according to their smallness: each is perfected in all its particulars, with none neglected. In establishing oneself, one necessarily establishes others as well; in attaining fulfillment, one does not attain it alone. One benefits all, excluding none. Is this not wisdom? Benevolence constitutes the substance, and wisdom constitutes its functioning. Our inherent nature possesses that which unites substance and functioning in a single source. Benevolence resides within, and wisdom manifests itself without; their names differ according to their sphere, but they unite the internal and external in a single Way.

If one has wisdom but has not attained benevolence, one’s impartiality is insufficient to establish the foundation for ordering affairs. If one has benevolence but has not attained wisdom, one’s discernment is insufficient to respond with subtle mastery to the workings of things. When benevolence and wisdom are both complete and the internal and external are one, their application to one’s own person, whether turning left or right, accords with what the time requires and never fails to fit the circumstances. Applied to all under Heaven, in matters great or small, they are put into practice at the proper time and never fail to be fitting. There is no employment in which they are not comprehensive, no application in which they are not beneficial: indeed, their abundance more than suffices. In handling ordinary affairs, one knows what is appropriate; in encountering exceptional affairs, one knows how to weigh circumstances. Indeed, there is no situation in which they are inadequate. So great is the efficacy of one who makes himself sincere! Is this why the gentleman necessarily prizes making himself sincere?

Generally speaking, when benevolence and wisdom are discussed separately, each embodies only its own virtue and is still insufficient for full practical efficacy. Thus it is said: “The benevolent see it and call it benevolence; the wise see it and call it wisdom. Few attain the Way of the gentleman.” Only when benevolence and wisdom are united are the undertakings of the great person complete. Applying them appropriately to the time is indeed the functioning of the sage, who transforms wherever he passes and whose presence is spiritual in its efficacy. When one who makes himself sincere reaches this point, then, in relation to the sage…

translation_en:
…comes close to the sage. Let the reader consider this carefully.

“If one's conduct leaves the heart dissatisfied, then one's qi becomes starved. This is why I say that Gaozi has never understood righteousness: he treats it as external.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Tang, Instructor: Mencius repeatedly refuted the claim that righteousness is external; its falsity becomes especially evident when tested against the cultivation of qi. This essay develops the matter almost exhaustively—a truly difficult achievement.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhou, Instructor: This topic is especially crucial to the chapter on cultivating qi. The flaw in Gaozi's claim that righteousness is external collapses without needing an attack. This essay offers real illumination. It is an excellent piece; include it.

Comment by Examiner Gu, Left Mentor: The writing fully elucidates the principle. It merits inclusion.

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting: His words suggest that he has grasped something of the matter.

By examining why qi fails to attain fullness, we recognize that righteousness cannot be described as external. Qi becomes full when properly nourished and starved when deprived of nourishment: all of this depends upon righteousness. How could someone who regards righteousness as external comprehend this? Mencius's meaning is that the vast, flowing qi can be generated through the accumulation of righteous acts; it cannot be seized through an isolated act of righteousness. The affairs that proceed from within and respond to what is outside vary in countless ways. If the weight assigned to them is at all inappropriate, shame manifests itself in one's every movement. Can the heart then feel at ease? Actions that issue from what is near and become manifest far away are likewise diverse. If their measure, whether long or short, departs at all from what is fitting, regret and self-reproach accumulate in the most hidden recesses. Can the heart then feel satisfied? From this …

text:
是氣之至大者雖曰初無限量也心無以為之
主而欿乎其小矣氣之至剛者雖曰不可屈撓
也心無以為之帥而索乎其微矣養氣必主乎
義如此然則義豈在外哉彼告子者乃曰義外
也非內也是不知而妄言者也彼義之見於事
者或輕或重若在外矣而本然之權則由中制
而非外也義之形於行者或長或短若在外矣
而本然之度則由內出而非外也以義為外而
不復以集義為事則盛大之體流行之用彼盖
===
有所未窺也不能養氣而徒欲不動其心則冥
然罔覺悍然不顧彼盖自以為至也謂之曰未
甞知義信乎其於義有所未達也歟大抵判心
跡於二途者異端之曲說合體用而一致者吾
道之大全也告子外義以求不動其心盖於佛
老之學絕事物以求心者類矣孟子性善養氣
之論擴前聖所未發而闢義外之說尤有功於

punctuated:
是氣之至大者，雖曰初無限量也，心無以為之主，而欿乎其小矣；氣之至剛者，雖曰不可屈撓也，心無以為之帥，而索乎其微矣。養氣必主乎義如此，然則義豈在外哉？彼告子者乃曰：「義外也，非內也。」是不知而妄言者也。彼義之見於事者，或輕或重，若在外矣，而本然之權則由中制，而非外也；義之形於行者，或長或短，若在外矣，而本然之度則由內出，而非外也。以義為外，而不復以集義為事，則盛大之體、流行之用，彼盖有所未窺也。不能養氣，而徒欲不動其心，則冥然罔覺，悍然不顧，彼盖自以為至也。謂之曰「未甞知義」，信乎其於義有所未達也歟！大抵判心跡於二途者，異端之曲說；合體用而一致者，吾道之大全也。告子外義以求不動其心，盖於佛老之學絕事物以求心者類矣。孟子性善養氣之論，擴前聖所未發，而闢義外之說，尤有功於後學。學者宜致思焉。

易
translation_en:
…Thus, although this qi, in its utmost greatness, originally knows no limits, without the heart to govern it, it dwindles into littleness; although this qi, in its utmost firmness, cannot be bent or broken, without the heart to command it, it withers into weakness. Nourishing qi must depend upon righteousness in this way. How, then, could righteousness be external? Yet Gaozi says: “Righteousness is external, not internal.” This is reckless speech born of ignorance. Righteousness manifested in affairs may give something lesser or greater weight and thus seem external; yet the inherent balance that weighs it is controlled from within, not from without. Righteousness embodied in conduct may allow a longer or shorter measure and thus seem external; yet its inherent standard issues from within, not from without. If one regards righteousness as external and no longer makes accumulating righteous deeds one’s concern, then one has surely not glimpsed the fullness of qi’s substance or the flowing activity of its functioning. Unable to nourish qi, yet merely wishing to keep his heart unmoved, he remains benighted and unperceiving, obstinately heedless, apparently considering himself to have reached perfection. To say that he “has never understood righteousness” is surely to say that there is something in righteousness he has failed to comprehend!

Broadly speaking, to separate the heart and its outward manifestations into two paths is the distorted teaching of heterodoxy; to unite substance and function in a single coherence is the completeness of our Way. Gaozi treats righteousness as external in seeking to keep his heart unmoved. In this he resembles those followers of Buddhist and Daoist learning who sever themselves from affairs and things in order to seek the heart. Mengzi’s discussions of the goodness of human nature and the nourishment of qi develop what earlier sages had not yet articulated; his refutation of the claim that righteousness is external has rendered an especially great service to later students. Students should ponder this deeply.

九五：渙汗其大號，渙王居，无咎。

同考試官教諭易批：濟渙莫要於此二事，周公詔後世之意，可謂喫緊。此作足以發之，而文亦精潔可愛，蓋深於易者。

考試官左諭德顧批：文有發明。

考試官侍讀學士汪批：詞足以發而不浮，非苟作者。

事合濟渙之宜，占獲補過之善，渙九五爻義也。蓋渙其號令、居積以濟渙，則事合宜而渙可濟矣。過不於是而補乎？爻易聖人之意若曰：渙之九五，陽剛中正，以居尊位，當濟渙之任，有濟渙之具者也。是故時過於豐，而紀綱不能無解弛；物極於豫，而人心不能無乖離，所謂渙也。王者值此，何以濟之？必推誠引咎，脩辭命以誥四方
translation_en:
Nine in the fifth place: Disperse his great proclamations as sweat spreads; distribute the king’s stores. No blame.

Comment by Associate Examiner Yi, an Instructor: Nothing is more essential to remedying dispersion than these two measures. The Duke of Zhou’s intention in instructing later generations may well be called urgently pertinent. This composition adequately brings it out, and its prose is also refined, spare, and pleasing. Its author evidently understands the Book of Changes deeply.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, a School Instructor: Those who compose essays on the meaning of the Book of Changes fall either into coarseness or into obscurity and rigidity, altogether departing from the proper character of such writing. Late in the process I obtained this essay: lucid, fluent, thorough, and elegant, it leaves out neither practical matters nor their principles. It should be recorded as a model for later students.

Comment by Examiner Gu, Left Admonisher: The composition brings out new understanding.

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting: Its language adequately develops the meaning without becoming superficial. This is no carelessly composed work.

To act appropriately in remedying dispersion, and to obtain through divination the good result of making amends for errors: this is the meaning of the ninth-in-the-fifth-place line of Dispersion. By disseminating proclamations and distributing accumulated stores to remedy dispersion, one acts appropriately, and dispersion can be remedied. Are not errors thereby made good? The sage’s intention in the line text of the Changes [?] seems to say: The nine in the fifth place of Dispersion is yang and firm, central and correct, and occupies the exalted position. It bears responsibility for remedying dispersion and possesses the means to do so. Thus, when an age passes beyond abundance, its governing order inevitably slackens; when circumstances reach the extreme of ease, people’s hearts inevitably become estranged. This is what is called dispersion. When a king encounters this, how can he remedy it? He must manifest sincerity and take responsibility for faults, carefully preparing proclamations to address the four quarters…

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
安內攘外布號令以新天下言出乎身加乎民
周流磅礴有以浹於民之肌膚令出惟行弗惟
反融液透徹有以切於民之疾苦開張公道而
幽枉畢達也掃除煩苛而風聲丕變也大號非
時所當渙者乎然徒事虛文不可也必敷實德
以拯塗炭之危託諸空言不可也必布大惠以
慰雲霓之望厚歛可懲而倉廩之粟在所必發
悖出可虞而府庫之財在所必散以四海為一
家大賚有不惜也視百姓猶吾子博施有不郚
===
也王居又非義所當渙者乎夫如是則施為有
序足以折釁孽之萌處置得宜可以消反側之
禍興滯補弊而紀綱為之復振說近來遠而人
心為之再安大業繫於苞桑始雖過而善於補
矣於義為无咎焉丕基固於磐石初雖失而不
遠復矣其占得无咎焉吁因一巳之渙以濟天
下之渙周公示占之意可謂深切著明矣抑考
渙之上體巽也巽象為風德為入有號令之義
其卦為陰陰主利有居積之義故姤以乾遇巽

punctuated: 安內攘外，布號令以新天下。言出乎身，加乎民，周流磅礴，有以浹於民之肌膚；令出惟行，弗惟反，融液透徹，有以切於民之疾苦。開張公道，而幽枉畢達也；掃除煩苛，而風聲丕變也。大號非時所當渙者乎？然徒事虛文不可也，必敷實德以拯塗炭之危；託諸空言不可也，必布大惠以慰雲霓之望。厚歛可懲，而倉廩之粟在所必發；悖出可虞，而府庫之財在所必散。以四海為一家，大賚有不惜也；視百姓猶吾子，博施有不郚也。王居又非義所當渙者乎？夫如是，則施為有序，足以折釁孽之萌；處置得宜，可以消反側之禍。興滯補弊，而紀綱為之復振；說近來遠，而人心為之再安。大業繫於苞桑，始雖過而善於補矣，於義為无咎焉；丕基固於磐石，初雖失而不遠復矣，其占得无咎焉。吁！因一巳之渙以濟天下之渙，周公示占之意，可謂深切著明矣。抑考渙之上體，巽也。巽象為風，德為入，有號令之義；其卦為陰，陰主利，有居積之義。故姤以乾遇巽
translation_en:
…to secure the realm internally and repel threats from outside, issuing proclamations and commands to renew all under Heaven. Words proceed from the ruler himself and extend to the people, circulating far and wide until they penetrate the people's very flesh and skin. Once commands are issued, they must be carried out, not reversed; they must permeate thoroughly and address the people's hardships directly. Open the public way of justice, and all hidden grievances will find a hearing; sweep away vexatious and harsh measures, and the prevailing moral atmosphere will be greatly transformed. Are great proclamations not what the times require him to disseminate?

Yet merely attending to empty formalities will not do: he must extend substantial virtue to rescue people from desperate suffering. Relying on empty words will not do: he must bestow great beneficence to satisfy their hopes, like those who look for clouds and rainbows in a drought. Excessive exactions should serve as a warning, and the grain in the granaries must be distributed. The prospect of wealth departing through wrongful means is cause for concern, and the riches in the treasuries must be dispersed. Treating all within the four seas as one family, he will not begrudge generous gifts; regarding the common people as his own children, he will bestow widely without [?]. Are the royal stores not also what righteousness requires him to disperse?

If he acts thus, his measures will be orderly, sufficient to cut off the beginnings of strife and calamity; his arrangements will be appropriate, able to avert trouble from the disaffected. By reviving what has languished and remedying abuses, he will restore the governing framework; by delighting those nearby and attracting those afar, he will bring renewed peace to people's hearts. His great enterprise will be secured as though bound to a clump of mulberry trees: although there were errors at first, he will have remedied them well, and in terms of right conduct there will be ‘no blame.’ His grand foundation will be as firm as a massive rock: although he initially went astray, he will have returned before going far, and the prognostication will yield ‘no blame.’ Ah! By dispersing what belongs to himself alone, he remedies the dispersal of all under Heaven. The Duke of Zhou's intention in setting forth this prognostication may indeed be called profound, pertinent, and manifestly clear.

Moreover, examining the upper trigram of Dispersion (Huan), we find Gentle Penetration (Xun). Xun's image is wind and its attribute is penetration, giving it the significance of proclamations and commands. It is a yin trigram, and yin governs material benefit, giving it the significance of accumulated stores. Thus, in Coming to Meet (Gou), Creative Heaven (Qian) encounters Xun…

則如風之被物而天道行矣能渙其居則是以
陽勝陰而天德粹矣尚何渙之不可濟哉爻易
取義各有攸當此又觀象玩辭者所當知

translation_en:
…the Commentary on the Great Image likewise says, “Issue commands.” In Jiaren (The Family), Li encounters Xun, and the statement for the six in the fourth place likewise says, “Enrich the family.” Although the nine in the fifth place occupies the body of Xun, its capacity enables it to act effectively. If it can disperse its commands, then, like the wind spreading over things, the Way of Heaven will operate. If it can disperse its accumulated stores, then yang will overcome yin, and Heaven’s virtue will be pure. What difficulty of dispersion could then remain unresolved? The lines and their changes [?] each draw their meaning from what is appropriate to them. This, too, is something those who contemplate the images and ponder the statements should understand.
“‘Numinous’ describes the wondrous working upon the myriad things. Nothing sets the myriad things in motion more swiftly than thunder; nothing stirs them more swiftly than wind; nothing dries them more thoroughly than fire; nothing delights them more than the marsh; nothing moistens them more than water; and nothing brings them to their end and their beginning more fully than Gen (Keeping Still). Thus water and fire reach one another, thunder and wind do not oppose one another, and mountain and marsh communicate their vital energies. Only then can transformation and change take place and bring the myriad things to completion.”
Comment by Associate Examiner Yi, Instructor: The study of the diagrams is inherently difficult, yet readers of the Book of Changes carelessly fail to examine it. Thus many plagiarize familiar phrases merely to fill out an essay. This composition says what others cannot say, and its language is also pure, elegant, and worthy of contemplation. Its author has evidently immersed himself deeply in the diagrams and gained understanding from them.
Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, Instructor: This topic places particular emphasis on the single statement concerning the numinous and its wondrous working upon the myriad things. This is the profound import of the study of the Prior Heaven and Later Heaven diagrams. Could Confucius have omitted Qian and Kun and spoken of the numinous without a purpose? Many write without understanding this. For profound and precise attainment, and for clear and exhaustive expression, none equals this …

說卦發明至神之無方必詳六子之造化以見
之也夫神妙萬物本無方也造化之見於六子
者孰非神之所為乎說卦聖人之意若曰造化
之迹固可見於六子陰陽之妙尤不外於一神
神也者寓乎氣而不倚於氣超乎物而不離於
物妙應不測變化無方之謂也果何以見之震
===
居東方動萬物而迅其機者雷也巽居東南撓
萬物以速其化者風也離居於南物長以燥火
之所燥也兌居於西物成而遂澤之所說也坎
居正北萬物歸藏皆水之所潤也艮居東北萬
物始終皆艮之所成也後天六子為陰為陽各
專其功即造化之推遷於四時者如此然豈無

translation_en:
…this essay; hence it has been selected for inclusion.
Examiner Gu, Left Admonisher to the Heir Apparent, comments: “The principle is indeed as stated.”
Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting, comments: “The exposition is lucid and clean.”
To elucidate the absence of any fixed direction in the supremely numinous, the Discussion of the Trigrams (Shuogua) must explain in detail the workings of creation and transformation in the six children—the six subsidiary trigrams—and thereby reveal it. The numinous, which works its wonders in the myriad things, is fundamentally without fixed direction. Of the workings of creation and transformation manifested in the six children, which are not the doing of the numinous? The sage’s meaning in the Discussion of the Trigrams is as though he were saying: the traces of creation and transformation can certainly be seen in the six children, but the wondrous workings of yin and yang are still encompassed by the single numinous power. The numinous resides in qi yet does not depend upon qi; it transcends things yet does not depart from things. It signifies wondrous responses that cannot be fathomed and transformations without fixed direction. How, then, can this actually be seen?
Zhen occupies the east: that which sets the myriad things in motion and quickens their incipient activity is thunder. Xun occupies the southeast: that which stirs the myriad things and hastens their transformation is wind. Li occupies the south: things grow and become dry through the drying action of fire. Dui occupies the west: things mature and reach fulfillment through the gladdening action of the marsh. Kan occupies due north: the myriad things return to storage, all moistened by water. Gen occupies the northeast: the beginnings and endings of the myriad things are all brought to completion by Gen. In the Later Heaven arrangement, the six children, whether yin or yang, each perform their particular work. Such is the progression of creation and transformation through the four seasons. Yet could this have no underlying basis?
Thus Li is positioned in the east and Kan in the west: water and fire reach one another in their operation without repelling one another. Zhen is positioned in the northeast and Xun in the southwest: the forces of thunder and wind mutually assist and augment one another without opposing one another. Gen is positioned in the northwest and Dui in the southeast…

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
山澤之氣彼此感通而不相隔焉後天六子一
陰一陽各得其偶即造化之象形於兩間者爾
夫位有對待斯用有流行體有配合斯氣有變
化於是陰變為陽陽化為陰往来不窮以司亨
毒之妙陰極復變陽極復化進退不已以鼓顯
蔵之機而凡物之盈於兩間生於四時者大造
而無間曲成而不遺矣然何莫非神之所為也
哉吁神之可見於先天後天卦位者如此宜聖
人發以示人歟抑此章去乾坤而專言六子豈
===
以二老不用歟曰非然也先天圖學所以明造
化之體乾坤陰陽也即天地也六子陰陽之經
緯乎其間者爾陰陽不測之謂神言神則乾坤
在其中矣後天退乾於西北退坤於西南六子
各易其位者所以著造化之用皆出於理勢之
自然爾然致役者母之養也戰者父之成也曰
坤者地則乾為天可知是二老君蔵之道亦未
嘗不在焉後天豈出於先天之外哉故曰帝曰
萬物曰神曰八卦曰六子合而言之一陰一陽
