punctuated:
考試官侍讀學士汪批〔善敷陳，末寓忠愛之意，足占所蘊。〕

人君欲治天下，正其心而已矣；欲正其心，務於學而已矣。夫君心，天下之大本也。天下之治忽係於心，心之邪正本於學。上古帝王暨我祖宗，心學淵微，先後一揆，是以天下善治，而道德功烈垂休無窮。漢唐宋諸君不知務學以正其心，是以事功卑汚，名譽不終，而卒詒後世非笑。於乎，可不鑒哉！請因執事之問而陳之。

自古及今，聖治之善莫過於唐虞，而君德之盛亦莫過於堯舜。禹湯文武，善法堯舜者也。是故克勤於邦，克儉於家，禹豈湎於旨酒者乎？防微杜漸，曰為後世慮，宜爾也。以義制事，以禮制心，湯豈黷於苞苴者乎？省愆思咎，曰遇災而懼，宜爾也。樂天知命，不顯維德也。獻女釋囚，閔夭之徒自獻耳，文王何歁乎？建極錫福，無競維
translation_en:
Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting, comments: 〔The exposition is skillful; its conclusion conveys loyal devotion, sufficiently revealing the qualities within the writer.〕

If a ruler wishes to govern All under Heaven, he need only rectify his heart; if he wishes to rectify his heart, he need only devote himself to learning. The ruler’s heart is the great foundation of All under Heaven. Order or disorder throughout the realm depends upon his heart, and whether his heart is wayward or upright depends upon his learning. The emperors and kings of high antiquity and our imperial ancestors shared the same profound and subtle learning of the heart, following one standard across the ages. Thus All under Heaven was well governed, and their moral virtue and meritorious achievements bequeathed blessings without end. The rulers of the Han, Tang, and Song did not understand that they must devote themselves to learning in order to rectify their hearts. Consequently, their achievements were lowly and sullied, their reputations did not endure, and they ultimately became objects of criticism and ridicule for later generations. Alas! Can we fail to take warning? Allow me to set this forth in response to your question.

From antiquity to the present, no sage government has surpassed that of Tang and Yu, and no rulers’ virtue has surpassed that of Yao and Shun. Yu, Tang, King Wen, and King Wu were skilled in taking Yao and Shun as their models. Thus, being diligent in affairs of state and frugal in his household, could Yu have been one to indulge in fine wine? Guarding against the slightest signs of evil and blocking its gradual growth, he spoke of concern for later generations: this was fitting. Regulating affairs through righteousness and his heart through ritual propriety, could Tang have sullied himself with bribes? Examining his transgressions and reflecting upon his faults, he spoke of fear when calamity struck: this was fitting. King Wen delighted in Heaven and understood its mandate: how illustrious was his virtue! As for presenting women to secure a prisoner’s release, it was Min Yao [?] and his associates who made the presentation on their own. What deception was there on King Wen’s part [?]? King Wu established the supreme standard and bestowed blessings; none could rival his…

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
烈也底貢厥獒西旅自貢耳武王奚累乎
之數聖人者學已至矣而憂勤之念不息
心已正矣而操存之功不忘觀其執厥中
而敷文命也顧天命而脩人紀也危平易
傾之道演於易也敬怠義欲之戒受於丹
書也德業之盛與天無極有由然哉漢唐
宋諸君不知法堯舜者也是故成帝外雖
尊嚴而內則湛於酒色陽阿禍水莫止披
香博士之唾漢業之遂衰宜也玄宗初雖
===
勵精而未幾溺於嬖幸華清麗質久垂栁
城胡孽之涎唐祚之不移幸也明帝尊師
重傅正坐自講似矣而迎佛書於天竺以
汙中夏文明之統右文者固若是乎憲宗
銳意勤政削平僭叛得矣而餌丹藥於方
士以速近習慘烈之變願治者固若是乎
瓊林之財大盈之積如民之膏血何不免
引虎貙而入室也德宗之聰明安在哉寶
籙之侈靡艮嶽之竒麗如國之膏肓何矧

translation_en:
…was his martial glory. As for the presentation of that mastiff in tribute, it was the western people of Lü who offered it of their own accord: how could King Wu be implicated? These several sages had attained the utmost in learning, yet their concern and diligence never ceased; their minds were already rectified, yet they never neglected the work of holding fast to and preserving them. Consider how they held to the mean and spread civilizing instruction; how they attended to Heaven’s Mandate and cultivated human relationships; how the principle that those conscious of danger attain security, while those at ease are overthrown, was expounded in the Book of Changes; and how the admonitions concerning reverence and negligence, righteousness and desire, were received from the Cinnabar Writing. There was indeed a reason why the magnificence of their virtue and achievements was as boundless as Heaven!

The rulers of the Han, Tang, and Song did not understand how to emulate Yao and Shun. Thus Emperor Cheng, though outwardly dignified, inwardly wallowed in wine and women. The calamitous beauty of Yang’a could not escape the spitting denunciation of the Erudite of Pixiang Hall. It was fitting that the Han imperial enterprise consequently declined. Xuanzong initially devoted himself energetically to government, but before long became infatuated with his favorites. The beauty at Huaqing had long made the barbarian miscreant of Liucheng drool with desire. It was fortunate that the Tang throne did not pass to another house.

Emperor Ming honored his teachers and esteemed his tutors, sitting upright to deliver lectures himself: this seemed right. Yet he brought Buddhist scriptures from Tianzhu, thereby polluting the succession of civilized learning in the Central Lands. Is this really how one who honors culture should act? Xianzong applied himself resolutely and diligently to government, suppressing usurpers and rebels: this was proper. Yet he took elixirs supplied by masters of esoteric arts, thereby hastening a dreadful upheaval at the hands of his intimates. Is this really how one who desires good government should act?

The wealth of the Qionglin Treasury and the stores of the Daying Treasury—what did these mean for the people’s lifeblood? He could not avoid bringing tigers and other fierce beasts into his own house. Where was Dezong’s intelligence? The extravagance of Baolu and the extraordinary splendor of Genyue—what could these do for the mortal illness of the state? How much more, then, …

text:
復决藩籬以媚盜也徽宗之技能奚用哉
之數君者氣質用事而不知所以務於學
情欲為主而不知所以正其心故倏而明
倏而昏倏而彊倏而懦用君子則治任小
人則亂崇正道則為中國惑邪說則為夷
狄身名俱辱而詒笑後世無足怪矣洪惟
我
太祖高皇帝肇造區夏

復决藩籬以媚盜也，徽宗之技能奚用哉？之數君者，氣質用事，而不知所以務於學；情欲為主，而不知所以正其心。故倏而明，倏而昏；倏而彊，倏而懦。用君子則治，任小人則亂；崇正道則為中國，惑邪說則為夷狄。身名俱辱，而詒笑後世，無足怪矣。
洪惟我太祖高皇帝肇造區夏，太宗文皇帝緝寧邦家，典則謀謨超乎禹文，功烈聲華軼於湯武。列聖相承，益隆繼紹，真宇宙間貞元之一會也！執事所謂脩為之方、持守之要，立極於前而垂統於後者，亦豈外於務學以正其心哉？愚嘗聞之：祖宗於聽政之暇，輒御便殿，召集儒臣，講論經理，切劘治道。雖在深宮，乃或乙夜，猶考閱往籍，研究聖賢之精微，鑒觀前代之得失，而於酒色燕遊佛
translation_en:
…and furthermore broke down the protective barriers to curry favor with bandits. Of what use were Emperor Huizong’s talents? These several rulers let their temperamental dispositions govern their actions, without knowing how to apply themselves to learning; they let their passions and desires take command, without knowing how to rectify their hearts. Thus they were now clear-sighted, now benighted; now strong, now weak. When they employed gentlemen, there was order; when they entrusted affairs to petty men, there was disorder. When they honored the correct Way, theirs was the central civilized realm; when deluded by heterodox teachings, they became barbarians. That both their persons and their reputations suffered disgrace, leaving them objects of ridicule to later generations, is hardly surprising.
We reverently consider how our Emperor Taizu Gao founded the realm of China, and Emperor Taizong Wen brought peace to the state. Their institutions, standards, plans, and counsels surpassed those of Yu and King Wen; their achievements and renown exceeded those of Kings Tang and Wu. The succession of sage emperors has further exalted the continuation of their legacy. Truly, this is a juncture of cosmic renewal! What you, honored examiners, call the methods of self-cultivation and the essentials of steadfast adherence—establishing the supreme standard for one’s own age and transmitting a governing tradition to posterity—surely cannot lie outside applying oneself to learning in order to rectify the heart. I have heard that, in their leisure from attending to government, our imperial ancestors would regularly take their seats in a private audience hall, summon Confucian officials, discuss the principles of the Classics, and refine their understanding of the Way of government through close discussion. Even within the secluded palace, sometimes as late as the second watch of the night, they would still examine ancient writings, investigate the subtle teachings of the sages and worthies, and scrutinize the successes and failures of earlier dynasties as a mirror for themselves. translation_en:
…Laoist teachings and esoteric arts, the amassing of wealth, and construction projects—all such pursuits of the rulers of the Han, Tang, and Song—not only never found expression in their deeds, but never even arose in their hearts.

Taizu once said: “The ruler’s heart is the foundation of government and moral transformation. If what he harbors within is not the heart of Yao and Shun, yet he wishes his administration to achieve the governance of Yao and Shun, this cannot be attained.”

Taizong once said: “A ruler truly must not have particular indulgences. Once he has an indulgence and becomes absorbed in it without turning back, desire will inevitably overcome principle. If his heart can remain still and empty, responding to affairs as they arise and, once they pass, resembling a bright mirror or still water, it will naturally consist entirely of heavenly principle. Whenever I withdraw from court, I invariably reflect that keeping this heart under control is essential.”

How great are these royal words! This is precisely the purport of the teaching concerning the precarious human heart and the subtle heart of the Way, and the need for refinement and single-mindedness. It is the Way of cultivating oneself to bring peace to the common people, attaining equilibrium and harmony, setting Heaven and Earth in their proper places, and nurturing the myriad things. Had he not deeply apprehended and earnestly practiced this, truly exerting himself in it, could he have spoken of it with such intimate understanding? The learning of the heart had a profound source, transmitted from father to son. Thus their virtue and glorious achievements directly emulated those of Yao and Shun and stood alongside them. Ah, how splendid!

Now the Son of Heaven continually advances in sagely learning, rectifying his heart and seeking good government. There is nothing more to add concerning how he brings glory to his predecessors and opens the way for his successors. In my humble view, if one wishes to emulate Yao and Shun, one need only emulate…

…to manage wealth; wealth serves to bring the people together, and the people serve to defend the state. This is the constant Way, unchanged through a hundred kings. Your policy question touches upon public finance: surely you are not one who merely talks of abstruse principles and regards matters of money and grain as beneath consideration. How could I fail to set forth what I have heard and observed in reply?

The land under Heaven was much the same in antiquity as it is today, and so were its financial resources and expenditures. Consider the Song: the Liao to the north and the Western Xia held portions of the central lands. Compared with the flourishing unity of today, its circumstances were decidedly inferior. Yet among its major expenditures were annual payments to these states, rewards bestowed at the suburban sacrifices, and stipends for temple sinecures—all expenses absent today. Our territory exceeds that of the past, while expenditure has diminished. Surely, then, our present wealth should consist of grain too abundant to consume before it rots, and strings of cash too abundant to spend before their cords decay. Yet those above and below remain anxiously concerned about shortages. This I truly cannot understand.

The Commentary says: “If those who produce wealth are many and those who consume it few, if production is swift and expenditure gradual, wealth will always suffice.” Might present insufficiency arise precisely from acting contrary to these words? Su Shi spoke of three approaches to managing a state: “To maintain nine years’ reserves, always left untouched and unused, is a plan for ten thousand generations. For one year’s revenue barely to cover one year’s expenditure is a plan for the moment. As for the lowest approach, devoid of foresight, it sets revenue according to expenditure: when resources do not suffice, ever more is exacted. text:

不終月之計也今之國計肉食者謀之非

論者多言之朝多倖位事有剰員此吏之

今日之冗，廟堂方議之，非草茅之所敢預也。竊見諸司有定員，而武功之賞大濫；軍士多失伍，而食粮之籍日增。其他不急之務、無名之費，盖未暇悉數也。則於是三冗者，得無全乎？唐李吉甫為《元和國計録》，丁謂因之為《景德會計録》，林特作於祥符，田况作於皇祐，韓絳作於熙寧，蘇轍作於元祐，所以總括天下財賦出入之數，而周知其有無多寡
translation_en:
…the expedient policies of an age of decline, without knowing what further measures could be taken should an emergency arise. This is a plan that will not last out a month. As for the state’s finances today, those who eat meat deliberate upon them; they are beyond the knowledge of those who subsist on bean leaves. Yet I have privately observed that orders allowing grain contributions in exchange for rank, and measures for collecting arrears and borrowing revenues in advance, have repeatedly been put into effect. Do these not approach what are called expedient policies? Those who discuss financial affairs often speak of three kinds of excess that harm the treasury. At court, many hold posts through favor, and there are surplus personnel conducting affairs: this is excess in official staffing. Soldiers are supported for generations, merely consuming provisions without working and burdening the farmers; yet when suddenly called upon, they may prove incapable of repelling the enemy: this is excess in military staffing. Some delight in construction projects; some seek rewards through frontier exploits; some confer rewards indiscriminately; some lavish devotion upon spirits and the Buddha: this is excess in expenditure.
The court is now deliberating upon today’s excesses; a man outside official service would not presume to intervene. Yet I have privately observed that although the various offices have fixed staffing quotas, appointments awarded for military merit are granted far too freely. Many soldiers have gone missing from their units, yet the rolls of those drawing grain rations increase daily. As for other nonessential undertakings and expenditures without justification, there has hardly been time to enumerate them all. Are not all three kinds of excess thus present? In the Rites of Zhou, the Grand Accountant cross-checks records to examine daily accomplishments, uses monthly summaries to examine monthly accomplishments, and uses annual accounts to examine annual accomplishments. He thereby gains comprehensive knowledge of administration throughout the realm and advises the king and the Grand Steward on dismissals and appointments. Alas! translation_en:
…His other policy essays are likewise of this standard and merit acceptance.

When a gentleman does good, does he intend to seek blessings? The answer is no. When a petty man does evil, does he intend to incur calamity? The answer is likewise no. Goodness is the foundation of blessings; evil is the agent of calamity. Goodness makes no appointment with blessings, yet blessings gather of themselves; evil makes no appointment with calamity, yet calamity comes of itself. This is the inevitable working of principle. Thus, it is not out of partiality toward his descendants that the gentleman bequeaths to them the blessings of doing good; nor is it out of hatred for his descendants that the petty man brings upon them the calamities of doing evil. They pursue different paths and encounter different outcomes: something that acts without anyone causing it to act naturally governs what happens between the two. Thus the wise men of antiquity were careful in choosing their course of conduct. They did not yield to immediate concerns but always considered what would follow their deaths; they planned not merely for the moment but for their descendants over hundreds and thousands of generations. They truly understood this principle.

You have posed this policy question to the assembled candidates, intending through their words to discern the subtleties of their dispositions and intentions. Allow me to set forth my thoughts. Descendants are of great importance to a person! Who will inherit and transmit the lineage and patrimony that we have received from our ancestors? The answer is our descendants. Thus, among the wise and foolish of past and present, who has not been concerned for his descendants? They differ only in the plans they make for them.

Xiao He rose to the position of Chancellor of State, yet did not improve the walls and houses for his descendants. He said: “If later generations are worthy, let them emulate my frugality; if they are unworthy, let there be nothing for powerful families to seize.” Was Xiao He indeed wise? If so, his…

text:
言可以鑒矣䟽廣懸車太傅不為子孫益
産業曰賢而多財則損其志愚而多財則
益其過廣果賢邪則其言可以省矣刺史
問龐德公何以遺子孫曰人皆遺之以危
吾獨遺之以安雖所遺不同未為無所遺
也夫以耕稼為安則遺子孫以官祿者非
危乎故人請楊伯起為子孫開産業曰使
後世稱為清白吏子孫以此遺之不亦厚
乎夫以清白為厚則遺子孫以貨賄者非
===
薄乎母績而勸以自安公甫文伯之孝也
奚至於絶嗣賢母之以身教其言固如此
爾君違不忘諫之以德臧哀伯之忠也奚
必於有後賢臣之自天佑其理固如此爾
王業偏安於鼎足是豈大丈夫之志哉其
曰鞠躬盡瘁又奚暇私家衣食之謀即此
以觀管樂之比盖自道焉爾兵權頓釋於
杯酒夫亦保全功臣之道哉雖曰成功不
居顧得世享田宅之利由是以知韓彭之

…his words may serve as a mirror. Shu Guang retired from his post as Grand Preceptor and did not increase the property of his descendants. He said: “If they are worthy, abundant wealth will weaken their resolve; if they are foolish, abundant wealth will increase their faults.” Was Guang truly worthy? Then his words deserve reflection. The Regional Inspector asked Pang Degong what he would leave his descendants. He replied: “Others all leave them danger; I alone leave them security. Though what we leave differs, it cannot be said that I leave them nothing.” Now, if farming constitutes security, is not leaving descendants official posts and emoluments a source of danger? An old friend urged Yang Boqi to establish an estate for his descendants. He replied: “Let later generations call them the descendants of an incorruptible official. Is not this a generous legacy?” If incorruptibility constitutes generosity, is not leaving descendants money and valuables a meager legacy?

When his mother was spinning, Gongfu Wenbo urged her to take her ease: this was his filial devotion. Why, then, did his line come to an end? Such indeed were the words through which a worthy mother taught by personal example [?]. When his ruler erred, Zang Aibo did not forget to remonstrate with him on grounds of virtue: this was his loyalty. Why must he necessarily have descendants? Such indeed is the principle by which a worthy minister receives Heaven’s aid [?].

With the royal enterprise confined to one region in a threefold division of power, could this have fulfilled a great man’s ambition? When he spoke of “bending every effort until utterly spent,” what leisure had he to plan for his own household’s food and clothing? Viewed in this light, his comparison of himself to Guan Zhong and Yue Yi was surely an expression of his own aspirations. Military authority was relinquished at once over a cup of wine: was this not also a way to preserve meritorious officials unharmed? Though they were said not to cling to their positions after achieving success, they nevertheless secured for successive generations the benefits of fields and residences. 而奕世貴顯殘民如周興來俊臣者寧免

善罰惡毫髮不差但教子孫以忠孝勤儉

…the calamity was of their own making [?]. Lord Yu served as a minor county functionary, adjudicating cases without injustice, and his descendants enjoyed wealth and distinction for generations. Could those who cruelly oppressed the people, such as Zhou Xing and Lai Junchen, escape the extermination of their clans? Deng Yu was a great general who never killed wantonly, and his entire household enjoyed distinction and prosperity. Could those who killed surrendered soldiers, such as Bai Qi and Li Guang, escape the destruction of their lineages?

Alas! The Way of Heaven is numinous and watches the world below each day. It detests arrogance and favors humility, rewards goodness and punishes evil, without the slightest error. Simply teach your descendants loyalty, filial devotion, diligence, and frugality; do not guide them toward conduct contrary to the Way. Rather let your descendants remain blameless for generations; do not burden them with gains acquired unrighteously. If I do not seek wealth and rank by improper means, how could I bear to kill people to further private designs [?]? If I do not seek wealth and rank by improper means, how could I bear to kill people to secure a position for myself [?]?

When meritorious deeds and beneficence reach the people, hereditary stipends and offices need not be a perilous course. When both reputation and actual achievement reach the sovereign, the promise that “you shall flourish and prosper” is certainly no empty saying. If labor is directed toward righteousness, farming is acceptable and spinning is acceptable: which is not a means of providing abundantly for posterity? If service in office truly accords with the Way, military affairs are acceptable and judicial affairs are acceptable: which is not a sphere for accumulating hidden virtue?

Who does not desire extensive fields and grand residences? But if what one establishes may not be carried on, why build so many walls and houses, and why manage such extensive estates? Who does not desire abundant baskets of gifts, clothing, and food? But if what one accumulates may not be preserved, why not decline an old acquaintance’s gift brought late at night, and why not use the sage ruler’s bounty to show kindness to one’s lineage?

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
人雖愚獨無是心哉彼任情縱欲固以牽
挽推拒於趨利避害之場不能自主矣又
見夫為善者偶得无妄之禍為惡者或享
非分之福則以天道寥遠未足憑據由是
作姦效尤肆無忌憚亡身喪家率由於此
善乎蘇軾之言曰盜跖之壽孔顏之厄此
天之未定者也善惡之報至於子孫而定
也久矣胡寅亦曰人之為善與惡天未必
逐逐然而禍福之也理存感應如寒暑雨
===
暘之消息自不可誣故人亦自脩而已人
能力於自脩而天有不定者乎脩之何如
曰立德行義久操而不渝積功累仁世濟
而無斁仰不愧於天俯不怍於吾心上不
負君父下不負生民中亦不負其所學如
此而其子孫不昌以永吾未之信也孔子
曰積善之家必有餘慶此又君子所恃以
為善而不移者愚也服膺斯訓久矣敢就
正於有道執事其幸教之

punctuated: 人雖愚，獨無是心哉？彼任情縱欲，固以牽挽推拒於趨利避害之場，不能自主矣。又見夫為善者偶得无妄之禍，為惡者或享非分之福，則以天道寥遠，未足憑據。由是作姦效尤，肆無忌憚，亡身喪家，率由於此。善乎蘇軾之言曰：「盜跖之壽，孔顏之厄，此天之未定者也。善惡之報，至於子孫而定也久矣。」胡寅亦曰：「人之為善與惡，天未必逐逐然而禍福之也。理存感應，如寒暑雨暘之消息，自不可誣，故人亦自脩而已。」人能力於自脩，而天有不定者乎？脩之何如？曰：立德行義，久操而不渝；積功累仁，世濟而無斁。仰不愧於天，俯不怍於吾心，上不負君父，下不負生民，中亦不負其所學。如此而其子孫不昌以永，吾未之信也。孔子曰：「積善之家，必有餘慶。」此又君子所恃以為善而不移者。愚也服膺斯訓久矣，敢就正於有道，執事其幸教之。
translation_en: …though petty people are foolish, do they alone lack this disposition? Giving free rein to their feelings and desires, they are pulled and pushed about in the pursuit of advantage and avoidance of harm, unable to govern themselves. Moreover, when they see that those who do good sometimes suffer undeserved calamities, while those who do evil sometimes enjoy blessings beyond their due, they conclude that Heaven’s Way is remote and offers no reliable basis for conduct. Thus they commit wicked deeds and imitate bad examples, acting without restraint or scruple. Their own ruin and the destruction of their families generally arise from this. Well did Su Shi say: “The longevity of Robber Zhi and the hardships of Kongzi and Yan Hui are instances in which Heaven’s judgment is not yet settled. When recompense for good and evil reaches their descendants, that judgment has long been settled.” Hu Yin likewise said: “When people do good or evil, Heaven does not necessarily hurry after each deed to bring them calamity or blessing. Yet the principle of stimulus and response exists, like the waxing and waning of cold and heat, rain and sunshine, and cannot be denied. People therefore need only cultivate themselves.” If people can exert themselves in self-cultivation, could Heaven’s judgment remain unsettled? How should they cultivate themselves? I answer: establish virtue and practice righteousness, maintaining their resolve over time without wavering; accumulate meritorious deeds and acts of benevolence, carrying them forward from generation to generation without wearying. Looking upward, feel no shame before Heaven; looking inward, feel no shame in one’s own heart. Toward those above, fail neither sovereign nor father; toward those below, fail not the people; and within oneself, remain true to what one has learned. That the descendants of such a person should fail to prosper enduringly is something I cannot believe. Kongzi said: “A family that accumulates goodness will surely have blessings to spare.” This, too, is what the gentleman relies upon in doing good without wavering. Foolish though I am, I have long cherished this teaching. I venture to seek correction from one who possesses the Way, and trust that you will kindly instruct me.

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
第五問
同考試官教諭易批此卷五策每篇數千
言皆有根據而於時務世故條悉無遺蓋用世之才不
特以博洽名而已敬羨敬羨
同考試官學正鄭批合三場所作足見體
用之學而五策尤奇崛不羣恨不能盡録耳
考試官左諭德顧批五策發盡感慨激烈
之抱而皆的確超迥非苟掇拾補緝以成文平居必久以
===
天下為心者矣場中俊傑如子誠不多見
考試官侍讀學士汪批此子發憤道世事蓋
有賈生之風且筆力過人能如其意之所往通前數卷莫
可低昻士氣如此可以占
昌運矣
有中國之大戒有治世之隱憂蓋中國之
與夷狄常相為盛衰而小民難保治亂之
機每倚伏於冥冥之中制治保邦之君子
誠不可以不加之意也請因明問而陳之

機每倚伏於冥冥之中制治保邦之君子

punctuated:
第五問

同考試官教諭易批：此卷五策，每篇數千言，皆有根據，而於時務世故條悉無遺。蓋用世之才，不特以博洽名而已。敬羨！敬羨！

同考試官學正鄭批：合三場所作，足見體用之學，而五策尤奇崛不羣，恨不能盡録耳。

考試官左諭德顧批：五策發盡感慨激烈之抱，而皆的確超迥，非苟掇拾補緝以成文。平居必久以天下為心者矣。場中俊傑如子，誠不多見。

考試官侍讀學士汪批：此子發憤道世事，蓋有賈生之風，且筆力過人，能如其意之所往。通前數卷，莫可低昻。士氣如此，可以占昌運矣。

有中國之大戒，有治世之隱憂。蓋中國之與夷狄，常相為盛衰，而小民難保，治亂之機，每倚伏於冥冥之中。制治保邦之君子，誠不可以不加之意也。請因明問而陳之。
translation_en:
Fifth Policy Question

Comment by Associate Examiner Yi, Instructor: The five policy essays in this script each run to several thousand words. All are well grounded, and their detailed treatment of current affairs and worldly matters leaves nothing out. Here is a talent suited to public service, someone whose reputation will rest on more than extensive learning alone. My respect and admiration! My respect and admiration!

Comment by Associate Examiner Zheng, Instructor: Taken together, the writings from all three sessions amply demonstrate learning that embraces both substance and practical application. The five policy essays are particularly striking and outstanding. My only regret is that they cannot all be reproduced here.

Comment by Examiner Gu, Left Admonisher: These five policy essays give full expression to deeply felt, impassioned convictions, yet all are precise and exceptionally penetrating. They are no mere compositions pieced together from borrowed scraps. In ordinary life, this candidate must long have kept the affairs of all under Heaven in his heart. Outstanding men like you are truly seldom seen in the examination hall.

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting: This candidate speaks of worldly affairs with impassioned indignation, showing something of the spirit of Jia Yi. Moreover, his command of the brush surpasses that of others and carries him wherever his thoughts lead. Considered together with his preceding scripts, none can be ranked above or below the others. Such spirit among scholars foretells a flourishing age.

There are grave matters against which the Central Kingdom must guard, and hidden anxieties even in an age of good government. The Central Kingdom and the Yi and Di peoples often wax and wane in relation to one another, while the common people are difficult to safeguard. The seeds of order and disorder often lie concealed, each harboring the possibility of the other. Gentlemen who establish good government and preserve the state must indeed give these matters their attention. Allow me to set them forth in response to your discerning question.

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
戎狄之患自古有之至元遂入主中國則
夷狄之極盛而中國之極衰也我
太祖起而逐之塞外復帝王所自立之中國華
夷之辨冠屨截然此中國之方盛而夷狄
之就衰也然彼以餘黎遺孽誕紀其緒而
與吾邊境鄰則吾之所以嚴為之備而預
為之防者固宜百倍於前代而後可今邊
關亭障萬里相屬可謂盛矣虜嘗竊入而
卒無大憂豈非
===
祖宗之法至精至密有以維持綱紀為不拔之
基哉近年以來虜宼犯邊往往深入腹裏
所過赤地無遺略無懲創而去識者盖久
憂之近日宣府之警羽檄交馳
朝野動色豨突鳥逝莫之誰何其為患盖未
可量也盜賊之起治世有所不免以近歲
言之盜起近畿而中原為之殘破盜起楚
蜀而環境為之繹騷至遣制帥動邊卒調
夷兵以成勦平之功然凋殘之餘生理未

戎狄之患，自古有之。至元遂入主中國，則夷狄之極盛，而中國之極衰也。我太祖起而逐之塞外，復帝王所自立之中國。華夷之辨，冠屨截然，此中國之方盛，而夷狄之就衰也。然彼以餘黎遺孽，誕紀其緒，而與吾邊境鄰，則吾之所以嚴為之備，而預為之防者，固宜百倍於前代而後可。今邊關亭障，萬里相屬，可謂盛矣。虜嘗竊入，而卒無大憂，豈非祖宗之法至精至密，有以維持綱紀，為不拔之基哉？近年以來，虜宼犯邊，往往深入腹裏，所過赤地無遺，略無懲創而去，識者盖久憂之。近日宣府之警，羽檄交馳，朝野動色。豨突鳥逝，莫之誰何，其為患盖未可量也。

盜賊之起，治世有所不免。以近歲言之，盜起近畿，而中原為之殘破；盜起楚蜀，而環境為之繹騷。至遣制帥，動邊卒，調夷兵，以成勦平之功。然凋殘之餘，生理未
translation_en:
The scourge of the Rong and Di has existed since antiquity. When the Yuan eventually came to rule China, the foreign peoples reached the height of their power, while China reached the depths of its decline. Our Taizu arose and drove them beyond the frontier, restoring the China in which emperors and kings had established themselves. The distinction between Chinese and foreign peoples became as clear as that between cap and shoe: China was then rising, while the foreign peoples were declining. Yet, with their remaining subjects and surviving scions, they perpetuated their line [?] and remained alongside our frontier. Thus, our preparations against them must be stringent and our precautions taken in advance; indeed, these must be a hundred times greater than those of previous dynasties to suffice. Today, frontier passes, watchposts, and fortifications stretch continuously for ten thousand li: these may be called formidable. The enemy sometimes slipped through, but ultimately caused no great trouble. Was this not because the institutions of our imperial ancestors were supremely refined and thorough, sustaining the governing order and providing an unshakable foundation? In recent years, however, enemy raiders have violated the frontier, often penetrating deep into the interior. Wherever they passed, they left the land utterly devastated, then departed virtually unpunished and unscathed. Those who understand affairs have long been troubled by this. Recently, alarms from Xuanfu have sent urgent military dispatches flying back and forth, causing consternation at court and throughout the country. The raiders charge like wild boars and vanish like birds, with no one to challenge them. The harm they may cause is surely beyond reckoning.

The emergence of bandits is something even a well-governed age cannot entirely avoid. To speak of recent years, bandits arose near the capital region, and the Central Plain was devastated by them; bandits arose in Chu and Shu, and the surrounding territory was thrown into turmoil. Matters reached the point of dispatching a supreme commander, mobilizing frontier troops, and transferring troops of non-Chinese peoples to accomplish their suppression. Yet, in the aftermath of this devastation, the people's means of livelihood have not yet…

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
復公私之積猶可哀痛而水旱之不時饑
饉之荐臻其為患亦未可量也夫禦戎無
上策論者曰當以氣勝之中國為陽夷狄
為陰君子道長小人道消則陽氣勝而陰
不能奸故二帝三王之世而夷狄之患無
甚君子道消小人道長則陰氣勝而陽不
能立故秦漢而下而夷狄之患始滋夫豈
無據之虛談哉宋儒朱熹告其君曰古先
聖王所以制馭夷狄之道其本不在乎威
===
彊而在乎德業其任不在乎邊境而在乎
朝廷其具不在乎兵食而在乎紀綱所謂上
策盖不出此數言而必以開納諫諍黜逺
佞邪杜塞倖門安固邦本四者為急先之
務此萬世不易之論也豈特可行於今日
而已乎若夫盜源之說盖曰衣食不足盜
之源也政賦不均盜之源也教化不脩盜
之源也一源慢則探囊發篋而為盜矣二
源慢則執兵刃劫良民而為盜矣三源慢

復，公私之積猶可哀痛，而水旱之不時，饑饉之荐臻，其為患亦未可量也。
夫禦戎無上策，論者曰：「當以氣勝之。中國為陽，夷狄為陰。君子道長，小人道消，則陽氣勝而陰不能奸，故二帝三王之世而夷狄之患無甚；君子道消，小人道長，則陰氣勝而陽不能立，故秦漢而下而夷狄之患始滋。」夫豈無據之虛談哉？宋儒朱熹告其君曰：「古先聖王所以制馭夷狄之道，其本不在乎威彊，而在乎德業；其任不在乎邊境，而在乎朝廷；其具不在乎兵食，而在乎紀綱。」所謂上策，盖不出此數言，而必以開納諫諍、黜逺佞邪、杜塞倖門、安固邦本四者為急先之務。此萬世不易之論也，豈特可行於今日而已乎？
若夫盜源之說，盖曰：「衣食不足，盜之源也；政賦不均，盜之源也；教化不脩，盜之源也。一源慢，則探囊發篋而為盜矣；二源慢，則執兵刃劫良民而為盜矣；三源慢
translation_en:
…have recovered, and the state of public and private reserves remains grievous. Floods and droughts come at irregular times, and famines arrive repeatedly; the harm they cause likewise cannot yet be measured.
As for defending against foreign peoples, there is no supreme strategy. One commentator says: “We should overcome them through vital force, qi. The Central Kingdom represents yang, and the foreign peoples represent yin. When the way of the gentleman advances and the way of the petty man declines, yang prevails and yin cannot intrude. Thus, in the age of the Two Emperors and Three Kings, the trouble caused by foreign peoples was not severe. When the way of the gentleman declines and the way of the petty man advances, yin prevails and yang cannot stand firm. Thus, from the Qin and Han onward, the trouble caused by foreign peoples began to multiply.” How could this be empty talk without foundation? The Song Confucian scholar Zhu Xi told his sovereign: “The means by which the sage kings of antiquity controlled foreign peoples rested fundamentally on virtuous achievements, rather than military might; responsibility lay with the imperial court, rather than the frontier; and their instruments were the governing order, rather than troops and provisions.” What is called the supreme strategy surely does not extend beyond these few words. Yet four matters must be given urgent priority: welcoming and accepting remonstrance, dismissing and distancing oneself from flatterers and the wicked, closing off avenues to unmerited favor, and securing the foundations of the state. This is a judgment that will remain unchanged through all ages. Could it be applicable only to the present day?
As for the explanation of the sources of banditry, it says: “Insufficient clothing and food are a source of banditry; inequity in administration and taxation is a source of banditry; failure to cultivate moral instruction is a source of banditry. If one source is neglected, people become thieves, picking pockets and breaking open chests. If two sources are neglected, people become bandits, taking up weapons and robbing law-abiding commoners. If three sources are neglected…”

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
則攻城邑略百姓而為盜矣豐世無盜者
足也治世無賊者均也化世無亂者順也
求其源而止之何盜之患若俟其起而平
之窮治則有不戢自焚之禍招降則有養
虎遺患之憂誠未見其一可也斯二患者
當今之急務也愚也不敏於邊防廢弛之
因軍士怨憤之情生民愁苦之狀官吏侵
漁之弊誠欲發憤痛哭一為執事陳之而
未暇悉數也伏望
===
朝廷於本原之地深加之意任老成為腹心
用臺諫為耳目
邦國大計安危所係必付之公論而勿參以
一髮之私則所以彊本折衝安內攘外之
道不期月而粲然可備舉矣芻蕘之言俾
得上達以備
采擇之萬一執事之賜也謹對

足也治世無賊者均也化世無亂者順也
求其源而止之何盜之患若俟其起而平
之窮治則有不戢自焚之禍招降則有養
虎遺患之憂誠未見其一可也斯二患者
當今之急務也愚也不敏於邊防廢弛之
因軍士怨憤之情生民愁苦之狀官吏侵
漁之弊誠欲發憤痛哭一爲執事陳之而
未暇悉數也伏望
===
朝廷於本原之地深加之意任老成爲腹心
用臺諫爲耳目
邦國大計安危所係必付之公論而勿參以
一髮之私則所以殭本折衝安內攘外之
道不期月而粲然可備舉矣芻蕘之言俾
得上達以備
采擇之萬一執事之賜也謹對
punctuated: 則攻城邑、略百姓而為盜矣。豐世無盜者，足也；治世無賊者，均也；化世無亂者，順也。求其源而止之，何盜之患？若俟其起而平之，窮治則有不戢自焚之禍，招降則有養虎遺患之憂，誠未見其一可也。斯二患者，當今之急務也。愚也不敏，於邊防廢弛之因、軍士怨憤之情、生民愁苦之狀、官吏侵漁之弊，誠欲發憤痛哭，一為執事陳之，而未暇悉數也。伏望朝廷於本原之地深加之意，任老成為腹心，用臺諫為耳目。邦國大計，安危所係，必付之公論，而勿參以一髮之私，則所以彊本折衝、安內攘外之道，不期月而粲然可備舉矣。芻蕘之言，俾得上達，以備采擇之萬一，執事之賜也。謹對。
translation_en:
…then they become bandits who attack cities and towns and plunder the common people. An age of abundance has no bandits because people have enough; an age of good government has no marauders because distribution is equitable; an age of moral transformation has no disorder because people are compliant. If we seek out the sources and stop them, what trouble need we fear from bandits? If instead we wait for them to rise before suppressing them, relentless punitive action risks the disaster of consuming ourselves in the flames of unchecked warfare, while inviting their surrender raises the fear of nurturing a tiger and leaving trouble for the future. Truly, I see neither course as acceptable. These two afflictions are urgent matters of the present day.

Dull-witted though I am, I sincerely wish, in indignation and bitter tears, to lay before you the causes of neglected frontier defenses, the resentment of the soldiers, the misery of the people, and the abuses of predatory officials. Yet there is not time to enumerate them all. I humbly hope that the court will give profound attention to these fundamental matters, entrusting seasoned men with the role of its closest advisers and employing censorial and remonstrance officials as its eyes and ears. Great plans of state, upon which security or peril depends, must be submitted to public deliberation, without the admixture of even a hair’s breadth of private interest. Then, before a full year has passed, the means of strengthening the foundations, repelling aggression, securing the interior, and warding off external threats can all be clearly established and put into effect. Should these humble woodcutters’ words be allowed to reach the throne, so that even the smallest part might be considered for adoption, it would be a kindness bestowed by you. Respectfully submitted in reply.

上命臣俊臣鼎臣主

punctuated:
順天府鄉試錄後序

正德十一年秋八月，上命臣俊、臣鼎臣主北畿試事。事竣錄成，鼎臣當序其後。竊惟古者迪士，材成而後進，論材授官，謹好尚，明考課，以先後之，故士知自重而有立。我國家學校之教、科目之法，最為近古。邇者士號明經，習為文，發解無餘事。朝取第，暮篋書，不復省覽者衆矣。仕習於法理簿書，不復知學；學矣，而徒攻於詞章，務枝葉，失本根，中無所主，就世之趨而靡焉。古之成材者固若是
translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination

In the eighth month of autumn in the eleventh year of Zhengde (1516), His Majesty commanded your servants Jun and Dingchen to preside over the examination in the Northern Metropolitan Region. When the examination was concluded and the record completed, it fell to me, Dingchen, to write its postface.

I venture to reflect that, in antiquity, scholars were guided and advanced only after their abilities had matured. Their abilities were assessed and offices conferred accordingly; care was taken over what was esteemed and encouraged, and performance evaluations were made clear, so as to determine their relative precedence. Thus scholars knew to value themselves and established firm principles. Our dynasty’s instruction in schools and its system of examinations come closest to those of antiquity.

Recently, scholars claim mastery of the Classics and practice composition, regarding success in the Provincial Examination as their sole concern. Many obtain their degree in the morning and by evening pack away their books, never to examine or read them again. Once in office, they become accustomed to legal principles and administrative paperwork and no longer know to pursue learning. Even when they do study, they merely devote themselves to literary composition, attending to branches and leaves while losing the roots. With no governing principle within, they yield to the prevailing tendencies of the age. Surely those whose abilities matured in antiquity were like this…

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄

馳類則士途則科目志行則夬
氓也是誠有負於經術迪士之
初意矣夫六經皆聖賢經綸之
迹其道極于天地通于神明學
者誦其言而通其意已非常人
况以是淑其身心蓄德脩業者
===
哉嘗聞
先朝名臣往往朴茂堅特若無他
技能而道德功業無愧於古其
所成立偉然一代之望豈當時
務實學尚質行所謂材成而後
進者歟夫亦有以振厲作興之
而不能自已也詩曰思皇多士

技能而道德功業無愧於古其
先朝名臣往往朴茂堅特若無他
𢦏嘗聞
punctuated:
乎？下此，决禮義之閑，困富貴之馳，類則士，途則科目，志行則夬氓也。是誠有負於經術迪士之初意矣。夫六經皆聖賢經綸之迹，其道極于天地，通于神明。學者誦其言而通其意，已非常人，况以是淑其身心，蓄德脩業者哉！
嘗聞先朝名臣，往往朴茂堅特，若無他技能，而道德功業無愧於古。其所成立，偉然一代之望，豈當時務實學、尚質行，所謂材成而後進者歟？夫亦有以振厲作興之，而不能自已也。《詩》曰：「思皇多士
translation_en:
…was this so? Below this level are those who break through the barriers of ritual propriety and righteousness and become ensnared in the pursuit of wealth and rank. In social category they are scholars, and their path is through the examinations, yet in aspiration and conduct they are vulgar fellows [?]. This truly betrays the original intention of guiding scholars through classical learning. The Six Classics all preserve traces of the sages’ and worthies’ ordering of the world. Their Way reaches throughout Heaven and Earth and communicates with the spirits. Those who recite their words and comprehend their meaning are already extraordinary people; how much more so those who use them to cultivate their persons and minds, accumulate virtue, and advance their undertakings!
I have heard that renowned ministers of former reigns were often simple, substantial, steadfast, and independent, seemingly possessing no other special skills; yet their moral character and achievements stood without shame beside those of antiquity. Through what they established and accomplished, they stood majestically as the admired figures of their age. Was this because people then pursued substantive learning and esteemed genuine conduct—being, as the saying goes, men whose abilities were fully formed before they advanced into office? There must also have been means of rousing and inspiring them, so that they could not cease their efforts. The Book of Odes says: “Oh, the splendid multitude of officers…

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
生此王國今兹百年禮樂之餘
畿甸俊造之選所謂其人夫豈少
哉矧登名是錄者類能上下古
今敷析理事醞齊以成文察人
以言藹然鹿鳴之賓豈復有如
前所云者哉必是之云者誠過
計而厚望焉耳諸士子其仰思
===
聖天子所以賓興我者之意不啻於
吏治君子之用世不在於浮華
益務績學砥行夷考老成典刑
泝而上之以求聖賢六經之道
進將舉所實有諸已者措之以
弼成采薇天保之治則主司之
心始慰而諸士子所自立亦偉

生此王國今茲百年禮樂之餘
畿甸俊造之選所謂其人夫豈少
哉矧登名是錄者類能上下古
今敷析理事醞齊以成文察人
以言藹然鹿鳴之賓豈復有如
前所云者哉必是之云者誠過
計而厚望焉耳諸士子其仰思
===
聖天子所以賓興我者之意不啻於
吏治君子之用世不存於浮華
益務績學砥行夷考老成典刑
濟而上之以求聖賢六經之道
進將舉所實有諸己者措之以
猷成采薇天保之治則主司之
心始慰而諸士子所自立亦偉
punctuated: 生此王國。今兹百年禮樂之餘，畿甸俊造之選，所謂其人夫豈少哉？矧登名是錄者，類能上下古今，敷析理事，醞齊以成文。察人以言，藹然鹿鳴之賓，豈復有如前所云者哉？必是之云者，誠過計而厚望焉耳。諸士子其仰思聖天子所以賓興我者之意，不啻於吏治。君子之用世，不在於浮華。益務績學砥行，夷考老成典刑，泝而上之，以求聖賢六經之道。進將舉所實有諸已者，措之以弼成《采薇》《天保》之治，則主司之心始慰，而諸士子所自立亦偉
translation_en:
…born in this royal realm.” Now, after a hundred years of rites and music, could there be few such men among the outstanding talents selected from the metropolitan region? Moreover, those whose names appear in this record can generally range across past and present, expound and analyze principles and affairs, and blend these into accomplished compositions. Judging the men by their words, we find an impressive gathering of guests worthy of “The Deer Call.” Could any still be as described above? If we nevertheless insist on speaking thus, it is only from excessive concern and high expectations for them.

You scholars should reverently consider the intention of the sagely Son of Heaven in honoring and recommending you: it extends beyond administrative service alone. A gentleman’s service to the world does not lie in superficial ornament. Devote yourselves still further to accumulating learning and honing your conduct. Carefully examine the exemplary standards of mature and experienced men, and trace them back to their source, seeking the Way of the sages and worthies in the Six Classics. When you advance to office, put into practice what you truly possess within yourselves, helping to bring about the governance celebrated in “Gathering Bracken” and “Heaven Protects.” Only then will the hearts of those presiding over the examination be consoled, and what you scholars establish for yourselves will also be magnificent…

title: 正德十一年順天府鄉試錄
text:
矣臣等祗奉
明詔既夙夜殫厥心力期以免不
明之責因念夫
南畿及諸省所薦士皆將登名
天府後先效用而令甲科試
朝覲之典相繼舉行是固人材進
退□機而
===
宗作□振厲天下之微意也示好
惡明賞罰公黜陟多士目擊於
觀光之餘長善遏惡以成其材
者亦將感且奮而不能已焉又
何假於言哉是爲序
奉訓大夫左春坊左諭德兼翰
林院侍讀顧鼎臣謹序

明之責因念夫

退機而
===
宗作振厲天下之微意也示好
惡明賞罰公黜陟多士目擊於
觀光之餘長善遏惡以成其材
者亦將感且奮而不能已焉又
何假於言哉是爲序
奉訓大夫左春坊左諭德兼翰
林院侍讀顧鼎臣謹序
punctuated:
矣。臣等祗奉明詔，既夙夜殫厥心力，期以免不明之責，因念夫南畿及諸省所薦士，皆將登名天府，後先效用。而令甲科試、朝覲之典相繼舉行，是固人材進退□機，而宗作□振厲天下之微意也。示好惡，明賞罰，公黜陟，多士目擊於觀光之餘，長善遏惡以成其材者，亦將感且奮而不能已焉。又何假於言哉？是爲序。
奉訓大夫、左春坊左諭德兼翰林院侍讀顧鼎臣謹序。
translation_en:
…indeed. We, your servants, have reverently received the illustrious edict and have already exhausted our mental and physical energies day and night, hoping to avoid the blame of failing to discern talent. We further reflect that the men recommended by the Southern Metropolitan Region and the various provinces will all have their names enrolled at the imperial court and, sooner or later, render service. The statutorily prescribed examinations [?] and the ceremonies of court audience are being conducted in succession. These are assuredly occasions for advancing or removing men of talent [illegible], and express the subtle intention of stirring and invigorating the realm [preceding wording corrupt: 宗作□].
By displaying approval and disapproval, making rewards and punishments clear, and administering dismissals and promotions impartially, the assembled scholars can witness these things while beholding the splendor of the court. Those who cultivate goodness and restrain evil to bring their abilities to fruition will likewise be moved and roused beyond restraint. What further need is there for words? This serves as the preface.
Respectfully prefaced by Gu Dingchen, Grand Master for Attendant Instruction, Left Admonisher of the Left Secretariat of the Heir Apparent, concurrently Reader-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy.
